name: Michigan Advance
title: Three licks and a question: Who is Gretchen Whitmer governing for?
description: How many betrayals does it take to get to the center of what many progressives now see as a corporate sellout? Just like the old 1970s Tootsie Pop commercial, the answer seems to be three. Three decisions in the course of a week have left organized labor, environmental advocates, and grassroots progressives seriously questioning whether […]
text:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer stands alongside business leaders, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (second from left) at a groundbreaking ceremony in Saline Township.  June 1, 2026 | Photo courtesy of Colin Jackson/MPRNHow many betrayals does it take to get to the center of what many progressives now see as a corporate sellout?
Just like the old 1970s Tootsie Pop commercial, the answer seems to be three.
Three decisions in the course of a week have left organized labor, environmental advocates, and grassroots progressives seriously questioning whether Gov. Gretchen Whitmer is still governing for the coalition that elected her — or for the powerful corporate interests with money and influence.
First came the veto of nine bills backed by House and Senate Democrats and organized labor. Union leaders didn’t describe the move as a simple policy disagreement. They called it a “betrayal.” They said they had been “stabbed in the back.” Those aren’t the words of Republicans trying to score political points. They’re the words of labor leaders who have spent years mobilizing members to elect Democrats.
‘Stabbed in the back’: Unions, House Democrats call Whitmer’s veto of 9 bills a betrayal

Then came another chapter in the administration’s aggressive push to attract massive data centers to Michigan. Whitmer’s data center plan unveiled Wednesday is not much more than a voluntary pledge. There isn’t much confidence that the same governor who smiled for the cameras as she posed with OpenAI’s Sam Altman, and was caught on a hot mic telling Oracle’s CEO “We’re used to people saying f*** no and doing it anyway,” will make sure those pledges are kept. 
To be fair, Whitmer’s office has denied that’s what she said in the video, the audio of which is garbled at times. The fact-checking website Snopes verified the authenticity of the video, but ultimately couldn’t determine her exact words. But let’s face it; when your defense is Snopes NOT making a determination, trust is hardly earned.
Yes, economic development matters, but progressives have learned to ask who pays the price when billion-dollar corporations are promised incentives and enormous amounts of electricity. Too often, ordinary Michiganders are left subsidizing deals that primarily benefit shareholders.
Then came strike three.
State agencies issued key permits for Enbridge’s controversial Line 5 tunnel beneath the Straits of Mackinac, advancing a project that environmental organizations and Tribal Nations have fought for years. 
While the administration points to the regulatory process, many environmental advocates see another concession to a powerful corporate interest at the expense of Michigan’s commitment to protecting the Great Lakes. After all, Whitmer came into office with a promise to “take action on the Line 5 pipeline.” Eight years later, Line 5 tunnel gets the go-ahead from agencies composed of her appointees. She’s the state’s executive. These are executive agencies. 
What makes it all the more frustrating for the environmental groups who have supported her is that in 2021, she acknowledged the oil flowing through Line 5 was “a very real threat of a catastrophic oil spill in the Great Lakes.” 
But as the League of Conservation Voters noted after last week’s decision, the governor has “softened her stance on Line 5 and largely stayed quiet on the issue, leaving the majority of the continued fight to Attorney General Dana Nessel.” The National Wildlife Federation was more pointed, calling the decision a “betrayal.” Sound familiar?
After just over a month in office, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signs environmental measures alongside Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist and then-DEQ chief Liesl Clark, Feb. 4, 2019 | Nick Manes
Both of those groups endorsed Whitmer in her 2022 reelection campaign. From endorsement to betrayal in four years is exactly why so many progressives are asking whether the governor who campaigned as a champion of workers and the environment looks a lot like the kind of corporate Democrat the party’s grassroots has long criticized.
Politics is about priorities. And the priorities Democrats and progressive voters saw coming out of Lansing last week are impossible to ignore.
The Democratic Party cannot continue expecting organized labor, climate activists, tribal communities, and grassroots progressives to show up every election while treating their concerns as negotiable once the ballots are counted.
These three decisions tell a story: Labor gets vetoes while oil companies and Big Tech get the go-ahead. 
With Democrats like that, who needs Republicans?

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Public Service Commission, take action on high bills and energy affordability now
description: Kentuckians are feeling the strain as residential energy bills sky-rocket and historic heat waves grip the region. Families need solutions that will lower energy burdens and monthly costs. For that reason, Sierra Club Kentucky – alongside six other community advocacy organizations – submitted a letter to the state’s Public Service Commission (PSC) asking tha[...]
text:
As power-hungry data centers proliferate, states are searching for ways to protect utility customers from the steep costs of upgrading the electrical grid, trying instead to shift the cost to AI-driven tech companies. (Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Kentuckians are feeling the strain as residential energy bills sky-rocket and historic heat waves grip the region. Families need solutions that will lower energy burdens and monthly costs.
For that reason, Sierra Club Kentucky – alongside six other community advocacy organizations – submitted a letter to the state’s Public Service Commission (PSC) asking that the Commission open an affordability docket to identify the drivers of rising energy costs and solutions to high bills. The PSC responded to the letter and confirmed that it has formed an internal working group to study affordability, but it hasn’t opened a formal docket to hear from Kentucky families.
No corner of our commonwealth has been spared from steeply rising energy bills. Kentuckians need answers and lower costs now, not more stalling. It is critical that the PSC working group open a formal affordability docket that includes extensive public outreach in all areas of the state, solicits feedback from all stakeholders, and brings together representatives from Kentucky’s utilities and all ratepayer classes.
We would like to see several issues addressed in the affordability docket. First, we are deeply concerned about Kentucky’s continued reliance on some of the country’s highest cost coal-burning plants. Within the last year, Kentucky utilities have proposed investing hundreds of millions more hard-earned Kentuckian dollars on projects that will extend the life of aging coal-fired plants once slated for retirement. Some of these plants are out-of-state and do not employ Kentucky workers or pay most Kentucky taxes.
Instead of doubling down on coal, a recent study found that the lowest-cost energy for Kentucky – capable of saving customers billions of dollars – will require a transition away from coal, better utilization of energy efficiency measures, and battery storage.
Second, we are concerned that the rapid deployment of data centers could increase costs for Kentucky’s utility customers. While Kentucky is not yet home to a single large-scale data center, a small number of proposals have generated significant local opposition. Data centers affect household energy bills before they ever reach the communities. Kentuckians deserve to know the facts, express concerns, and participate in transparent dialogue about what’s in our state’s best interest.
Governor Andy Beshear has stated publicly that any data center interested in operating in Kentucky will “have to pay for 100 percent of its own energy.” We believe that data centers should be required to pay for 100 percent of the costs that they cause on a utility’s system, including the cost of driving up energy prices in the communities in which they locate.
As the only state agency charged with determining data center electric rates and electric energy cost allocation, the PSC is uniquely placed to lead a discussion between utilities, industry stakeholders, and the public that sets out the approval processes required to connect data centers to the grid and lays out how information about potential data centers is made public. Without shared expectations around public disclosures, the inevitable result will be local frustration over the use of non-disclosure agreements, public mistrust, and, likely, extended litigation. This could all be avoided should the PSC address these issues in an affordability docket.
Lastly, we want to ensure that Kentucky utilities do not invest in expanding electric generating capacity to power hypothetical data centers that may never exist. There are far more data center projects in utilities’ economic development pipelines than will ever conceivably be built. A Sierra Club report found that just two dozen utilities had been approached with over 700 GW of potential data center development. That’s enough energy to consume every unit of electricity produced in North America in 2024.
An affordability docket should provide a helpful forum for the PSC, utilities, and the public to explore these critically important issues before ratepayers are saddled with decades of unnecessary energy costs from new and retrofitted fossil generation.
As part of any affordability docket, we hope that the Commission will do all in its power to hear from everyday Kentuckians about their experiences with rising energy costs. It’s clear, Kentuckians need relief now. The interests of Kentucky families must stay front of mind as the PSC engages in the important work of ensuring an affordable energy future for our state.
Let the PSC know you support an affordability docket that seeks solutions for these three drivers of higher energy costs, among others. Call and tell the PSC you appreciate their studying affordability and the sooner they open a formal docket the better off you’ll be. The number to call? 502-564-3940.

text:
A storm surge forecast from the National Hurricane Center released Monday morning, July 20, 2026. (Image from NWS)A tropical depression prompted storm surge and tropical storm watches for Florida’s western-most areas.
By Monday night or Tuesday, the depression is expected to become a tropical storm, according to the National Weather Service’s National Hurricane Center.
The Monday afternoon report from NWS says “an isolated tornado or two are possible over the Florida Big Bend region today.”
As of Monday afternoon, maximum sustained winds from the depression were about 35 mph. “Gradual strengthening is expected for the next day or two,” the report states.
The NWS issued a storm surge watch, beginning at the Alabama-Florida border, stretching west to Louisiana. That watch means there is a “possibility of life-threatening inundation, from rising water moving inland from the coastline,” according to the NWS.
The surge is expected to reach 1-3 feet from Indian Pass to Chassahowitzka, as pictured above.
A tropical storm watch, as of Monday afternoon, was in effect for the Ochlockonee River west of Tallahassee, and extending further west from there, meaning tropical storm conditions are possible within the next 24-28 hours.
Associated rainfall could cause flash flooding.
The NWS said more watches or warnings could be issued Monday or Tuesday.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida disaster fund spent more on immigration than all 2025 missions combined
description: The DeSantis administration spent nearly two-thirds of Florida’s emergency fund last fiscal year on fighting illegal immigration, dwarfing spending for severe weather, international rescues, and other emergency missions for which the fund was created. State records show that the Florida Division of Emergency Management, the agency in charge of the so-called[...]
text:
Two-thirds of the money spent last year from the Florida emergency fund went to immigration. (Getty Images. Courtesy of NC Policy Watch).The DeSantis administration spent nearly two-thirds of Florida’s emergency fund last fiscal year on fighting illegal immigration, dwarfing spending for severe weather, international rescues, and other emergency missions for which the fund was created.
State records show that the Florida Division of Emergency Management, the agency in charge of the so-called “Alligator Alcatraz” and “Deportation Depot” lockups, shelled out $890 million in taxpayer dollars between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. 
Of that, $564 million — about 63% — went to immigration enforcement, meaning emergency managers spent more on immigration than all emergency missions combined last year.
The rest paid for assistance to counties and other states, costs associated with rescuing Americans from Israel after the Oct. 7, 2023 attack, and severe weather — including snow in the Panhandle, storms in Northwest Florida, and heavy October rainfall. 
The spending represents a significant shift in the purpose of the Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund, a trust created in 2022 to allow Gov. Ron DeSantis to quickly pay for disasters like hurricanes, floods, and more without legislative approval.
But in 2023, the trust became a financing vehicle for one of DeSantis’ top priorities: immigration. Gearing up for a presidential run and enjoying an iron grip over the GOP Legislature, DeSantis declared a state of emergency on immigration — one that he’s renewed at least 20 times since.
This opened the fund’s dollars to immigration enforcement, allowing FDEM to spent $573 million out of it since 2023 — 98% of which was paid for in the past year. This is largely because of the so-called “Alligator Alcatraz” and “Deportation Depot,” facilities, state-run detention centers erected last summer, lauded by President Trump, and mirrored by Republican states nationwide.
But these costs represent just a fraction of the total to be spent on immigration. As the Phoenix previously reported, immigration contracts signed by FDEM are valued at roughly $1.01 billion. This doesn’t include isolated immigration costs like food, supplies, or travel.
FDEM still owes the vendors that built and ran the facilities at least another half a billion dollars.
Despite those outstanding costs, the fund has under $7 million left. Lawmakers approved another $250 million for the trust in June, but FDEM hasn’t asked for the money yet.
The agency also missed the deadline for a new quarterly report detailing the fund’s health and cash projections, a requirement lawmakers added this year. Representatives of the Senate president and House speaker told the Phoenix they had not received the report, which was due five days ago. FDEM did not respond to questions about when it would submit the information.
Immigration spending from the fund last fiscal year exceeded the individual costs of several past emergency responses, including Hurricane Idalia, Hurricane Debby, Hurricane Nicole, and evacuation flights for Americans from Israel and Haiti.
The estimated $1.01 billion in immigration-related contracts, meanwhile, would rank as the third-largest use of the trust since its creation, behind only Hurricane Ian ($2.5 billion) and Hurricane Milton ($1.5 billion).

name: Michigan Advance
title: AOC addresses apparent Will Lawrence snub at Lansing rally for Abdul El-Sayed
description: An odd moment at a weekend rally featuring Bernie Sanders stumping for Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed left some scratching their heads: U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who has endorsed El-Sayed, failed to mention progressive 7th Congressional District candidate Will Lawrence in her address and left the stage as he arrived for [[...]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, center, and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence, right, at a rally in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. The rally also included U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)An odd moment at a weekend rally featuring Bernie Sanders stumping for Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed left some scratching their heads: U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who has endorsed El-Sayed, failed to mention progressive 7th Congressional District candidate Will Lawrence in her address and left the stage as he arrived for a final bow with Sanders.
It may not have been out of bad blood, however, as Ocasio-Cortez later said that a lack of an outright endorsement wasn’t necessarily a rejection of Lawrence.
The representative from New York has not endorsed Lawrence, who has fashioned himself as the frontrunner in the three-way August primary race between him, former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam. Lawrence has taken flak recently for past comments he made on a podcast about Black Democrats, saying their place in upholding the establishment served to “defang the white left.”
Several reporters and other observers noticed that Ocasio-Cortez kept Lawrence out of her remarks on Sunday, and avoided being seen on stage with him at the rally’s final moments.
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, right, at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Lawrence also spoke at the rally, and had the crowd of 1,600 people energized during the daylong progressive revue at the downtown Lansing Center convention space.
A spokesperson for the Lawrence campaign declined to comment on the incident on Sunday.
Ocasio-Cortez has not endorsed Democratic 13th Congressional District candidate Donavan McKinney, either, and did not mention him during her address during a Sanders for Abdul tour stop in Detroit Saturday. McKinney is running in a primary challenge against incumbent U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Detroit).
That said, Ocasio-Cortez did take a final bow with the full slate of speakers at the Detroit rally, which included Sanders, El-Sayed, McKinney and U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Detroit).
In Monday’s Politico Playbook feature, Ocasio-Cortez spoke about the rally and said: “I think that there’s nuances to a candidate — I think — or to any campaign, that are holistic, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t important.”
The interview occurred backstage at the Sunday evening portion of the tour stop, when the revue landed in Grand Rapids that night to pack the DeVos Place with a crowd of more than 2,500 people.
“That doesn’t mean that not endorsing in a race is rejection by any means, but I think that me choosing to enter a race has a high bar because of — I put a lot of energy into every candidate that I endorse,” Ocasio-Cortez told Politico.
As to why she didn’t appear with Lawrence, Ocasio-Cortez said: “I’m always careful before I issue any endorsements.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen rescinds ImagiNE Act tax incentives for new Nebraska data centers
description: LINCOLN — New data center projects coming to Nebraska will no longer benefit from tax incentives provided under the ImagiNE Act, according to a new executive order. Gov. Jim Pillen signed the executive order Monday alongside State Sens. Mike Jacobson, Rob Clements, Tony Sorrentino and Eliot Bostar, Department of Economic Development Director Maureen Larsen a[...]
text:
Gov. Jim Pillen signs executive order regulating data centers next to State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte. Behind him are Director of Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment Jesse Bradley, Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, Sen. Tony Sorrentino of the Elkhorn area, Sen. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln, and Director of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development Maureen Larsen. (Erin Bamer/ Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — New data center projects coming to Nebraska will no longer benefit from tax incentives provided under the ImagiNE Act, according to a new executive order.
Gov. Jim Pillen signed the executive order Monday alongside State Sens. Mike Jacobson, Rob Clements, Tony Sorrentino and Eliot Bostar, Department of Economic Development Director Maureen Larsen and Department of Water, Energy and Environment Director Jesse Bradley.
The order prohibits any new data center applications from being approved for tax credits under the ImagiNE Nebraska Act. While Pillen initially said this would apply to large-scale data centers, he later clarified that it would apply to all new data center projects.
The order also directs the state Department of Water, Energy, and Environment to create a task force that will offer recommendations to the Nebraska Legislature about how to best protect state resources like water and electricity. Pillen did not specify what officials would serve on the task force, but said several people have already come forward with interest in participating.
Currently, Nebraska houses 39 data centers across the state. According to conservative thinktank the Platte Institute, Nebraska ranks 9th in the U.S. for the number of data centers per capita. Neighboring Iowa ranks 2nd, with 105 data centers statewide.
The governor did not know how much money data centers have received in ImagiNE Act credits to this point, but said it was “too much.”
Jacobson, who Pillen said gave him the idea for the executive order, clarified that no general fund dollars have gone to data centers, and that any incentives they received were refunds of tax payments they made to the state.
Financial services company Moody’s estimated that there will be at least $3 trillion invested in global data centers by 2030. Pillen said that convinced him that new data center projects don’t need Nebraska to ease their development, but instead they should give back to the state.
“We need to make sure that we attract givers, not takers,” Pillen said.
Pillen said Nebraska ranks second in the U.S. for the percentage of electricity spent on data centers, at 11.5%. He said this has prevented other businesses from expanding in Nebraska when they would have otherwise.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
One piece of protecting Nebraska’s electricity came through Legislative Bill 1261, which Pillen celebrated with a ceremonial signing in early June. The bill alters the authority of public power districts to allow private companies to build energy infrastructure, like power plants, without the risk of having a public power board take them over using the power of eminent domain.
During that signing, Pillen said he called for a pause on building new data centers, but also expressed support for further investments in artificial intelligence. He said Monday that he still supports artificial intelligence, but argued the executive order would help ensure Nebraska “doesn’t give the farm away” by doing it.
Former State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, the Democratic nominee challenging Pillen’s bid for reelection, accused Pillen in an email statement of changing his tune on incentives from what he was pushing during this year’s legislative session.
“Nebraskans deserve to know the truth,” Walz said. “Less than four months ago, he was lobbying senators to pass these same incentives. We are tired of politicians saying one thing and doing another.”
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln noted that she brought an amendment to LB 1261 that would have accomplished a similar goal to Pillen’s executive order. Her amendment stated that no privately owned electric generation facility would receive tax incentives under the Nebraska Advantage Act, or the ImagiNE Nebraska Act.
Conrad’s amendment was rejected during floor debate, with Jacobson and Sorrentino voting against it. Bostar voted yes, while Clements was present-not-voting.
Jacobson said he couldn’t speak to how he voted on a specific amendment, but noted that “things were moving rapidly” at that point in the session, with only two weeks to go before lawmakers adjourned. He said “the heat has turned up” on conversations about data centers since then, and he intends to introduce a bill codifying the governor’s executive order in 2027.
When asked why he didn’t act sooner to rescind credits for data centers, Pillen said “the glass of milk was spilled” long before he took office. He noted that he was the first governor to call for a “timeout” on new data centers roughly three years ago.
Since then, at least 12 Nebraska counties have passed moratoriums on data centers. Pillen repeatedly clarified that his executive order was not a moratorium, and said he hopes the task force it establishes will help teach the counties some of what he has learned over the last three years.
“We’ve all had moments when we’ve used the word ‘never,’” Pillen said. “I’m old enough to admit that whenever I used the word ‘never,’ it was a mistake.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan Supreme Court declines to hear habeas corpus case for chimpanzees in Upper Peninsula zoo
description: The Michigan Supreme Court has declined to hear a case brought by the Nonhuman Rights Project, a legal advocacy organization focused on animal rights, which argued that seven chimpanzees, currently all at the DeYoung Family Zoo in Wallace, Mich., should be granted habeas corpus rights over living conditions that the lawyers consider to be violations […]
text:
A chimpanzee identified as Tommy pictured in a 2017 letter by PETA to the USDA requesting an investigation of the DeYoung Family Zoo. | Courtesy of the Nonhuman Rights ProjectThe Michigan Supreme Court has declined to hear a case brought by the Nonhuman Rights Project, a legal advocacy organization focused on animal rights, which argued that seven chimpanzees, currently all at the DeYoung Family Zoo in Wallace, Mich., should be granted habeas corpus rights over living conditions that the lawyers consider to be violations of the bodily liberty of chimpanzees housed there. 
“We are not persuaded that the questions presented should be reviewed by this Court,” the order stated. 
The Michigan Court of Appeals heard the case in October and denied the petition for a writ of habeas corpus to the chimpanzees, affirming a decision from the trial court that chimpanzees are not “persons” under the law. Lawyers for the Nonhuman Rights Project had been seeking a court order to show the merits of the case. That decision was officially appealed in December. 
“On the face of the complaint, the chimpanzees at defendants’ zoo are not eligible for habeas relief,” the Court of Appeals decision read. “The chimpanzees are animals, and as the common law authorities all make clear, animals—including wild animals, such as these chimpanzees—are treated as property.  No exception exists for ‘intelligent’ animals, which in any event has no natural stopping point.”
Lawyers representing seven chimpanzees at the DeYoung Family Zoo in Wallace, Mich. gathered outside the Michigan Hall of Justice after a hearing in their case. Oct. 14, 2025 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance
That question of the “stopping point” for animal rights was a key question in the Court of Appeals hearing, in which Jake Davis, the attorney for the Nonhuman Rights Project, argued that the threshold should be based on autonomy, which can be defined as “self determined behavior based on freedom of choice.”
Only one justice, Justice Elizabeth Welch, wrote a dissenting opinion in which she argued that the Court of Appeals incorrectly relied on “questionable applications of social contract theory” in defining personhood. 
“This case raises profound questions about bodily autonomy and whether the law should expand to offer protection to other living beings,” Welch wrote in her dissent. “Because the common law can evolve over time and indeed has evolved with respect to habeas relief, and because our scientific understanding of the animal kingdom is constantly evolving, I believe that we should explore this issue further.”
Michigan Supreme Court Justice Elizabeth Welch. March 11, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Welch continued on to say that, despite the court’s decision, the Legislature could reconsider its animal welfare laws. 
A statement from Davis following the Supreme Court’s decision called Welch’s dissent a “landmark development for the Nonhuman Rights Project and the broader movement to secure fundamental legal rights for nonhuman animals.”
“While our work is far from over, opinions like this strengthen the legal foundation upon which the Nonhuman Rights Project and future advocates will continue building toward meaningful legal recognition of nonhuman animals’ fundamental rights,” he continued. 
The Menominee County Circuit Court first dismissed the case in December 2023, determining that the law’s use of the word “person” made the chimpanzees ineligible for the relief that their lawyers were seeking — transfer out of the DeYoung zoo, which they called in the hearing an “unjust confinement,” to a designated sanctuary. 
The Nonhuman Rights Project filed its appeal of that decision in January 2024, arguing that Michigan common law — not a statute that includes the word “person” — should determine the outcome of the case, instead relying on the autonomy of chimpanzees.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Former Ole Miss employee contends in appeal of dismissed lawsuit that Chancellor Glenn Boyce caved to hecklers
description: University of Mississippi students walking through The Grove near Farley Hall, Thursday, March 26, 2026, in Oxford.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
A former University of Mississippi employee is arguing in a federal appeal that a judge’s dismissal of her lawsuit against Chancellor Glenn Boyce would allow a government employer to punish a worker for protected political speech because of backlash from outside critics. 
Lauren Stokes, the former Ole Miss employee, is asking the appeals court to reverse the dismissal and allow the lawsuit to proceed. The brief, filed Thursday in the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, contends that firing a public employee over protected political speech violates the First Amendment. 
Stokes’ appeal also contends that if the ruling dismissing her lawsuit stands, it would have important and risky implications for free speech.
“If the district judge is correct, a government employer may terminate an employee for no better reason than external hecklers disagree with her political point of view. No other facts matter,” the appeal states. “The First Amendment itself has nothing at all to say about it. 
Chancellor of the University of Mississippi Dr. Glenn Boyce, center, speaks during a Institutions of Higher Learning meeting Thursday, Jan. 16, 2020. 
“That is not the law, but the district judge’s orders set a dangerous precedent that affects everyone, whatever their politics.”
Stokes, a former executive assistant in the university’s development office, was fired in September after she shared to her private Instagram account commentary about the assassination of Charlie Kirk, the right-wing activist and CEO of the political organization Turning Point USA. Stokes sued Boyce in federal court, claiming he violated her First Amendment rights. 
On March 16, U.S. District Judge Glen Davidson ruled in favor of Boyce’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit. Davidson determined that Stokes failed to prove the chancellor violated her constitutional rights. Davidson also ruled that Boyce, in his role as chancellor, is entitled to qualified immunity, which protects him from liability stemming from doing his job.
When reached for comment, Stokes’ attorney Alysson Mills said the brief speaks for itself. 
Jacob Batte, a spokesperson for Ole Miss, said the university does not comment on pending litigation. Boyce’s attorney, Cal J. Mayo Jr., could not immediately be reached for comment. 
Challenging a ‘heckler’s veto’
After Kirk was shot and killed, Stokes shared to her Instagram account a post from someone else that criticized the activist’s views on issues including race, gun control and abortion. The post generated immediate backlash for Stokes, who later deleted it. She also apologized to anyone the post offended, saying, “In all facets we strive to be kind and hold space for all. My husband and I do not support violence of any sort.”
Stokes said she shared the post in a “heated moment” and apologized again, saying she looked forward “to getting off the internet to reevaluate kindness, privacy, and respect for all.”
But she was too late, the appeal notes. Stokes was already being doxxed, and people were sharing screenshots of her post.
Conservative activists and state leaders, including Mississippi State Auditor Shad White, a vocal critic of what he calls “woke” initiatives in higher education, shared a screenshot of Stokes’ post on X, formerly known as Twitter, and tagged the university.  As of Monday, White’s post has received about 60,000 views, 130 comments and has been reposted 1,300 times. 
Stokes said she received death threats and bomb threats against her restaurant that forced it to close for two weeks.
The recent appeal claims that backlash, not Stokes’ actions, led to her firing. That equates to a “heckler’s veto” of Stokes’ politics, the appeal contends, and “the government cannot punish speech ‘simply because it might offend a hostile mob.’” 
The appeal comes at a time when public employers across the country, including other colleges and universities, are facing lawsuits over whether workers can be disciplined for political speech posted on their personal social media accounts.
2026-07-16 [19] Appellant’s brief FILEDDownload
On July 1, the University of Tennessee System Board of Trustees agreed to pay a $1.9 million settlement to a former professor who sued after being fired for comments she made about Kirk. 
In May, Ball State University in Indiana paid a $225,000 settlement to its former director of health promotion and advocacy. She had been fired over a Facebook post in which she said Kirk’s killing was tragic but reflected “the violence, fear, and hatred he sowed.”
In the new brief, Mills notes that among numerous cases challenging a government employer’s firing of an employee for posting about Kirk’s death on social media, Stokes’ may be the first to go before a court of appeals “because it is the only such case to have been completely dismissed.”
Stokes’ case has also drawn the attention of free speech advocates, including The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, or FIRE, a nonprofit that frequently litigates First Amendment cases involving higher education. 
Stokes’ appeal could have implications for how public universities discipline employees over political speech on personal social media accounts, said Greg Harold Greubel, senior litigation attorney for FIRE. He said the group plans to file an amicus brief supporting Stokes this week. 
Greubel said he also thinks Stokes’ firing was driven by online outrage  — a heckler’s veto — rather than actual workplace disruption. 
Stokes maintains that her termination was not justified.
“I did nothing wrong,” Stokes said in an email to Mississippi Today. “I didn’t deserve to be fired.”
Education Editor Marquita Brown contributed to this report.

State Rep. Marcia Morey of Durham County is one of the many experts who’ve expressed concerns about how the state budget debate played out.  While she’s happy about raises that some teachers will get, she’s concerned about those teachers and state employees who will receive a relative pittance.
And as Morey also pointed out to Newline during an extended conversation this past week, there were a lot of other very important (and in some instances deeply concerning) provisions in the budget – some of which have only come to light in recent days as she and other lawmakers and advocates have finally gotten a chance to fully dissect the hurriedly enacted 600-plus page document.
In Part Two of our discussion, we examined some other policy matters of importance as the legislature prepares to return to Raleigh in late July, including the recent and troubling spate of late-night teen takeovers in some communities that have raised discussion of issues like curfews and gun regulation, as well as ongoing Republican efforts to further alter state voting laws and election oversight for partisan purposes.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Democratic Party votes to oppose property tax amendment
description: The Florida Democratic Party has voted to formally oppose Amendment 3, the measure designed to expand the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and set the state on a path towards eliminating those taxes. A statement released by the party Monday said members adopted the position over the weekend amid concern the amendment would remove […]
text:
Sen. Bryan Avila closes on the resolution he sponsored to reduce property taxes during a special session on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The Florida Democratic Party has voted to formally oppose Amendment 3, the measure designed to expand the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and set the state on a path towards eliminating those taxes.
A statement released by the party Monday said members adopted the position over the weekend amid concern the amendment would remove billions of dollars from local governments that fund public safety and other essential services.
“We need real affordability relief, but Amendment 3 would hurt our local communities and cut local services while giving huge tax breaks to billionaires and corporations,” said FDP Chair Nikki Fried in a written statement. “This is a scam that would either raise other taxes on working families or rob their communities of essential services like public hospitals, EMTs, fire rescue, disaster preparedness, road maintenance, children services, libraries and parks.
The Republican Party of Florida has yet to announce where it stands on the proposal.
There is growing momentum opposing the measure.
Last week, the Florida Fire Chiefs’ Association became the first major statewide public safety organization to formally oppose Amendment 3, saying that providing tax-relief and reliable emergency services “are not mutually exclusive, but both require responsible long-term planning.”
“Until a comprehensive funding plan is established that preserves local governments’ ability to provide these essential services, the Florida Fire Chiefs’ Association cannot support the amendment in its current form,” the organization said in a statement. “We remain committed to working with state leaders to develop solutions that protect both Florida taxpayers and the emergency services that safeguard every community.”
According to state economists, the proposed amendment would reduce local-government property-tax revenues by an estimated $5 billion in its first year and $11.8 billion per year after five years.
“We thank the Florida Democratic Party for standing up for the people of Florida and opposing Amendment 3,” said Jackson Peel, communications director for Save Our Services, one of several organizations formed to advocate against the property tax proposal.
There doesn’t appear to be any organized support for the amendment as of yet, even though Gov. Ron DeSantis and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia campaigned in public over the past year in support of such a proposal. But after the GOP-controlled Legislature approved his plan with some changes, DeSantis has noticeably cooled in his public support for it.
The governor has said the measure would be “good for taxpayers” and that he will vote for it, but will not actively campaign for the amendment before it appears on the Nov. 3 ballot.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana put on alert ahead of likely Tropical Storm Bertha
description: A tropical depression that is getting better organized — and likely to become Tropical Storm Bertha later Monday — has Louisiana officials putting residents on alert for possible flooding and wind damage.
text:
The National Weather Service forecast map for Tropical Depression 2 as of 10 a.m. Monday, July 20, 2026.A tropical depression that is getting better organized — and likely to become Tropical Storm Bertha later Monday — has Louisiana officials putting residents on alert for possible flooding and wind damage.
As of late Monday morning, the depression was roughly 110 miles south of Panama City, Florida, and moving to the northwest at 3 mph with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph. The National Hurricane Center expects the system to move slowly northwest through Monday night before turning west-northwest and eventually west. 
The system is forecast to reach tropical storm strength by Tuesday morning, but conditions are currently not favorable for further intensification. By Wednesday, the storm’s center is expected to be near southeastern Louisiana, and its forecast track takes it to southeast Texas by the weekend.   
The National Hurricane Center put a storm surge watch into effect Monday morning along the Gulf Coast from the Alabama-Florida state line to the mouth of the Mississippi River. A tropical storm watch is also in effect from the Ocholocknee River, which meets the gulf just east of Panama City, to the Jefferson-Plaquemines parish line in Louisiana. 
The National Hurricane Center is expected to update its watches and warnings as the storm advances.
Louisiana Insurance Commissioner Tim Temple said residents should prepare for heavy rain and localized flooding this week. In a news release, he recommended property owners trim trees, clear gutters and storm drains and secure outdoor items ahead of the storm.
“You should also review your homeowners and flood insurance policies, discuss potential out-of-pocket costs with your agent and keep your insurance information close at hand in the event you need to file a claim,” Temple said.
More resources related to insurance are available through the state Department of Insurance website or by calling 1-800-259-5300. The new LDIConnect app also provides access to the agency’s Storm Claim Center and its consumer services office. The app is available through the App Store and Google Play.

The family-owned farm has become a destination for children and[...]
text:
Photo Courtesy of Cozy Quarters
Where Kids Can Paint Ponies and Meet Mini Donkeys: Cozy Quarters Farm Brings Family Fun to Delaware City
By John Riddle, Contributing Journalist, Delaware LIVE
Tucked away on Madison Street in Delaware City, Cozy Quarters Farm is giving families an opportunity to trade screen time for farm time.
The family-owned farm has become a destination for children and adults looking for hands-on experiences with horses and other animals. Visitors can enjoy guided walking rides, riding lessons, pony parties, farm experiences, summer camps, and opportunities to interact with a variety of friendly farm animals.
One of the farm’s most popular attractions is its Farm Experience program. Children can ride a pony, paint a live pony using washable non-toxic paint, feed goats, visit with ducks and chickens, collect eggs, meet a pig named Paisley Mae, and spend time with miniature donkeys and miniature horses.
According to information on the farm’s website, the goal is to provide a more hands-on and interactive experience that allows children to engage directly with animals while learning about farm life.
Birthday parties have also become a major attraction. Party packages include continuous pony rides, wagon rides, pony painting, and access to a covered party area. School groups, daycare centers, summer camps, and youth organizations can also schedule special farm visits through the farm’s Giddy Up Package.
For older children and adults, Cozy Quarters Farm offers guided walking rides through Delaware City. The rides are designed for beginners and require no previous riding experience. Helmets are provided, and riders are guided throughout the experience.
The farm also provides horseback riding lessons, horse boarding, horse leasing, and trail ride opportunities. Its social media pages describe the operation as a family-owned horseback riding farm that is home to horses, ponies, and donkeys.
Visitors have responded enthusiastically to the experience.
In a recent online review, one parent described a birthday celebration at the farm as “a huge success” and said all of the children loved the activities, including pony painting, pony rides, and a tractor ride.
Another visitor who attended a party at the farm wrote that “the environment is calm and welcoming” and praised the healthy animals and friendly staff.
Beyond the animals and activities, Cozy Quarters Farm has also become a popular backdrop for photographers. The farm partners with several local photographers who use the property for family portraits, seasonal photography sessions, and special events.

The combination of horses, farm animals, open spaces, and family-friendly activities has helped make the farm a unique attraction in Delaware City. Whether visitors are celebrating a birthday, learning to ride, attending summer camp, or simply spending an afternoon meeting animals, the farm offers an experience that feels far removed from everyday routines.
As Delaware continues to grow, places like Cozy Quarters Farm provide families with an opportunity to reconnect with animals, enjoy the outdoors, and create memories that often last much longer than a typical day trip.
For more information about riding lessons, farm experiences, guided rides, camps, or party packages, visit CozyQuartersFarm.com.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Economists predict fewer people in temporary cash assistance program but higher grant amounts
description: The number of Florida residents relying on temporary financial assistance to make ends meet is decreasing but the average amount of grants awarded is on the rise. July data released by the state Office of Economic and Demographic Research (EDR) show the state expects 24,234 people to benefit from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families […]
text:
State economists attributed the decreasing caseload "primarily" to   "persistently falling child poverty rates." (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The number of Florida residents relying on temporary financial assistance to make ends meet is decreasing but the average amount of grants awarded is on the rise.
July data released by the state Office of Economic and Demographic Research (EDR) show the state expects 24,234 people to benefit from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program, referred to as TANF, in state fiscal year 2026-27.
That’s a 30% reduction from the 34,718 people previously estimated to benefit from the program between July 1 and June 30, 2027 and that legislators relied on when crafting the state budget.
The 24,000-plus people represents 14,574 caseloads. The economists who serve on the EDR previously anticipated there would be 19,346 caseloads for FY 26-27.
Overall, the program is expected to cost $47.6 million this fiscal year, which is less than the $63.1 million included in the current year budget to cover the costs.
Sitting as the Social Services Estimating conference, the economists said in an executive summary the decreasing caseload is “primarily related to persistently falling child poverty rates.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
TANF is a federally funded program that provides cash assistance and support services to lower-income families with children. The TANF program in Florida is called Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA) and is administered by the Department of Children and Families.
TCA provides up to 48 months of financial support to low-income Florida families to help cover essential needs. To qualify, an applicant must be a U.S. citizen or qualified noncitizen, have a Social Security number, have an annual income of less than 185% of the federal poverty level or $61,050 or less a year, and have a child living with them. Families must cooperate with child support enforcement.
Young children (those under age five) must be vaccinated while children aged 6-18 must regularly attend school to qualify. Additionally, the rules require most adults to participate in at least 35 hours per week of approved work activities, which include job searches, community service, or training.
Caseloads and people served aren’t the only data points being revised downward by economists. The average family size went from just under 1.8 people per caseload to about 1.6 per caseload.
Bucking the downward trend, however, is the average size of the grant per person.
Data show economists predict a $143.24 TANF grant per person in FY 26-27, which is slightly higher than the previous estimated award of $134.34 per person.

text:
Public Ed Works executive director David Rice 
After more than a full year of delay at the legislature, North Carolina finally has a new state budget and as is almost always the case, what the new budget does and doesn’t do for public education is among the matters receiving the most attention.
The good news is that a lot of teachers will get some decent raises this fall. Unfortunately, the bad news is that those raises don’t apply to all teachers or school personnel. What’s more, thanks to inflation and the rising cost of health insurance premiums, most teachers remain stuck in the mud financially or even worse off than they were just a couple of years ago.
So, what should we make of this situation? Are lawmakers making encouraging strides in lifting up our public schools or is the new budget just the latest in a series of inadequate measures. Newsline caught up with the veteran executive editor of the nonprofit group Public Ed Works, David Rice, to learn more.

name: Source New Mexico
title: US Sen. Heinrich, New Mexico tribes seek rules to rein in prediction markets
description: Heinrich (D-N.M.), along with local Indigenous tribes and pueblos, are urging Republican senators to restrain online gambling apps.
text:
U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) led a dozen Democratic Senate colleagues in urging Republican majority senators to crack down on online sports gambling platforms, which he says undermine tribal sovereignty and state-tribal gaming compacts. (Casino photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM; Heinrich photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), along with local Indigenous tribes and pueblos, are urging Republican senators to restrain online gambling apps, saying the unregulated platforms pose an “existential threat” to tribal gaming rights and sovereignty. 
Heinrich on Friday sent a letter to Republican chairmen of two U.S. Senate committees that are considering separate pieces of legislation that deal with digital assets like cryptocurrency. As drafted, according to the letter, both the CLARITY Act and Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act remove accountability for online platforms that allow users to bet on sports and other events online. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The “rapid expansion” of the apps, which allow users to bet on sports and otherwise engage in casino-style gambling, “poses an existential threat to tribal sovereignty by undermining the revenue that tribes rely on for government services,” Heinrich and 11 other Democratic senators wrote. 
The letter argues that the apps bypass federal tribal gaming laws and also undermine states’ abilities to regulate gambling. In New Mexico, sports gambling is illegal except in-person at tribal casinos, which tribes rely on to fund services including education, public safety, healthcare and housing. 
Sixteen tribes and pueblos in New Mexico signed on to the letter, according to a news release from Heinrich’s office, as did the national Indian Gaming Association and National Congress of American Indians. 
The two bills are currently being negotiated in the U.S. Senate’s Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs and Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Heinrich’s letter warns that if enacted, the legislation would “effectively allow prediction markets to offer online casino-style gaming and sports betting across the United States, entirely bypassing the localized tribal-state regulatory systems required” in federal law. 
Heinrich’s letter to leadership of both committees comes amid lawsuits from New Mexico’s attorney general and a group of tribes and pueblos seeking to crack down on Kalshi, one of the platforms that local plaintiffs accuse of subverting state and tribal law. Both lawsuits remain pending in state and federal courts. 
U.S. Sens. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) and John Boozman (R-Arkansas) chair the committees that are reviewing the legislation. Spokespersons for both senators did not immediately respond to Source NM’s emailed requests for comment Monday morning. 
The letter urges senators to amend the bills to prohibit the platforms from enabling sports betting and also make explicit that the platforms cannot be used to circumvent existing tribal-state gaming compacts. 
Without those amendments, unregulated online gambling will undermine federal treaty obligations to tribal governments and their rights to self-determination, which represent a “primary pillar of tribal sovereignty,” the letter reads.

title: ICE officers to wear body cameras at traffic stops, White House border czar says
text: WASHINGTON — In the wake of two fatal shootings in Texas and Maine, U.S. Immigration Customs and Enforcement officers will wear “at least one body camera” during traffic stops, Tom Homan, the president’s border czar, said over the weekend. Homan, who President Donald Trump has tasked with leading his mass deportation campaign, said in a Sunday interview on Fox News that ICE’s acting director has instructed officers to wear a body camera “whenever possible” during vehicle stops. This month, two immigrants — 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero and 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo — were shot and killed by ICE agents who stopped their vehicles. Neither man was an initial enforcement target, the Department of Homeland Security said.During Sunday’s Fox and Friends Weekend program, Homan said he supported body cameras because “they exonerate more law enforcement than they convict.” “I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action,” Homan said. Federal immigration officers have shot 22 people and killed six, including three U.S. citizens, during the second Trump administration. Most shootings have stemmed from traffic stops, which Homan said officers were continuing. After the back-to-back shootings of Salgado Araujo in Texas and Guerrero in Maine, DHS instructed agents to pause vehicle stops, but Trump quickly reversed those plans. Congressional standstillHoman blamed Democrats for the reason immigration agents don’t have body cameras, pointing to the weeks-long shutdown of DHS. He also accused traffic stops of becoming more dangerous because of Democrats criticizing ICE.“They're more dangerous now than ever because Democratic members of Congress, Democratic mayors and governors have preached for the past year ‘ICE isn’t a real law enforcement agency. ICE has no authority. Resist,’” he said. Democrats refused to approve funding for DHS unless restraints were placed on ICE and Border Patrol officers, such as the requirement for body cameras, after two U.S. citizens were killed by federal immigration officers in Minnesota in January. Congressional Republicans last year used a special legislative maneuver to allocate roughly $175 billion to DHS for immigration enforcement, detainment and deportations, without needing Democratic support. GOP lawmakers used the same move following the shutdown this year to fund $75 billion for ICE and Border Patrol until September of 2029.In a separate interview, on CBS’s Face the Nation Sunday, Homan again gave his support for body cameras on ICE officers and blamed Democrats for a lack of body cameras. “I think body cameras are the way to go,” he said. After the two killings in Minnesota in January, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said DHS would be issuing body cameras to immigration officers.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC elections board vote makes it easier to throw out mail-in ballots
description: Republicans say the change would enhance election security. Democratic critics say it would disenfranchise legitimate voters, and could be applied arbitrarily with political motives.
text:
Photo: Adobe StockThe North Carolina State Board of Elections approved on Monday a measure to disqualify certain absentee ballots ahead of the 2026 midterms. 
Members voted 3-2 along party lines. 
The measure allows county elections board staff to take further action on ballots with “irregularities.” Examples include not properly sealing a ballot or using the wrong type of envelope. Staff should contact voters, but without appropriate action, the ballots may be tossed. 
Republicans say the change would enhance election security. Democratic critics say it would disenfranchise legitimate voters, and could be applied arbitrarily with political motives. 
“I think it’s confusing,” Democratic board member Siobhan Millen said. “We’re going to lose perfectly sound ballots due to over-fussiness.”
“I don’t think it’s fussy. I don’t think it’s picky. I don’t think it’s hard,” responded Republican board member Angela Hawkins. Hawkins says voters confused by the container return envelope used in  absentee voting may contact their local elections board for clarification. 
She pointed out the proposal is legal under current state’s laws.
“If the General Assembly wants to change it, then that’s fine,” Hawkins  said. 
At the national level, President Donald Trump has slammed mail-in voting, claiming it contributed to “fraud” in the 2020 election. His allegations have not been proven. 
North Carolina’s Rules Review Commission, made up of Republican appointees, needs to approve the change before it takes effect. 
Last week, the elections board voted in favor of a rule to make it easier to throw out voters’ ballots if they don’t show photo identification. 
NC elections board moves to make it easier to toss voters’ ballots

Under the measure, an elections board could toss a ballot by majority vote if they think a voter is lying about their lack of photo ID. Current rules require bipartisan agreement.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma’s plan to comply with mental health consent decree is approved one year after deadline
description: More than a year after it was due, the state’s plan to provide court-ordered treatment for Oklahoma defendants found incompetent to stand trial has been approved by the consultants overseeing a high-profile consent decree. The state entered the consent decree to settle a 2023 lawsuit that accused the Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse […]
text:
The Oklahoma Forensic Center in Vinita provides court-ordered mental health treatment to criminal defendants who have been deemed incompetent to stand trial. (Photo by  Sierra Pfeifer/KOSU)More than a year after it was due, the state’s plan to provide court-ordered treatment for Oklahoma defendants found incompetent to stand trial has been approved by the consultants overseeing a high-profile consent decree.
The state entered the consent decree to settle a 2023 lawsuit that accused the Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services of violating the civil rightsof people in the criminal justice system with severe mental illness who sometimes wait months in jail for treatment before their cases can resume.
Four versions of the plan previously submitted by the department were rejected by court consultants and class counsel for a lack of detail and a failure to collaborate with the settlement parties, according to court consultant Neil Gowensmith. He approved the latest draft in a letter filed in federal court in Tulsa on July 13.
“While we approve the Plan, we consider this to be the first serious effort on the part of ODMHSAS to implement the Decree,” Gowensmith wrote on behalf of the three consultants in charge of monitoring the department. “More than a year has gone by since entry of the Decree, much of that time wasted by a lack of real focus on the Decree.”
He said the plan is just one step toward meeting the standards of the consent decree and that the department has a short amount of time left to begin “the real work.”
The department’s plan was originally due by June 9, 2025, but as of January, consultants said the plan didn’t exist, and the number of people waiting in county jails for mental health treatment had increased by 58%.
Ultimately, the consent decree requires the state to provide criminal defendants with court-ordered treatment within 21 days. In May, 203 people were waiting an average of 104 days in county jails for treatment, according to the agency’s approved strategic plan.
The Department of Mental Health has already been fined $3.5 million for failing to reduce treatment wait times and make other functional improvements for class members. The agency will face another round of fines beginning in October after the consent decree’s yearly cap resets, according to the lead attorney for the plaintiffs, Paul DeMuro.
He said the newly approved plan represents a substantial shift in the department’s handling of the consent decree. DeMuro credited agency leadership changes and a federal judge’s ruling that the state had failed to make “best efforts” to comply with the decree.
“I’m confident, if the department maintains this level of focus and collaboration, we can get this done,” DeMuro said. “There may be some bumps in the road, or disagreements or things might not happen as quickly as people on the ground would like, but I am confident we can get it right.”
Still, more than a year after the final consent decree was approved, DeMuro said he had hoped the state would be further along in making improvements.
“If you talk to public defenders, district attorneys and judges, they are still not seeing the changes,” DeMuro said. “We’ve got a long way to go.”
To be successful, the department must create a treatment system for criminal defendants that “serves courts, counties, treatment providers, and individuals more effectively,” the plan authors wrote.
“We’re grateful for the Court Consultants’ approval of our Consent Decree Strategic Plan,” a spokesperson for the department said in a statement. “While there is still important work ahead that will take time and collaboration with our partners across the state, this marks a meaningful step in the right direction.”
This article was originally published by KOSU.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Independent New Mexico governor candidate drops out, endorses Republican nominee Gregg Hull
description: Ken Miyagishima, a former longtime mayor of Las Cruces who couldn’t get on New Mexico’s November ballot as an independent gubernatorial candidate, on Friday announced he was officially dropping out of the race and backing former Rio Rancho mayor and Republican nominee Gregg Hull.
text:
Ken Miyagishima, a former Las Cruces mayor who ran for governor as an independent after unsuccessfully mounting a Democratic campaign, pictured in the New Mexico Secretary of State’s office on June 25, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Ken Miyagishima, a former longtime mayor of Las Cruces who couldn’t get on New Mexico’s November ballot as an independent gubernatorial candidate, on Friday announced he was officially dropping out of the race and backing former Rio Rancho mayor and Republican nominee Gregg Hull.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Miyagishima had initially planned to challenge former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland and Bernalillo County District Attorney Sam Bregman for the Democratic nomination, but was unable to obtain the necessary signatures. He switched to running as an independent in hopes of making the Nov. 3 ballot, but was similarly unable to collect enough signatures. He subsequently lost a lawsuit challenging the state’s ballot access requirements.
Although he initially ran as a Democrat, on the campaign trail, Miyagishima often billed himself as a centrist and said he planned to use “policies from all parties.”
“I have known Mayor Hull for almost 12 years. He is intelligent, hardworking and a man of integrity,” Miyagishima wrote in a statement announcing his departure from the race and endorsement. “His record reflects his dedication to the people of both Rio Rancho and New Mexico.”
While the two spent much of their political careers in opposing parties, they share a mayoral distinction — Miyagishima and Hull were the longest-serving mayors of Las Cruces and Rio Rancho, the state’s second- and third-largest cities, respectively.
Hull previously told Source NM he believed his experience as a mayor, which is a non-partisan office, marked a meaningful difference between him and other gubernatorial candidates.
His campaign sent a fundraising email to his supporters over the weekend with the subject line: “A Democrat mayor just endorsed me.”
“Ken and I did not enter this race from the same political party. We served different cities in different parts of our state,” Hull wrote in the email. “Yet as mayors, we faced many of the same challenges, and we learned that potholes are not Republican or Democratic, public safety is not a partisan issue and creating good jobs should never take a back seat to political games.”

name: National
title: Trump administration ramps up pressure on indefinite immigrant detention
description: Seeking to stop a “flood” of court cases freeing immigrants from mandatory detention, the Trump administration is asking an appeals court to put three immigrants back in detention. The immigrants were freed by Texas federal judges in February and March in a case that was upheld by an appeals court panel for Louisiana, Mississippi and […]
text:
Fomer U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi speaks last year  at Louisiana State Penitentiary to announce the opening of Camp 57, a facility at the prison that will house immigrant detainees. An appeals court covering Louisiana and other states with large detention centers is at the center of a court fight over mandatory detention for many immigrants. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)Seeking to stop a “flood” of court cases freeing immigrants from mandatory detention, the Trump administration is asking an appeals court to put three immigrants back in detention.
The immigrants were freed by Texas federal judges in February and March in a case that was upheld by an appeals court panel for Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas, which found that such immigrants have the right to bond hearings within 90 days of being detained. That decision was reversed by the full 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which will hold a full hearing on the case in September. 
Appeals court reverses decision on immigrant detention, leaving no-bond policy in place

In court papers filed earlier this month, the Trump administration noted the thousands of recent court cases, called habeas petitions, in which judges determined that the mandatory detention policy violates the U.S. constitution. In many cases, those determinations were made even by judges appointed by Trump.
“This flood of habeas petitions has inflicted a devastating toll on U.S. Attorneys’ Offices as well as district courts — draining those Offices’ resources and impeding numerous other significant priorities,” administration attorneys wrote in the filing. The administration asked for a decision by Monday, July 20, that would put the three men back into immigration detention as a precedent for other judges to follow.
Rebecca Cassler, a senior litigation attorney with the American Immigration Council, which represents the three men, told Stateline the men were all pulled over in traffic stops, have no criminal record and have children who are U.S. citizens, and have each lived in the U.S. more than 10 years. They are subject to the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy because they crossed a border illegally. 
“This is a highly irregular motion to file at this stage of the case, and it would work tremendous hardship on the clients and their families,” Cassler said. 
In immigration detention, the men “experienced rotten food, inadequate medical care, maggot- and fungus-ridden mattresses, and devastating separation from their families,” according to court papers filed Friday by the American Immigration Council. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: WyoFile
title: Meta wants hearing, $10K fine refunded in data center water case
description:
In appeal of “significant noncompliance” in Cheyenne, tech giant says it should not be on the hook for cleanup costs either.
The post Meta wants hearing, $10K fine refunded in data center water case appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Meta, parent company of Facebook, has told the Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities that a $10,000 fine Meta paid for a pollution citation at a data center construction site is not supported by evidence and should be refunded.
In a six-page appeal of a “notice of noncompliance” Meta asserts that the Cheyenne agency named the wrong party, didn’t explain the legal basis for the fine and provided no evidence that a dangerous bacteria came from Meta Cheyenne Data Center as charged.
The appeal asks for a hearing with the state’s independent office that examines administrative conflicts. The Meta appeal also states that Cheyenne has not established that cleanup costs it may seek to recover were caused by Goat Systems, a company Meta used to conduct business before it unveiled its plans for the center in 2024.
The Cheyenne utility agency has balked at answering questions regarding the discovery of Cupriavidus gilardii bacteria, known to be deadly, which it said it traced to an industrial user. But the Meta appeal provides some information about the incident, including that Cheyenne indicated it will seek to recover cleanup costs stemming from what it called “significant remediation efforts.”
The bacteria was found in the city’s wastewater reclamation system, which cleans and recycles sewage for use on city fields like golf courses and parks. Discovery of the bacteria required “draining and disinfecting the entire reuse water system,” over the course of two months, the city said.
Fouling part of the city’s water system — even though the bacteria was in the reclaimed sewage system and not in drinking water — has implications for a metropolis that can’t sustain its needs locally. Cheyenne pulls half of its water from the far side of the Continental Divide 115 miles away. The city used potable water to cleanse the reclaimed sewage system and water fields during the time the recycling system was off line.
“Given the flaws outlined above, BOPU has failed to prove the causal basis for any such increased costs,” Meta states of the cleanup. It asks the utility board to “[d]isapprove, withdraw, or vacate” the citation as “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, unsupported by substantial evidence, and not in accordance with applicable procedures.”
Fill, flush, fine
Although Cheyenne cited Goat Systems for the bacteria it discovered, it was the construction company Fortis that held the permit to discharge wastewater into the Cheyenne sewage system, according to the appeal. Cheyenne verbally ordered Fortis, not Goat Systems, to stop discharging on March 24, 2026, the appeal states.
“Goat Systems was not engaged in any activities on the site related to the discharges and could not have caused a discharge of the bacteria in question,” the appeal states. Cheyenne discovered the bacteria at the data center “discharge point” on March 18, according to the appeal, but provided no evidence that the sample collected “was representative of the alleged discharge or any activities associated with Fortis’ fill/flush activities.”
Cheyenne said it traced the bacteria to the Meta Cheyenne Data Center after “extensive field investigations and targeted sampling.” Cupriavidus gilardii has high resistance to metals and is used in advanced manufacturing and industrial systems, the utility said.
Fill-flush activities are conducted on data center cooling systems, essential systems that keep data center computers from overheating. The Meta Cheyenne Data Center is designed to use a closed-loop system — akin to a car’s radiator, instead of consuming water by cooling through evaporation. Such systems need a fill-flush cleaning before startup.
“Goat Systems was not engaged in any activities on the site related to the discharges and could not have caused a discharge of the bacteria in question.”Meta
Meta also challenges the discovery of the bacteria itself, saying it hasn’t received information and data about quality analysis and control to support the charge against Goat Systems.
There is not now any “significant noncompliance,” Meta says.
“The [citation] does not reflect the fact that discharge from the construction operations was permanently halted in March 2026,” the appeal states. “Since that time, all wastewater has been hauled offsite. To the extent any bacteria contamination occurred, it has already been fully remediated.”
Cheyenne revoked the discharge permit permanently following the discovery.
Construction contractor Fortis “began its own water testing with an independent environmental specialist which has found no trace of the substance,” Meta said. That conclusion came from “four separate testing rounds across discharge samples, passivation water, source water, stagnant water from uncleaned systems, and samples with added dirt,” Meta said.
Meta is “committed to being a good neighbor,” a spokesperson said, “and will continue encouraging collaboration between Fortis and the [utility] board until this situation is resolved.
“It is important that the community has all the information about what happened,” Meta said in a statement.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Challenger drops recount of 14-vote GOP primary margin for state Sen. Liz Brown
description: The Republican primary challenger to state Sen. Liz Brown has dropped his push for a recount of their 14-vote margin race.
text:
Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, speaks during an Indiana Senate session on Feb. 24, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Republican primary challenger to state Sen. Liz Brown has dropped his push for a recount of their 14-vote margin race.
Darren Vogt submitted a petition Monday to the state Recount Commission to dismiss the recount request he filed May 19, two weeks after primary voting ended in what was a bitter campaign.
Certified vote tallies for Senate District 15, which is entirely in Fort Wayne’s Allen County, gave Brown a lead of 5,241 to 5,227 over Vogt.
The Recount Commission was scheduled to take up the State Board of Accounts review of voting materials in race during a Tuesday meeting.
Republican state Senate candidate Darren Vogt of Fort Wayne. (Ballotpedia)
Vogt’s filing asks to dismiss his recount petition “in its entirety” but did not explain his decision.
Vogt, a staffer to U.S. Sen. Jim Banks and a member of the Northwest Allen County Schools board, did not immediately return a phone message from the Indiana Capital Chronicle seeking comment.
Brown is seeking her fourth state Senate term while Vogt had support from Banks and state Attorney General Todd Rokita, both of whom clashed with Brown over her handling of immigration crackdown legislation.
Brown said she was glad to see the end of what she called a “costly, time-consuming and unnecessary recount.”
“This was a long primary season, with a Senate District 15 primary fight that never needed to happen,” Brown said in a statement. “Voters had a clear choice of two very different candidates. They chose the unwavering pro-life conservative who stands on principle, no matter the cost, rather than the candidate fielded last summer by an attorney general and U.S. senator hungry to hold influence.”
Rokita gave $90,000 from his campaign fund to Vogt’s campaign, with Banks giving $35,000 from his campaign account, according to state Election Division filings.
Brown is set to face Democrat Julie McGill in the November election in what has typically been a strongly Republican area.
Vogt’s decision to drop the recount follows the June 25 withdrawal of his attorney just days before auditors conducted their ballot review on June 30 and July 1 in Fort Wayne. Vogt didn’t hire another attorney and filed Monday’s petition on his own behalf.
The Recount Commission has a July 28 hearing scheduled in another state Senate race, where Sen. Spencer Deery of West Lafayette leads his President Donald Trump-endorsed opponent, Paula Copenhaver, by a three-vote margin.
