name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ public school enrollment falls to lowest level in quarter century
description: The number of public school students fell by nearly 24,000 in 2025-26, pushing enrollment to its lowest since the 2001-2002 school year.
text:
The number of public school students fell by nearly 24,000 in 2025-26, pushing enrollment to its lowest since the 2001-2002 school year. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Enrollment in New Jersey public schools fell to the lowest levels recorded in almost a quarter-century during the state’s most recent annual count, diving past pandemic lows to reach depths not seen since the turn of the millennium.
According to figures from October recently released by the state Department of Education, public school enrollment declined by 23,732 students in the 2025-2026 school year to about 1.4 million, the lowest level since the 2001-2002 school year, a drop that appeared driven mostly by falling birth rates.
“It’s like a giant clock with a lot of moving parts, but it adds up to enrollment declines. And since state aid is tied to enrollment, it’s going to have an effect,” said Betsy Ginsburg, executive director of the Garden State Coalition of Schools. “It’s already having an effect. It’s going to have an even bigger effect.”
New Jersey’s youngest public school students were born chiefly in 2020, a year the state recorded 18,775 fewer births than it did 13 years earlier, a decline of roughly 16%. The latter group of students graduated last year.
Declining births are likely to prompt further drops in public school enrollment over the coming years. New Jersey cumulatively recorded 27,412 fewer births between 2021 and 2024 than it did in the same range 13 years earlier.
“You take any 13-year gap, and if you’ve got a lower number now than you did 13 years ago, you’re likely to see a somewhat corresponding decline in enrollment,” said Steve Baker, a spokesperson for statewide teachers union the New Jersey Education Association.
The enrollment changes are not uniform across districts, and some are growing while others shrink. Of the 663 public school districts and charter schools that reported enrollment to the state in October, 227 reported they had more students than they did the previous year.
The overall decline is not unique to New Jersey. Birth rates have fallen across the United States, and schools nationwide have seen corresponding drops in enrollment. The National Center for Education Statistics in May 2024 forecast nationwide public school enrollment could fall by roughly 1.3 million, or about 2.7%, between 2025 and 2031.
Sen. Vin Gopal (Photo by Hal Brown/New Jersey Monitor)
“It’s a moment in time. I think things will fluctuate back and forth, and we’re seeing a generational change a little bit,” said Sen. Vin Gopal (D-Monmouth), the chamber’s education chairman.
But New Jersey’s enrollment decline appears faster, and losses due to its declining birth rates alone could cut public school enrollment by as much as 3.3% by the 2029-2030 school year.
Michael Yaple, a spokesperson for the Department of Education, said state education officials are aware of enrollment declines but had not done an analysis to determine their causes.
 Non-public schooling
Rises in home schooling or non-public school enrollment can also push down public school enrollment, but it’s unclear how much of a role either of those factors has played in New Jersey’s recent declines.
Private school attendance likely played some part, but it’s difficult to say how large because the state does not track statewide non-public school enrollment.
Take Lakewood as an example. The Ocean County township is the fastest-growing municipality in the state due largely to its large Hasidic community, and its population ranks among the youngest of any political subdivision in the country.
Nearly half its residents are less than 18 years old, and the township’s population grew by 6% between April 2020 and July 2025, more than double the statewide average rate of 3%. Despite this growth in Lakewood overall, public school enrollment there has fallen 32% since the 2019-2020 school year.
Lakewood’s school-aged population is north of 48,000, but fewer than 4,000 were enrolled in the township’s public schools this year. That’s because, overwhelmingly, children there attend private religious schools called yeshivas. As a result, they are not captured in the state’s enrollment statistics.
Gopal said the state should begin tracking non-public enrollment.
“That should be easily available information. That should be public information,” he said.
State data on homeschooling is also thin. New Jersey does not require parents to notify the Department of Education or their local school district unless a public high school student is moving to in-home education.
U.S. Census data shows a rise in homeschooling contributed to enrollment declines during the pandemic. About seven months into the COVID-19 crisis, statewide public school enrollment was down to 1.362 million. It would fall to 1.361 million the in the 2021-2022 school year before rebounding.
Meanwhile, homeschooling rates more than doubled, rising from 5% in late April and early May of 2020 to 10% that October, according to Census data. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimated those rates declined to 4% in the 2023-2024 school year.
Immigration enforcement — and deportations in particular — can also affect public school enrollment, but the degree of that effect is unclear.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to an inquiry asking how many New Jersey residents aged 18 and under had been removed from the United States since January 2025, but enrollment data suggests removal operations may have accelerated declines in some cities.
This year’s enrollment declines were larger in municipalities with large Hispanic communities, like Paterson (where the number of students dropped 8%), West New York (6%), and New Brunswick (6%). But the effect was far from uniform. In Perth Amboy, where more than 80% of residents are Hispanic, enrollment fell by only 1%.
Mark Magyar, director of Rowan University’s Steve Sweeney Center for Public Policy, said he thinks immigration enforcement has contributed somewhat to the enrollment decline.
“I think a fear has been aroused that’s been a factor,” Magyar said. “A crackdown on immigration has a disproportionate impact on New Jersey as a state, more so than it would on New Hampshire or Massachusetts or Connecticut or Pennsylvania because people come here then they spread out from here.”
Other factors, like the availability and cost of housing, the strength of local and regional economies, and the desirability of a given municipality to the people actually having children, can affect enrollment levels by prompting migration to or from a state or region.
Those factors have contributed to slower population growth in New Jersey’s rural northwestern counties, while destructive storms and gentrification have pushed some year-round residents out of Jersey Shore communities, Magyar said.
“Younger people want to live in walkable environments,” he said. “They want to live near mass transit, so one of the things that we have been seeing is if you look at where the population of New Jersey has had the largest declines, it was Sussex, Warren, and parts of Hunterdon.”
A school bus transports students in Newark. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
 Funding and staffing schools
Enrollment declines have a knock-on effect throughout the state’s education system as districts with shrinking student bodies decide whether to keep staff and facilities or shed them to meet the diminished demands of their communities.
Schools’ populations help determine the amount of state aid a school receives, and state lawmakers have for years edged toward mandating districts where few students are enrolled to merge with others to reduce property taxes or at least slow their growth.
“I have a small district that’s about 30% full, the building. Their per-pupil cost is about $60,000 per kid. They’re looking at possibly cutting their music and art programs, and there’s nowhere in the town where redevelopment’s happening where families are moving in,” Gopal said. “What does that look like for the next 15 years?”
Efforts to rework the school funding formula, which determines how much state aid a district receives based on factors like enrollment, property values, and income, are slow-moving but ongoing.
Gopal and a range of other officials inside and outside state government have said Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s administration is examining the formula to see where changes might be made, but it’s not clear when those proposals might arrive. Ginsburg said those changes ought to be made during a special summer legislative session to avoid timing conflicts with the state’s and school districts’ budget cycles.
Because enrollment is one of the factors that determines a district’s level of state aid, a shrinking student body will cause a corresponding decrease in aid that could force a district to cut staff or reduce course offerings, while rising enrollment could force a district to expand its faculty or secure new class space.
“Rising enrollment has its own set of challenges,” Baker said. “Districts that have increasing enrollment, now you’re talking about construction cost, you’re talking about building new facilities, you’re talking about transportation costs go up, all that kind of stuff.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Our vote is our only real power. Let us not abdicate or waste it
description: We have some very important elections this year. Elections have consequences, and a lot is riding on how we vote, or worse, if we choose not to vote at all. There are concerted efforts at the national level and across many states to make it more difficult to exercise that power. We cannot afford to […]
text:
(MicroStockHub/iStock Images)We have some very important elections this year. Elections have consequences, and a lot is riding on how we vote, or worse, if we choose not to vote at all.
There are concerted efforts at the national level and across many states to make it more difficult to exercise that power.
We cannot afford to sit silently by and allow such efforts to win.
First, follow any proposed changes in voting requirements and make sure you are still able to vote.
Then, determine where you stand on the candidates, and the issues.  
What is the profile of the man or woman who potentially could represent you in Jefferson City and Washington? Do you really know the candidates and their positions on the issues that will impact your life, your family, your neighborhood, your city, for the next two, four, or six years — even beyond?
In Missouri, there are very important ballot issues seeking your vote in August and November. Take the time to find out and understand what you are truly being asked to vote for.
All across the country there are legislative offices — at the municipal, county, state and federal level — with candidates vying for our vote. Our involvement and vote, or failure to vote will determine the outcome for those critical offices. 
In Missouri, the list of the issues, offices and the candidates vying for them gives you an idea of how much is at stake and up for grabs. 
To understand what the candidates really stand for, once in office who they will really represent, the details of public policies, or impending legislation can be daunting, if not indeed overwhelming. Most of us are preoccupied with daily issues of making ends meet, raising a family, keeping a job, and other demands.  
There are ways we can achieve a “comfort zone” around who can best represent us, and how we should vote on ballot issues before us.
You might find this approach helpful. 
1) Take some time to examine and reflect on the issues that are important to you — whether they are your personal quality of life, economic development, community revitalization, jobs for youth, quality health care or some other concern. What has been the overall political and policy direction and decisions taken by those whom you have entrusted to lead?
2) Develop a score card on paper or in your mind and see how you, and your community, city, county, state or our nation has fared. Ask yourself a few critical questions: Are things better off than they were two, three or four years ago? If not, why not? Who and what actions or inactions are responsible?
3) Consult creditable local and national organizations and other trusted sources for factual information. 
Many of the issues and conditions impacting your community, city or state are the same across the country. Some are different. But the important thing is how they are dealt with, and what are the attendant results short-term and long-term by the people you vote to put in office.
We only have to look at a few critical indicators to reach some rather poignant conclusions:

Our ability to keep up with the cost of living.
The availability and affordability of housing in our communities.
Access to quality health care services at affordable prices.
Access to services such as a good grocery store, pharmacy, auto services, etc.
The state and quality of education our children are receiving.

We cannot afford to just look at our personal situation, or just one area, in a vacuum when so much of where we find ourselves is interconnected. 
Your vote for a particular candidate can be the change. Find out what actions the incumbents have taken or failed to take on issues that are most important to you. Ask the challengers for their specific plans to address them should they be elected. 
When you tally your scorecard, what are your conclusions about the incumbent and the challenger?
Our current political environment is flooded with divisiveness, disinformation, misinformation, no information, downright lies, personal agendas, finger pointing and the blame game dominating the news and public square. It is very difficult to shut out the noise and give serious thought about the conditions all around us.
This unproductive morass should compel us to ask what moral values are being adhered to. History has proved that no civilization or nation survives without them.
The representatives we elect to represent us will respond when we insist they do with the power of our vote and vigilance once they are in office. If you want elected officials who are honest, ethical, and responsive, vote and hold the elected officials accountable throughout his/her term.
Good government, like a good family, a good church, or a good school, takes having the right people at the top making good decisions. But it also takes the rest of us to play our part.
We have time to research, discuss, and mobilize the vote.
Tell a neighbor, a family member, or a colleague who you think will be best to work and fight for the issues you care about — for your family, your neighborhood, your city, your state, and our country. 
Our vote has the power to make the difference and the changes we need.
We can’t afford to not use that power, or waste it.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Leadership vacuum: Agencies in New York and beyond pass the buck on opioid cash oversight
description: Advocates are demanding accountability for how local officials spend tens of billions in opioid settlement cash. But whose job is that?
text:
Alexis Pleus’ son Jeff Dugon died of a heroin overdose in 2014 at age 28. She says his addiction began in high school, when he was prescribed opioid painkillers for a knee injury. In 2023, Pleus protested outside the Supreme Court while justices heard a case about Purdue Pharma, the company many people consider a driver of the opioid crisis. (Mia Hause)Companies accused of recklessly marketing and distributing prescription opioid painkillers are paying roughly $58 billion to settle lawsuits over their role in fueling the addiction crisis. It’s a pot of gold eyed by addiction treatment providers, companies creating the latest opioid-related products, and government officials struggling to balance budgets.
Nearly half of that money is going to local governments, to be distributed by county commissioners and city councilors. The idea is that local leaders know their communities best and can do justice to these payouts, often described as “blood money” by people who’ve lost loved ones to an overdose.
But many local leaders have little to no training in addiction policy and may lack robust local health departments and policy guardrails to assist them.
That has resulted in spending decisions that many clinicians, researchers, and addiction recovery advocates say are unlikely to save lives or treat substance use disorders.
In New York, where about 46% of the opioid settlement money is directly controlled by local governments, counties have spent tens of thousands of dollars on surveillance cameras, technology to help police access data on locked cellphones, and goggles that simulate being drunk, according to public records obtained by the nonprofit advocacy group Legal Action Center and shared exclusively with KFF Health News. Though the purchases were likely legal, many people consider them a slap in the face because they don’t directly help people struggling with addiction or their families.
Without oversight, counties have the chance “to go rogue” with this money, said Jasmine Budnella, director of drug policy at VOCAL-NY, an advocacy organization that is tracking settlement money as part of its mission to serve people affected by the war on drugs.
When advocates and families of overdose victims raise concerns to the various state agencies that could hold localities accountable, those agencies often punt to one another, Budnella and other local advocates said.
It feels “like the Spider-Man meme, where it’s like everybody’s pointing at each other,” Budnella said. “Somebody needs to be able to have the stick and slam their hand on the table and be like, ‘You’re doing this wrong and this is the consequence.’”
The experience in New York provides a microcosm of regulators evading oversight responsibility nationwide while varied interests vie for the financial windfall.
Years of data collected by KFF Health News, the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, and the addiction nonprofit Shatterproof have found that settlement money was spent on law enforcement gear, such as night-vision goggles and bulletproof vests; unproven prevention initiatives, such as a drug-awareness magician for kids; and budget stopgaps.
It’s unclear who should — or will — take action on such expenditures that many people harmed by the crisis consider questionable.
In each state, control of the money is split among various entities, creating a leadership vacuum. The federal government plays little to no role. Advocates and families who’ve lost loved ones have pushed for accountability but have limited power. A few states have passed new laws, but change is slow and uneven.
The settlement agreements require the majority of the money to be spent on “opioid remediation,” with more than 100 suggested expenditures. But the list is broad and open to interpretation. Further complicating the issue, many states — including New York — designate some portion of the settlement dollars as unrestricted, which allows for general spending.
Meanwhile, federal budget cuts have threatened addiction-related services and created more demand for funding. And though overdose deaths have decreased since peaking in 2022, they still claim about 186 lives per day.
Jeff Dugon (right) spent Easter with his mother, Alexis Pleus, and brothers in 2014. He died four months later of a heroin overdose. Now, Pleus is fighting to ensure opioid settlement money is spent in ways that can spare other families such heartache. (Mitchell Sosnicki)
“We really are wasting this opportunity to use these funds to turn the epidemic around,” said Alexis Pleus, a Binghamton, New York, resident, whose 28-year-old son, Jeff Dugon, died of a heroin overdose in 2014.
He was a chef who loved to rib Pleus about her bad knife skills. She thinks of him and smiles every time she peels garlic the way he taught her. If the money could spare other families such heartache, that would give her solace.
“We need oversight,” said Pleus, who runs a nonprofit that is receiving opioid settlement cash from her county to serve people who use drugs and provide support groups for families.
In New York, there are three prime watchdog contenders: the Office of Addiction Services and Supports, the attorney general, and the comptroller.
 The lead state agency
New York’s opioid settlement documents designate the Office of Addiction Services and Supports as the “lead state agency.”
It distributes a portion of settlement dollars via grants, according to recommendations from the state’s Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Board. It also has the power to “engage in oversight and audits of projects and programs” funded by settlement cash and “may withhold future funds” from local governments that do not comply with certain requirements, according to the agreement.
Agency spokesperson Jerry Gretzinger told KFF Health News the office has not yet exercised its power to withhold funds but understands its oversight role.
“OASAS has a duty to ensure these funds are used responsibly and strategically to build programs that will have a lasting impact in reversing this crisis,” Gretzinger wrote in a statement.
The office is currently auditing 19 local governments’ use of the money to ensure compliance with “reporting and recordkeeping requirements,” he said. However, that may not encompass the broader question of whether money was spent on appropriate uses, which many advocates want addressed.
Some people are frustrated with the narrow role OASAS has carved out.
For example, language included in last year’s state budget required local governments for the first time to publicly report how they spent settlement money. OASAS collected links to those reports on its site. But it does not review the accuracy or detail of that data, instead relying on “the information as it is provided” by localities, Gretzinger said.
“That doesn’t feel like oversight,” said Christine Khaikin, a deputy director at the Legal Action Center, which obtained public records about local spending in New York.
Members of the state’s Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Board have also pushed the office to provide more data and evaluation of how dollars are being used. But at a February 2025 meeting, OASAS Commissioner Chinazo Cunningham deflected.
“OASAS has no oversight over these portions of dollars,” she said of the 46% of settlement money that goes directly to counties and cities. “In terms of what kind of data each county collects,” she added, “we cannot dictate exactly what that information is.”
 The top law enforcement officer
New York Attorney General Letitia James has been one of the leading national voices on prosecuting pharmaceutical companies that fueled the overdose crisis. Her office has issued dozens of press releases on the topic, touting her role in securing billions of opioid settlement dollars for the state.
But when asked about the attorney general’s role in ensuring this windfall is spent appropriately, her office passed the buck to other agencies.
“While our partners in state and local governments distribute and oversee these funds, we will continue our work to hold accountable the companies responsible for fueling the spread of addictions and overdoses,” spokesperson Grant Fox wrote in a statement.
That stance contrasts starkly with many people’s views of the office’s responsibility.
A state senator, a member of the opioid settlement advisory board, and several advocates named the attorney general’s office as a key enforcement entity.
“The money is here because of their efforts,” said Democratic state Sen. Nathalia Fernandez, who chairs the committee on alcoholism and substance use disorders and has introduced several pieces of legislation related to settlement funds. “I believe it is under the Office of the Attorney General to enforce.”
Budnella, the advocate with VOCAL-NY, agreed, saying, “It would be a shame for all of their work that they have done to secure all this funding for it to be misspent.”
Attorneys general in Michigan and Kansas have taken more active roles, issuing lists of ways opioid settlement money cannot be spent. The lists include many law enforcement expenditures that have raised concerns for advocates in New York.
James’ office did not respond to a specific question about whether she’d consider creating a similar list.
 The fiscal watchdog
Some people have suggested that the state comptroller, as a steward of New York’s finances, could play an oversight role, perhaps by conducting or requiring audits.
Early this year, the Reason Foundation, a libertarian think tank, released a model law that would create audit requirements for organizations receiving settlement cash. The blueprint suggests recipients of more than $1 million in opioid settlements be required to undergo an independent review of financial statements and transaction testing to determine whether funds were used for their intended purpose. Smaller grantees, receiving less than $1 million, could simply provide an unaudited accounting of the funds.
It’s “not telling states what is and what isn’t an appropriate use,” said Mariana Trujillo, a co-author of the Reason Foundation plan. “We’re simply trying to ensure recipients follow through with their promises.”
No state has adopted the model law yet. But the office of New York Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli told KFF Health News it is already conducting an audit.
The process, which began in February, “is looking at OASAS’ oversight” of the opioid settlement money, said spokesperson Mary Mueller. It includes settlement money controlled by the state and local governments.
Mueller said any future enforcement action “will depend on the results of our current work and our ongoing monitoring.”
The office is following in the footsteps of comptrollers and auditors in New Jersey, Missouri, and Nashville, Tennessee, who have taken action on settlement cash.
These initial steps have given some advocates and researchers hope for the future of opioid settlement dollars, which are expected to flow for more than a decade.
“We’re already years in and we’ve seen the craziest stories” of this money funding concerts and a police shooting range, said Layal Bou Harfouch, a co-author of the Reason Foundation’s model law. “If we can prevent that at least a little and have these funds be a bit more focused, I don’t think it’s too late.”
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Transportation network eyes new tax to pay for ambitious Oklahoma public transit expansion
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A transportation network plans to propose a new sales tax next year to pay for a expanded commuter rail service in the Oklahoma City metropolitan area.  The sales tax plan, which would also pay for the expansion of existing light rail and bus transit services, is expected to cost a penny per […]
text:
An Embark bus drives past the Downtown Transit Center on July 9, 2026 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A transportation network plans to propose a new sales tax next year to pay for a expanded commuter rail service in the Oklahoma City metropolitan area. 
The sales tax plan, which would also pay for the expansion of existing light rail and bus transit services, is expected to cost a penny per taxable transaction and would fund a commuter rail service connecting Oklahoma City to Edmond and Norman, among other projects, said John Sharp, deputy director over the Association of Central Oklahoma Governments. 
If approved by voters, the sales tax is expected to generate a similar amount of revenue to previous penny sales tax measures, which have generated over $130 million a year. 
It would be decided by voters living within Oklahoma, Cleveland and Canadian counties, which compose the boundaries of ONE Transit, said Armando Reyes, a spokesperson for the governmental agency. ONE Transit, formerly known as the Regional Transportation Authority of Central Oklahoma. The organization prioritizes policies increasing access to public transit in Central Oklahoma.
If passed, the tax would stay in effect as long as ONE Transit is in operation, Reyes said. 
The exact cost of the commuter rail service is not currently known as negotiations with the Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway Company continue, but it will be “one of the largest capital projects within the region to date,” Reyes said. 
ONE Transit’s plan was developed in conjunction with transit providers in Oklahoma City, Norman and Edmond and the Association of Central Oklahoma Governments. 
Services would be connected through regional corridors centered around the hub at the Santa Fe train station in downtown Oklahoma City. The north-south corridor would connect the three cities through the commuter rail. An airport corridor would be built for the light rail service. 
The transit fares for these services have not been determined yet, said Ethan Mazzio, a transportation planner for Association of Central Oklahoma Governments, a group that leads regional collaboration efforts between cities. 
The plan will focus on improving local communities through programs such as the commuter rail in the first 10 years. Larger projects, such as light rail, would come further down the line, he said.
It is the first major proposal for public transportation in the Central Oklahoma region since 2005, Mazzio said.
Opposition to the plans hasn’t emerged yet, but groups or individuals interested in keeping sales tax rates as low as possible, limiting railway traffic or keeping demand for car-oriented infrastructure as high as possible could push back as the plan gets closer to appearing on the ballot, Mazzio said.
Rail would allow for suburb-to-suburb connections that are pivotal for the growth of the Oklahoma City metropolitan area, Mazzio said. 
“People have forgotten that government can do really big things,” he said. “Things like a commuter rail could give people job opportunities between communities that they can’t currently access.”
As the Oklahoma City metropolitan area continues to grow it will be necessary to increase public transportation access to sustain that growth, said David Chapman, ONE Transit director representing Edmond.
“Oklahoma City is the largest metropolitan area without rail,” Chapman said. “(The Oklahoma City metro area is) projected to be at two million residents by 2040, so we feel like it’s critical that we have a comprehensive regional transportation system once we get to two million people.” 
It will become difficult for residents of Oklahoma City’s suburbs to access the city’s amenities as the area continues to grow, he said. 
“What really makes an area attractive to jobs, people and amenities is the metropolitan statistical area,” said Chapman. “Oklahoma City, unfortunately, is a huge city in terms of area, so the population in those suburbs, where the growth is really happening, is further out. If you look at a place like Detroit, it’s a very small city, so the suburbs are very close in. This makes it easier for them (residents) to get to the amenities, to get to the bigger city.” 
Having rail as an option to access the amenities in Oklahoma City could be necessary as traffic on the highways continues to get worse, Chapman said. 
As for bus travel, EMBARK, the company currently running the bus systems in Oklahoma City and Norman, would become part of ONE Transit. Edmond, which currently has its bus system run by Citylink, would also have the option to turn over all of its services to ONE Transit, said Chapman.
Having the bus services in all three cities run by the same company would make travel a lot more efficient, Chapman said.
Commuter rail would also be a “game changer” for Oklahoma City’s suburbs. 
“Our downtown is becoming an entertainment venue, and it is becoming a commercial destination, but you really need rail to get down there from the venues in Oklahoma City,” Chapman said.
Editor’s note: This story was produced through a reporting partnership between Oklahoma Voice and the University of Central Oklahoma’s journalism program.

title: Rich politicians loaning money to their own campaigns puts the average Oklahoman’s interests at risk
description: “Be afraid. Be very afraid” seems like a fitting slogan for Oklahoma elections this year. While the tagline first originated in 1986 horror movie “The Fly”, it’s a relevant warning for all Oklahomans watching their election system be hijacked by wealthy candidates who loan their campaigns copious amounts of money. The Oklahoman analyzed campaign finance […]
text:
A roll of money is pictured. (Photo by Getty Images)“Be afraid. Be very afraid” seems like a fitting slogan for Oklahoma elections this year.
While the tagline first originated in 1986 horror movie “The Fly”, it’s a relevant warning for all Oklahomans watching their election system be hijacked by wealthy candidates who loan their campaigns copious amounts of money.
The Oklahoman analyzed campaign finance reports filed through June and found that Oklahoma candidates reported loaning themselves a combined $27.5 million.
Even more alarming, nearly 40% of those personal loans have been assumed by one candidate — Republican gubernatorial hopeful Mike Mazzei, who also happens to be President Donald Trump’s pick for the office.
Ahead of the June primary election, Mazzei reported loaning himself over $10.8 million, using his business assets as collateral, The Oklahoman reported. By that time, he’d only raised about $650,000 from donors.
Mazzei’s opponent in the Aug. 25 primary runoff election, state Attorney General Gentner Drummond had loaned himself $3 million while raising $3.8 million, campaign finance reports showed.
Big spending might seem like business as usual in U.S. elections, which have gotten increasingly expensive following a 2010 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that has allowed unlimited campaign spending by outside groups.
But personal loans, particularly the gigantic ones accumulated by Mazzei, should set off alarms.
We’re still months away from the contested general election, and his campaign has already far outpaced the amount Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt loaned himself eight years ago. 
Stitt, who boasts he’s a self-made millionaire, loaned himself $4.9 million in his 2018 gubernatorial campaign and $2 million when running for his second term in 2022.
Early on while I was still learning the ins and outs of campaign finance, I used to shrug my shoulders at personal loans. After all, the common perception is when you’re starting a business or a new hobby, sometimes you have to be your biggest cheerleader and be willing to invest in yourself.
But doing the people’s work isn’t starting your own business.
The dirty secret tied to affluent politicians who loan their own money to their campaigns is that if they win, they generally expect to one day recoup those expenses.
While business owners recoup their investments from customers and sales, in politics, everyday Oklahomans generally don’t have the cash flow to foot the bill for $10 million personal loans.
You know who has deep pockets?
Lobbyists, political action committees and other groups with connections generally aren’t pitching in thousands of dollars because they’re good-natured philanthropists.
Most are likely handing candidates money in hopes of swaying the decisions made by elected officials or having a public official on speed dial when things aren’t going well.
That’s why traditionally the losing candidates, who loan themselves money, rarely recoup their losses and wind up writing off their loans as a cost of doing business.
High personal loan spending in state politics could kick the door wide open for dark money to run our state.
Don’t believe me? Here are a couple of hypotheticals of how special interests could factor in:
— Want to hike the costs of utilities again? It would sure be handy to have the ear (and goodwill) of an Oklahoma Corporation Commissioner, who decides the fate of such requests.
In fact, an Oklahoma Voice analysis of campaign finance data from 2018 through mid-year 2024 found that commissioners accepted hundreds of thousands of dollars from the same businesses that we task them with regulating. It’s perfectly legal, but it sure raises some pesky ethical questions about whether there’s preferential treatment or access.
— What happens if the insurance industry doesn’t like a bill that the Legislature advances to help homeowners facing some of the highest costs in the nation? An industry lobbyist or executive who has an “in” with the governor or insurance commissioner might find it useful to pick up the phone and press him to veto or intervene. (We were one of your supporters, they might gently remind them.)
And, I don’t know about you, but I find myself suspicious of a candidate’s motives when they spend millions more of their personal funds than they stand to make in that public office. A four-year stay in the governor’s mansion, for instance, pays $185,000 a year. Due to eight-year term limits, the most a winner can expect to make is $1.48 million.
But even more alarming is that the growing practice of candidates loaning themselves enormous amounts of money makes it impossible for average people to launch a successful campaign for statewide office regardless of what great ideas they might have to Make Oklahoma Great Again, to borrow Stitt’s catchphrase. 
It may only be a matter of time before we start seeing that mentality trickle down to state House and Senate races.
Lobbyists, political action committees and dark money are the winners in Oklahoma right now.
If our lawmakers cannot find a way to level that playing field – perhaps by capping how much candidates can loan themselves – Oklahomans will find their voices further relegated to the sidelines.

title: Don’t Let Fraud and Scams Ground Your Summer Vacation
description: As you make your summer travel plans this year, or perhaps you’ve already hit the road or you’re on your way to the airport, one thing to keep in mind – without putting too much of a damper on your trip – is to stay financially vigilant when finalizing your vacation plans. The travel and […]
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
As you make your summer travel plans this year, or perhaps you’ve already hit the road or you’re on your way to the airport, one thing to keep in mind – without putting too much of a damper on your trip – is to stay financially vigilant when finalizing your vacation plans.
The travel and events sector is especially susceptible for fraud and scams as people are looking for deals in locations that might be unfamiliar, with bad actors savvier than ever when it comes to separating travelers from their money. Once travelers figure out their plans, they’re ready to hand over the funds to make their dream vacations happen – and scammers are more than happy to take it.
Theresa Horne, Chase Community Manager in Jackson, Mississippi, offers these tips to help you avoid the latest and most common travel scams so you can relax and enjoy your trip.
Vacation rental scams
So you’ve found a great house on a vacation rental website and email the property through the website. You might have received a call back from the “owner,” who asked you to send your deposit through Zelle or another peer-to-peer app. The “owner” will often pressure you into sending a deposit to hold the property, saying there’s a lot of demand for the location, and may ask to move the conversation from the official website to a private messaging app
As your trip gets closer, you might reach out to confirm the details or assume all is well and travel to the property at the start of your trip. That’s when you discover the location is already booked, not available to rent or doesn’t exist at all.  
The listing you saw could have been fake, or a fake phone number was posted to a real listing, and the true owner has no idea about your reservation. Either way, you’re stuck without lodging and your payment, with little chance of getting your money back.
Most major property rental sites offer fraud guarantees, but only if you pay and communicate with the owners through the site. To avoid lodging scams, try to see properties in person if possible, read reviews from other travelers, and pay through the official platform.. Sending deposits through wire transfers or P2P apps is like sending cash — once you send it you may not be able to get it back.
“Free” trips
Unless you’ve won a legitimate contest or sweepstakes – and even those should be examined – there’s no such thing as a free vacation. If you get a call, text, email or other notification that you’ve won a free vacation, it may be a scam, especially if you don’t remember entering a contest.
Watch out for automated calls or texts offering free vacations or “vacation deals.” There may not be a vacation package available at all, or you’ll be asked to pay processing fees, taxes and other costs to claim your “free” trip, which might include substandard accommodations.
If you did enter a contest and are told you’re the winner, you won’t be asked to send money to claim your prize. The Federal Trade Commission is a good resource for information on recognizing legitimate versus fraudulent contests.
Flight scams
If you hear about a charter flight or other private flight deal to a destination, sometimes including a tour or hotel stay, be extra careful. Too many would-be travelers find out after paying their money that the flight, and sometimes the entire trip, is nonexistent.
The U.S. Department of Transportation maintains updated lists of approved charter flights so you can make sure the company you’re considering is legitimate.
Concert/event ticket scams
The event ticket industry is ripe for scammers. You might find an amazing deal for a sold-out show on social media, send money to the seller and never hear from them again. Not only do you not have concert tickets, there’s also no way to get your money back.
While some social media sellers might be legitimate, the best sources for ticket deals are verified resale sites that handle transactions and guarantee authenticity. If something goes wrong, there’s a digital “paper trail” that can help you get your money back.
Reminders 
While even the most prepared consumers can fall victim to a well-executed scam, remember these tips to protect your vacation plans.

Zelleand other P2P payment apps should be reserved for family, friends and businesses you know and trust. Treat your transactions like cash — once scammers get the money, you may not get it back.
Scammers are advertising on social media and social marketplaces. Whenever possible, shop through official websites and be cautious of deals that seem too good to be true before sending any money.
Scammers can make caller ID, emails and texts display as messages from your bank or other businesses. If you are ever unsure, end the conversation and reach out to the company directly through their official website or call the number on the back of your card

title: Supporting mental health care is not ‘woke.’ It’s the Wyoming way.
description:
Rep. Cody Wylie asks, “When did Wyoming become a place that backs away from a problem just because the answer is hard?”
The post Supporting mental health care is not ‘woke.’ It’s the Wyoming way. appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Every election cycle, candidates make their rounds and talk about the issues they think matter most. This year, one of the things I have heard over and over again at people’s doors, at meet-and-greets, at community events and in everyday conversations across Wyoming is the topic of mental health.

Opinion

Not as a talking point or some trendy issue of the month — as a real problem affecting real Wyoming families. 
I have heard from parents worried about their kids. I have heard from people who have watched friends, coworkers or family members struggle. And like many Wyomingites, I have been touched personally by the kind of tragedy that can come when someone loses their battle with mental health.
That is why I get frustrated when I hear people try to turn mental health into another cheap political argument. Somehow, if you support doing something about it, you are “liberal.” If you think Wyoming should invest in treatment, access or prevention, you’re called “woke.” If you believe we should at least try to help people before they end up in crisis, suddenly you are soft or reckless with taxpayer money.
I do not buy that for a second.
There is nothing “liberal” about believing a Wyoming kid should be able to get help before anxiety or depression takes over their life. There is nothing “woke” about wanting a veteran, a rancher, an oilfield hand, a teacher or a young mother to have somewhere to turn before things spiral out of
control. And there is nothing “conservative” about shrugging your shoulders at a problem this serious and pretending the answer is to do nothing because solving it might cost money.
Mental health is not a slogan. It is not a culture war issue. It is not something to be mocked because it does not fit neatly into somebody’s political brand. It is a real challenge in a state where isolation is real, access to care is limited and too many families know exactly what it feels like to get a phone call they can never take back.
Now, I am not naive enough to pretend there is a silver bullet here. There is not. Mental health is complicated. Suicide prevention is complicated. Some programs will work better than others. Some investments will pay off, and some will need to be fixed or replaced. That is the truth.
But since when did Wyoming become a place that backs away from a problem just because the answer is hard?
If someone in your family had cancer, would you tell them treatment was too expensive, too uncertain or too politically inconvenient? Would you say, “Well, there is no guarantee this works, so I guess we should just save the money”? Of course not. You would fight for every option, every treatment and every chance to keep that person here.
That is how I look at mental health.
We are not guaranteed a perfect solution, but every Wyomingite ought to be guaranteed a chance. A chance to get help. A chance to be heard. A chance to find treatment before it is too late. A chance to stay here for their family, their kids and the people who love them.
I have said before that if we can save even one life, it is worth the investment. I still believe that. Not because I think government can solve everything. It cannot. Not because I think every dollar spent automatically means success. It does not. But because I know doing nothing has a cost, too. In this case, that cost is measured in funerals, broken families and lives that could have gone differently if someone had gotten help in time.
Want to have a conversation about accountability? Good. We should. Want to make sure money is spent wisely and programs actually work? I am all for it. That is our job. But there is a big difference between demanding accountability and using words like “woke” or “liberal” as an excuse to avoid the issue altogether.
That is not leadership. That is laziness.
Wyoming has never been at its best when we sit around pointing fingers and congratulating ourselves for saying no. We are at our best when we face problems head on, trust our communities and get to work. We do not need to copy every bad idea from Washington and we do not need a blank check approach, either. What we need is the same thing Wyoming has always needed: common sense, local leadership, strong families and the willingness to tackle hard problems without turning everything into a political performance.
If you want to represent Wyoming’s future — especially the future of our kids, — then you ought to have the backbone to say this clearly: Mental health matters, and helping people is not weakness.
It is not “woke” to care whether kids in our communities can get help before they fall through the cracks. It is not “liberal” to think a struggling father, a stressed-out mother or a teenager in crisis deserves a shot at getting better. It is not reckless to believe Wyoming should do what it can to keep its people alive.
That is not a left-wing value. That is not a right-wing value.
That is a Wyoming value.
The post Supporting mental health care is not ‘woke.’ It’s the Wyoming way. appeared first on WyoFile .

title: The Wyoming Freedom Caucus exists for the people
description:
Despite a statewide movement to oust the Freedom Caucus from the Legislature, we will continue to fight for the rights of Wyomingites, writes Rep. Joe Webb.
The post The Wyoming Freedom Caucus exists for the people appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Recently, I sat in the living room of some politically active community members that I have known for several years. They shared with me what they feel is the greatest threat to Wyoming’s future. 

Opinion

It was not the anti-energy policies of the Democratic Party, driven by the Biden administration, which have nearly destroyed Wyoming’s economy, costing our state billions of dollars in revenue. 
It wasn’t the strain on our water resources posed by new tech industries. 
It was not about the coastal states blocking exports of clean, beautiful Wyoming coal to Pacific markets. 
It wasn’t even about the democratic socialist movement in America. 
To these people, the greatest threat to Wyoming is a group of locally elected legislators who fight to put money back into the hands of taxpayers, place control back into the hands of parents and restore confidence in our elections. 
They looked me in the eyes and told me the biggest threat to the state’s future is the Wyoming Freedom Caucus. They said “we” are doing everything possible this election — statewide — to oust the Freedom Caucus from the Legislature. To me, this is an organized, statewide movement. 
On Independence Day, the thought and feeling hit me that I have never been prouder to be a member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus and the people associated with it. 
After huge property tax increases, we are fighting to keep money in your pocket. 
After millions of illegal aliens entered our country under the Biden administration, we worked hard to protect your voice by requiring proof of citizenship and proof of Wyoming residency to vote in Wyoming elections. We also banned illegal aliens from driving on our highways. 
We stood up to protect women’s sports and spaces, even after our governor called such measures  “draconian” and “discriminatory.” 
But according to these folks, fighting for these basic conservative values poses a greater threat to Wyoming than the left-leaning actors who are actively trying to destroy Wyoming and our country. 
We will continue the fight for parental rights, tax reform, government transparency, streamlined infrastructure funding and more. The Freedom Caucus exists for the people of Wyoming.

title: Idaho’s honor flight organizations need our support to thank our veterans for our freedom
description: Honor Flight Boise is scheduled to make its inaugural trip to the nation’s capital Oct. 3-5, and Patrick Teixeira – a World War II veteran – says he can hardly wait. He will join about 25 other war veterans, from World War II to Vietnam, giving them an opportunity to see the memorials and share […]
text:
Patrick Teixeira will join about 25 other war veterans, from World War II to Vietnam, giving them an opportunity to see the Washington, D.C., memorials and share experiences. (Photo by Chuck Malloy)Honor Flight Boise is scheduled to make its inaugural trip to the nation’s capital Oct. 3-5, and Patrick Teixeira – a World War II veteran – says he can hardly wait.
He will join about 25 other war veterans, from World War II to Vietnam, giving them an opportunity to see the memorials and share experiences.
The 97-year-old Army veteran has gone most of his life not thinking about rewards that went with military service. Most of his post-war focus was on raising five kids, all of whom are living happily. But now he thinks he has earned this trip down memory lane, and those associated with Honor Flight fully agree.
“People should remember World War II,” he said. “I don’t think there is anybody who is left from the World War II era who say were there at the beginning (he was in Hawaii when Pearl Harbor was attacked on Dec. 7, 1941) and cleaned up at the end (at Hiroshima).” 
He was 12 years old on that fateful day in 1941, but he wasn’t thinking about the magnitude from his mountainside viewpoint.
“I was thinking, ‘Whoa, look at the fire,’” he said. “At 15, I tried to enlist, but I was refused because I was too young. But I wanted to enlist and do my part.”
He took a civilian job at Pearl Harbor and successfully enlisted for a three-year stint when he was 17. He was honorably discharged in 1949.
Honor Flight Boise, which serves counties in Southwest Idaho, is one of three hubs in Idaho. The Southeastern Idaho group, based in Pocatello, will have its inaugural flight on Sept. 1-2 for nearly 50 veterans. The Inland Northwest Honor Flight, based in Spokane and includes North Idaho, has been in operation since 2009. More than 3,000 veterans have gone to the nation’s capital over those years, and about 100 are scheduled to fly out Oct. 13-14.
The cost of the flights are not cheap, and the three nonprofits are on their own as far as raising funds. Julie Crider, executive director of Honor Flight Boise, estimates it will cost $100,000 for its trip.  
Photina Haumschilt, the board president and executive director of the Eastern Idaho Honor Flight, says Anheuser-Busch, is paying for the veterans to take the flight. From there, the organization relies on private donations and money raised from an annual fundraiser called “Legacy of Honor.”
Linda Peters, board secretary for Inland Northwest, says a golf event and gala (casino night) are the major fundraising events. From there, she says, “We beg for it … we have amazing volunteers.”
And what a way to honor veterans as America celebrates its 250th birthday. World War II and Korean War veterans are dwindling in numbers, and many of the Vietnam veterans have bitter memories about their homecomings.
“I’ve heard so many stories, and some are reluctant to make the honor flights because of that, said Haumschilt. “I know of one who remembers the smell of being pelted with rotten tomatoes and a head of cabbage being thrown to his head.”
Receptions are far different with the honor flights, she says.
Peters says she’s been on a about a dozen flights. “I love it. My heart is in it. It’s such a humbling experience, and such a pleasure to tell them what they have done and what their service has meant to us.”
Crider is a native and former resident of San Diego, where the military is part of the community’s lifeblood. Her husband, Clark, served 20 years in the Army.
“I’ve watched honor flights in San Diego for 15 years, and I’ve seen many military homecomings. I became interested in the Honor Flight program when I was there, and I thought it would be good to start one here when we moved in 2025,” she said. “It’s a labor of love for me, and I will be thrilled when we make this first flight. I think it all will be easier after that.”
And, hopefully, this will be the start of a long tradition.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Family demands answers after Memphis Task Force agent kills man at Burger King
description: The family of a man killed by an officer with the Memphis Safe Task Force is calling for a swift and public accounting of the May 13 shooting. Darrin Pigram, 41, was working the breakfast shift at a Burger King when he was shot and killed at about 9:30 a.m. by a Drug Enforcement Administration […]
text:
MEMPHIS, TN - July 16, 2026: Melvin Pigram, Darrin Pigram’s younger brother, at Darrin’s memorial near the Burger King where he was killed by a member of the Memphis Safe Taskforce. The May 13 fatal shooting of Darrin Pigram, 44, was by a Drug Enforcement Agency officer assigned to the task force. (Photo: Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)
The family of a man killed by an officer with the Memphis Safe Task Force is calling for a swift and public accounting of the May 13 shooting.
Darrin Pigram, 41, was working the breakfast shift at a Burger King when he was shot and killed at about 9:30 a.m. by a Drug Enforcement Administration officer serving a warrant, according to a brief description of the incident by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, which investigates officer-involved shootings. 
Pigram was shot eight times inside the restaurant as horrified coworkers looked on, according to Andre Wharton, the family’s attorney, citing communications with the Shelby County district attorney. 
A TBI statement said the officer fired after Pigram “reached for a gun in his waistband.” 
Melvin Pigram, Darrin’s Pigram’s 33-year-old brother, said his family does not trust the official account. He said it does not square with restaurant video footage viewed by the family in the offices of the Shelby County district attorney.
“Me and my family are still seeking answers on what the officer did and why they took the actions they did versus apprehending my brother,” Melvin Pigram said. 
“My brother should be here. He wasn’t out on a shooting spree or anything like that. He was at work.”
Man fatally shot in second Memphis Safe Task Force use-of-force incident this week

None of the footage screened by the family shows Darrin Pigram reaching for or holding a gun, he said. Wharton, the family attorney, confirmed Melvin Pigram’s description of the video.
The footage included several angles captured by restaurant cameras. Because the cameras are stationary, there are gaps in the footage as interactions between Darrin Pigram and the officers shifted out of view, Wharton said.
What the family could see was Darrin Pigram opening the door separating the counter from the public restaurant space, then backing away as an officer reached for him, Melvin Pigram said.
“The video my family saw did not show my brother reaching for a gun or posing a threat toward the officer,” Melvin Pigram said. “We were so confused with the footage we watched and how they could come up with … that story behind it.”
Officials have not revealed whether a gun was retrieved from the restaurant. Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy did not respond last week to a message seeking information about the incident, and a spokesperson for the TBI said the agency does not comment on ongoing investigations.
“We are trying to get some clear answers on the firearm, if one was recovered, including where it was recovered from,” Wharton said. 
Wharton said his own investigation into the shooting “remains steadfast and ongoing, including seeking full transparency on the entire sequence of events.” 
Four fatal shootings in two months
Pigram’s was the first in four fatal shootings over a two-month span by members of the task force, established “to smash the grip of the violent criminals on this iconic American city,” President Donald Trump said during a visit to Memphis earlier this year.
With 2,700 personnel — 1,450 Tennessee National Guard and hundreds of agents from 13 federal agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security and the U.S. Marshals Service — the Task Force is now the largest single law enforcement entity in Tennessee. 
Since its launch in September, use-of-force incidents by the task force have surpassed those committed by any other state or local law enforcement agency in Tennessee. 
Of 18 fatal shootings by officers in 2026, the task force has been responsible for four.
One week after Pigram’s death, 25-year-old Jonah Neal was fatally shot by a Homeland Security Investigations officer, according to TBI. Neal’s mother told NPR she called 911 after her son threatened suicide. A TBI statement said task force agents found multiple weapons and that it wasn’t clear “whether Neal died as a result of the agent firing upon him or if it was self-inflicted stab wounds.”
National Guard troops on patrol in Memphis fatally shoot 20-year-old man,  according to TBI

Tyrin Johnson, 20, died July 5 after two Tennessee National Guard members opened fire while chasing him on foot after he allegedly brandished a gun, according to the TBI. 
Four days later, Alfonso Ivy, 47, was fatally shot in a Memphis hotel after allegedly pointing a handgun at officers serving a warrant for felony drug charges, a statement by TBI said. All four men killed were Black.
Task force officers have been involved in at least three other non-fatal incidents involving use-of-force: two shootings and one instance in which a task force officer hit a suspect with his vehicle, according to the TBI. 
The violence has prompted community outrage. The NAACP, in a letter to acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, asked for a “thorough, transparent federal investigation.” 
Calling the task force a “dangerous operation,” the NAACP demanded its immediate suspension.
Shootings raise questions about training, culture
Wharton said the incidents raise questions about the training and culture of the task force. He’s also representing Johnson’s family.
“The question that remains is: What was the strategy employed by the task force when they came? What were their dictates, their boundaries?” he said. “Was this framed as a war on Memphis?”
“Because without the right guardrails and parameters, it can create reckless encounters by folks who may not be familiar with the local citizenry. That can be concerning when you’re having these interactions, when you’re serving warrants, when you’re making sudden arrests,” he said.
Lauren Bonds, executive director for the National Police Accountability Project, said federal law enforcement officers are generally “ill-equipeed and poorly trained” to do the work of local police. 
Bonds cited recent fatal shootings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Texas and Maine, and past deployments of National Guard and federal officers to Los Angeles, Chicago and Washington, D.C.
“We’ve seen federal deployments in other contexts, whether that’s ICE surges, whether that’s the National Guard presence in D.C., and I think one of the common things we’re seeing across the board is more misconduct,” she said. “I think that really speaks to the fact that policing is local for a reason, and there’s a misfit between the skill set of federal law enforcement and rank-and-file policing duties.”
‘That’s not who my brother was’
Melvin Pigram said his family’s grief has been compounded by terse official statements about his brother.
In a statement, the DEA described Darrin Pigram as “armed and dangerous, with a violent criminal history.”  
MEMPHIS, TN – July 16, 2026: Melvin Pigram, Darrin Pigram’s younger brother, shows one of his brother’s funeral programs while at Darrin’s memorial near the Burger King where he was shot and killed by a member of the Memphis Safe Taskforce. (Photo: Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)
Shelby County court records show Pigram has a single misdemeanor conviction in Memphis. He pleaded guilty last year to assault after he threatened to harm his stepfather during an argument, according to the documents.
On the day he was killed, task force officers were serving a warrant for aggravated assault, aggravated burglary and employing a firearm in the commission of a felony. 
The charges stem from an accusation that Pigram threatened neighbors with a firearm over loud music in January, court records show.
Melvin Pigram said his brother was not a violent man. He was a hard worker who had just been promoted to shift lead at Burger King, responsible for working with the manager to open the store. He was an artist. He loved to play golf and spend time with nieces and nephews.
“Every time you hear about a killing with the task force, it’s always some ‘armed criminal.’ It’s always the same story, different person,” he said. “That’s not who my brother was.”
Pigram said his family wants to see the officer who shot his brother fired.
“We want the officer’s badge removed so he cannot do this to anyone else and so no other family has to experience the pain my family is going through,” he said.
