name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabamians are facing more debt collections lawsuits than ever, says report
description: A study published last week found debt lawsuits in Alabama reached their highest level in 2025, affecting some of the most vulnerable people in the state. The study by Pew Charitable Trusts, with analysis from January Advisors, found about 108,308 collection lawsuits were filed in the state last year, a 140% increase over 2019. “And […]
text:
Six percent of adults — 16 million people — in the United States have debt above $1,000, according to KFF's 2022 analysis. Debt collectors are filing an increasing number of lawsuits in state courts to force people to repay their outstanding obligations, according to a July study. (Getty Images)A study published last week found debt lawsuits in Alabama reached their highest level in 2025, affecting some of the most vulnerable people in the state.
The study by Pew Charitable Trusts, with analysis from January Advisors, found about 108,308 collection lawsuits were filed in the state last year, a 140% increase over 2019.
“And that is the highest number we have seen recorded in Alabama data, as far as debt collection lawsuits go, going back to 2010 when the state website was tracking this data,” said Lester Bird, senior manager for the courts and communities project at Pew Charitable Trusts.
“The core driver behind the rise in litigation is a systemic breakdown in communication. Litigation is typically a last resort, pursued only after cooperative outreach has been exhausted and primarily with consumers who can pay but choose not to engage,” ACA International said in a statement on Sunday, a trade organization that represents debt collection agencies.
That figure accounts for debt collection lawsuits, many of which are medical debts and credit cards, and they have increased significantly since 2023, according to experts. Although the data did not separately aggregate the different types of lawsuits, the data shows debt filings went from about 54,000 in 2023 to more than 108,000 last year as it reached its high-water mark.
The Pew Charitable Trusts study shows that most debt collection lawsuits account for medical debts and credit cards. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
“The people who are most vulnerable are people of color, primarily Black Americans for a range of systemic racist laws, women with children because kids are so expensive – daycare is more than some people earn in a month,” said Deborah Thorne, a professor of sociology at the University of Idaho. “Seniors, and people who are sick with chronic illnesses.”
Some majority-Black counties saw major increases based on the data from the Office of the Courts and an analysis from the Alabama Reflector. In Greene County, where Black Alabamians comprise about 81% of the population, the number of debt collection filings jumped 500% from 2010 to 2025. Sumter County, with a Black population of 73%, saw the number of debt filings go from 43 in 2010 to 242 in 2025, an increase of 463%.
Majority-white counties also saw increases. In Cleburne County, with a population that is almost 93% white, filings went from 219 to 309, an increase of 41%. In Winston County, where 91% of residents are white, filings increased by 82%.
The suits have also become a greater share of all civil cases filed in the state. In 2023, debt collections accounted for about one-quarter of all cases. Last year, they took up about 38% of the nearly 290,000 civil claims filed in the state, according to the Alabama Administrative Office of the Courts website.
The increases happening in Alabama mimic a trend unfolding across the country, Bird said.
Alabama had the fourth-highest increase in debt collection suits among the eight states that Pew and January Advisors studied. No. 1 was Missouri, where numbers have jumped 188% since 2019, according to the study. The next highest state was Texas at 177%, then Massachusetts at 153%, followed by Alabama.
“It does seem like a pretty significant increase in at least several of these states, going up 25%, 50%, 75% in just a few years,” said Daniel Wilf-Townsend, an associate professor of law at Georgetown University. “It certainly seems like a significant rise to me.”
Before the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, civil claims for debt collection had been increasing in state courts. Claims were relatively stable for a few years after but started rising again in 2023.
Wilf-Townsend said increases in debt collection filings could be due to people falling further into debt, collection agencies pursuing debts more aggressively or procedural changes.
The amount of outstanding credit card debt, one of the main components for debt collection filings, have continued to increase. According to the New York Federal Reserve Bank’s Household Debt and Credit Report, U.S. households had about $819 billion in aggregate credit card balances at the end of 2020. It increased to $1.28 trillion at the end of 2025, an increase of about 56%.
Robert Lawless, a professor at the University of Illinois College of Law, said that the number of lawsuits regarding debt collection increased because of technology.
“Part of it is that it is also easier to track what people owe, and to track people,” he said. “Debt collection has also been more specialized. It makes more business sense to pursue cases that maybe 25 years ago would not have been worth it.”
Many of the companies who sue over debt are not the original creditors. Many times, other firms purchase the unpaid amount from the original creditor who will then own the claim.
“The car lender will sell that claim to a debt buyer, who will pay pennies on the dollar,” Lawless said. “The debt buyer buys a $2,000 claim for $200. The debt buyer is betting that it can collect more than $200. These sell cheaply because it is a truism that you can’t get blood out of a stone.”
Debt collection agencies purchase a collection of debts and spread the risk across an amalgam of debtors.
ACA International said the reason for the increase in litigation comes from a breakdown in communication between creditors and debtors. The hurdles come from regulatory barriers imposed by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, credit reporting limits and misinformation.
“Social-media ‘finfluencers’ often tell consumers to ignore legitimate outreach,” the statement said.
The organization also said laws are already in place to protect debtors from having their assets seized.
“The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act requires collectors to provide written validation notices, prohibits harassment and deceptive practices, and gives consumers the right to dispute debts and request verification,” ACA International said in the statement.
“If you specialize in auto loan deficiencies, you have a pretty good sense of what is collected in the end,” Lawless said.
The process is also steep in legalese, and debtors may not understand what they need to do with the court. The report from Pew states that less than 4% of defendants have an attorney to assist with their cases. Other times, consumers are entitled to protections that they may not receive.
Some states protect some of the money in people’s bank accounts, or funds are protected if they come from specific sources, such as Social Security payments and veterans’ benefits.
Delaware law does not allow debt collectors to garnish money from people’s bank accounts because of a lawsuit. Other states, such as California, limit the amount that debt collectors can take.
“But often, in order for those protections to apply, the defendant has to go to the court and affirmatively assert them,” Wilf-Townsend said. “So, if the person doesn’t know those protections exist, then the person doesn’t end up being able to get the benefit of them.”
A man who had kidney surgery displays some of his medical bills at his home in Temple Hills, Md., in June 2023. Medical debt is one of the main reasons that people are in debt and collectors file lawsuits to recover money owed. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)
The National Center for Access to Justice at Fordham University reviewed the rules established in 50 states and Washington, D.C., and created a ranking for how well they promote fairness when people are being sued over alleged debt.
No state earned even a passing grade, but the nation’s capital ranked the best with a score of 58 out of 100. Alabama placed 9th with a score of 32.
Alabama received a higher score in the index because some of its laws gives consumers some protection from debt collectors. For example, Alabama does not require consumers to pay a fee when they file court paperwork in response to a lawsuit filed by a debt collector. The state also received a higher mark because it requires debt collectors to provide banks with a court order before seeking to garnish people’s money.
“While Alabama was 9th on the list, which is high relative to some states, it is still well below a passing score,” said David Udell, executive director of the National Center for Access to Justice. “And that low score of 32 signals that there are many safeguards that can be incorporated into state law that make the process fairer, but that Alabama does not yet have in place.”
The center recommends that Alabama establish pleading requirements mandating debt collectors who file lawsuits to state the name of the original creditor, enabling courts and defendants to learn the origin of the claimed debt; their standing in the case, enabling courts and defendants to determine if the plaintiff is legally entitled to bring the suit; and an itemized list of the charges that remain outstanding, enabling courts and defendants to understand the amounts claimed.
Other recommendations include rules ensuring the debt is actually valid, and that Alabama automatically protect enough weekly income from wage garnishment to keep a family of four above the federal poverty level.
The Pew report recommended protecting people’s bank accounts, ensuring that people have the correct information about the debts in the lawsuit and adequate notification about litigation.
“Some of the fixes are not going to come from the legal system. They are going to have to come from our economic-employment system,” Wilf-Townsend said. “Debt is not just a problem of litigation. It is also a problem of social organization, economic organization, and income security and income inequality. It is also going to have to happen with policy measures to improve people’s income and their income security.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC budget offers rural childcare businesses financial help they’ve sought for years
description: It’s been a difficult year for Mary Moody, owner of the top-rated Silver Bluff Kids Early Learning Center in Haywood County. She said her business has struggled since federal pandemic funds used to keep childcare centers open ran out in 2025.  Moody didn’t want to cut staff salaries after the federal money ran out, she […]
text:
The NC budget raises subsidy rates for rural childcare providers. (Photo: Getty Images) It’s been a difficult year for Mary Moody, owner of the top-rated Silver Bluff Kids Early Learning Center in Haywood County. She said her business has struggled since federal pandemic funds used to keep childcare centers open ran out in 2025. 
Moody didn’t want to cut staff salaries after the federal money ran out, she said in an email, but avoiding wage cuts and paying higher operational costs meant the center had to end contributions to retirement plans and employee health insurance reimbursements “because the money simply wasn’t there.”
The center also had to cut back on art and craft supplies and some activities. 
The new state budget tosses a financial life preserver to rural businesses like Moody’s that provide subsidized childcare, offering them some hope of stability after a long period of hardship.
The budget commits $97 million in federal funds to raise subsidy rates, and it also sets a minimum rate, called a “rate floor,” that will end up sending more money to rural childcare providers than they otherwise would have received. Subsidies help low-income families cover childcare costs. 
“This is what we have been begging for for years,” said Mandy Mills, executive director of the Southwestern Child Development Commission.
Rural providers collect fewer subsidy dollars per child than urban providers. Payments are based on market rate studies, as well as the quality of the childcare center or home and the age of the child. 
Rural providers have argued for years that the rates they’ve been paid fall far below their actual costs. 
Mills’ commission administers subsidies for 14 western counties and operates the childcare resource and referral service for 37 counties. The rate floor will make a huge difference in rural western countries, she said. 
“It’s going to be a game changer,” she said. “We have had programs closing right and left.”
It’s not just childcare providers who called for a rate floor. Child advocates and businesses did, too. The NC Chamber Foundation called the rate floor a “breakthrough” and “the single most consequential childcare provision in the budget.”
Establishing a rate floor was also a top recommendation from Gov. Josh Stein’s Task Force on Child Care and Early Education. 
Rural centers and home-based childcare operators that had been struggling are in line for significant increases.
A top-rated, five-star center in Randolph County receives a $867 subsidy per month for each infant, said Leanna Martin, director of early childhood education policy and research at NC Child. Starting in October, that same center will see subsidies increase by $500 a month for each infant.
‘Distraught and pissed off’: Businesses, providers sound alarm over cracks in NC child care industry

In another example, reimbursements for five-star home-based care for 3- to 5-year-olds in Alleghany County will increase from $407 per month to $900 a month. 
The hope is that childcare options will expand in rural areas, with the increased payments encouraging centers and homes to accept more children. 
“When reimbursements were so low, they were losing so much money,” Martin said. 
There’s a tremendous need for infant care, but costs for providers are higher for babies because childcare centers need one staff member for every five babies. Staff-to-child ratios are higher for older children. 
Centers throughout western North Carolina closed classrooms because they could not hire or keep enough staff, said Mills. When centers needed to cut back, infant care was the first thing to go. 
Moody at Silver Bluff Kids is anxious to restore employee benefits and hire a new teacher. 
“The subsidy rate floor will, number one, allow us to avoid the big financial burden we have had. It will allow us to reinstate either a health insurance policy or a health insurance reimbursement plan with higher reimbursement rates than we were previously able to contribute to employees’ insurance. We will also contribute again to the staff’s retirement plans,” Moody said. 
The center is fully enrolled with 54 children. Moody couldn’t afford to hire a new teacher, so she and the assistant director have been filling in. Moody said she spends her nights and weekends doing paperwork. 
“The rate floor, in my opinion, will allow centers to thrive,” she said. “ I think it will be a game-changer for retaining highly qualified staff and recruiting additional staff. This investment will allow many centers like ours to continue providing the high-quality care we are known for, without the financial stress of trying to figure out how to fit it all into the budget creatively.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Democratic nominees for Congress​ in Colorado outraise Republican rivals
description: Colorado’s Democratic nominees for Congress have outraised their Republican rivals by more than a 2-to-1 margin in the 2026 election cycle, Federal Election Commission data shows. But some Democratic candidates are entering the general election season in better financial shape than others. As Democrats look to regain control of the House of Representatives,[...]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, left, and Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel, right. (Colorado Newsline photos)Colorado’s Democratic nominees for Congress have outraised their Republican rivals by more than a 2-to-1 margin in the 2026 election cycle, Federal Election Commission data shows. But some Democratic candidates are entering the general election season in better financial shape than others.
As Democrats look to regain control of the House of Representatives, all four of Colorado’s incumbent Republican members of Congress have drawn well-funded challengers this year. By contrast, the House delegation’s four Democratic incumbents have so far drawn only token opposition from candidates who have reported little or no fundraising activity to the FEC.
In Colorado’s 8th District, the state’s top battleground seat, an expensive head-to-head primary contest has put Democrats at a steep financial disadvantage to begin the general election. State Rep. Manny Rutinel of Commerce City spent more than $3.7 million on his way to a landslide victory over former state Rep. Shannon Bird of Westminster in the June 30 primary election.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Though he outraised Bird throughout the primary, Rutinel had a little over $600,000 remaining in cash on hand at the end of June, according to FEC reports. That’s less than one-sixth of the funds held by incumbent GOP Rep. Gabe Evans, the first-term Republican whom Rutinel is hoping to unseat in November.
Evans has amassed the largest campaign war chest of any Colorado GOP candidate, entering the general election with more than $3.8 million in cash on hand. Despite winning his seat by fewer than 2,500 votes in 2024, Evans who has aligned himself closely with House Speaker Mike Johnson and President Donald Trump and is ranked as one of the country’s most vulnerable Republican House incumbents.
The 8th District spans from Denver’s northern suburbs into parts of southern Weld and Larimer counties.
In the 5th District, centered on Colorado Springs, Democrat Jessica Killin, an Army veteran and political operative, also prevailed in a head-to-head Democratic primary last month, defeating opponent Joe Reagan by 22 percentage points.
But Killin also maintained her financial edge over incumbent GOP Rep. Jeff Crank, entering the general election with $1,592,642 in cash on hand, compared to Crank’s $1,465,048.
Though Crank won his seat by more than 14 percentage points in the 2024 election, Killin has been included alongside Rutinel in the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” program, a list of the party’s top congressional targets in the 2026 midterms.
Meanwhile, Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd of Grand Junction easily turned back a 3rd District primary challenge from far-right former state Rep. Ron Hanks last month, and begins the general election with $1.8 million in campaign funds. The 3rd District encompasses most of Colorado’s Western Slope, along with Pueblo and the San Luis Valley.
Democrat Dwayne Romero, a former state economic development director who made a late entry into the race in March, is in the worst financial position of any Democratic challenger after defeating financial executive Alex Kelloff in the June 30 primary. Romero’s campaign reported just $84,208 in cash on hand at the end of June.
Colorado’s best-funded congressional challenger is running in the district that analysts say Democrats are the least likely to win: in the 4th District, where incumbent U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert won a 12-percentage-point victory over Democrat Trisha Calvarese in 2024. The district’s nine-point GOP lean, according to the Cook Political Report’s Partisan Voting Index, makes it the most heavily Republican district in Colorado. It covers the Eastern Plains.
Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official, has raised more than $10 million since announcing her 4th District candidacy in May 2025, more than seven times Boebert’s haul over the same period.
Despite once being one of Colorado’s strongest congressional fundraisers, Boebert has struggled financially this cycle, and reported just $247,201 in available campaign funds as of the end of June — only a small fraction of Laubacher’s $3.6 million in cash on hand.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: US Supreme Court to hear North Dakota property rights case
description: The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to answer whether a group of McKenzie County landowners is entitled to attorney fees from a pipeline company. The lawsuit stems from the landowners’ yearslong legal battle with WBI Energy after the company used eminent domain to take a portion of their properties for a pipeline project in 2018. […]
text:
Leonard Hoffmann is part of a group of North Dakota landowners asking the Supreme Court to find they're entitled to attorney fees they incurred while settling an eminent domain dispute with pipeline company WBI Energy. (Photo provided by Institute for Justice)The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to answer whether a group of McKenzie County landowners is entitled to attorney fees from a pipeline company.
The lawsuit stems from the landowners’ yearslong legal battle with WBI Energy after the company used eminent domain to take a portion of their properties for a pipeline project in 2018. The federal Natural Gas Act allows companies to take land for public natural gas infrastructure so long as landowners are fairly compensated. 
The property owners — Leonard and Denae Hoffmann, Randall Stevenson and Rocky Prestangen — were paid for their land under a confidential settlement reached in federal court in 2021. They claim they’re also entitled to legal costs.
North Dakota part of 12-state coalition urging Supreme Court to take up property rights case

The plaintiffs and WBI disagree on whether federal or state law should decide who pays attorney fees. The Natural Gas Act doesn’t specifically direct WBI to cover this expense.  However, North Dakota statute does, the McKenzie County property owners claim. 
The landowners want the Supreme Court to find that companies are required to follow state statute in this area.
Robert McNamara, the lead attorney representing the plaintiffs, told the North Dakota Monitor previously that courts have long recognized that state property laws should be honored in federal eminent domain cases. Eminent domain was exclusively a state power until the late 19th century, said McNamara, deputy litigation director for the Institute for Justice, a libertarian legal group.
North Dakota U.S. District Court Judge Daniel Hovland in 2024 ruled in favor of the landowners, and ordered WBI to pay them roughly $380,000. That decision was overturned by the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit last spring.
The 8th Circuit is the only federal appeals court to rule this way, McNamara said.
WBI Energy says that state law doesn’t apply in this instance because it seized the land under a federal statute. The Natural Gas Act essentially delegates the federal government’s power of eminent domain to natural gas companies, WBI writes in court records, and the federal government is not required to cover property owners’ legal expenses in most cases. It says the Natural Gas Act is intended to make the process for building natural gas pipelines more uniform across the country, so it wouldn’t make sense for companies to have to follow different laws for attorney fees in every state.
WBI also claims that even if state law did govern in this scenario, North Dakota law would not require it to cover this expense, either. North Dakota law allows judges the discretion to award attorney fees in eminent domain actions filed in state court, but does not mandate that they be provided, the company argues.
WBI declined a request for comment Tuesday.
Bill supports North Dakota landowners caught in costly legal battles

The landowners petitioned the Supreme Court to take up the case last year. 
In September, a coalition of 12 states led by North Dakota filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the justices to decide the suit on the side of the landowners. The U.S. Department of Justice in May filed a brief advising the court to decide the issue in favor of WBI.
“What you’re kind of seeing here is the age-old fight of federalism,” McNamara said.
The high court agreed to review the suit late last month.
In the coming months, each party will file additional documents with the court outlining their arguments. McNamara said he expects the Supreme Court to hold oral arguments in the case this fall. The justices will likely issue their decision between three and six months after that
WBI is proposing a major new natural gas pipeline between McKenzie County and eastern North Dakota. It has said it expects the project, known as the Bakken East pipeline, to be operational by 2030. 
“It would be nice if everyone knew what the rules were before deciding to build a new pipeline,” McNamara said.
WBI Energy President Rob Johnson previously said the company will only use eminent domain for the project as a last resort.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV advocates want to know who owns the land proposed for data center development in Tucker County
description: Tucker County residents are, once again, seeking more information regarding the massive data center and natural gas power plant complex proposed between the mountain towns of Thomas and Davis.
text:
An anti-data center yard sign sits on the side of the road outside of the Billy Motel & Bar outside of Davis in Tucker County, West Virginia, on Saturday, Nov. 1, 2025. (Photo by Caity Coyne/West Virginia Watch)Tucker County residents are, once again, seeking more information regarding the massive data center and natural gas power plant complex proposed between the mountain towns of Thomas and Davis.
Members of Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club sent a letter to the state Department of Environmental Protection on Thursday requesting the agency to investigate who actually has control of the land where out-of-state company Fundamental Data is proposing to build some of its facilities. 
The request from the advocates was spurred by conflicting information officially provided by Fundamental Data regarding the location of the proposed natural gas- and diesel-fired power plant.
In Fundamental Data’s air quality permit application to the DEP, the company asserted that it gained control of the property for the proposed site through a land purchase and sale in July 2024. The DEP issued that air quality permit to Fundamental Data last August.
In a letter this month, however, the state Department of Commerce — which oversees the development of high impact data center projects in the state — raised alarms about what parcels of land Fundamental Data actually owns. The department, per the letter, “conducted a search” of property records at the proposed sites and “did not find any property in Tucker County owned by Fundamental Data, LLC or any of its affiliated companies.”
According to a parcel map from the Tucker County Assessor’s Office, parcels included in the company’s air quality permit are listed as being owned by Western Pocahontas Properties, LTD. All addresses associated with Fundamental Data through the West Virginia Secretary of State’s office are in Virginia, while the company is incorporated in Delaware.
Jim Kotcon, conservation chair for the West Virginia chapter of the Sierra Club, said that if the company does not own the land they claimed to own, then there is a clear violation of the DEP’s policies that led to the company receiving its air quality permit.
“West Virginia’s rules are quite clear that, to get their pollution permit, the applicant must demonstrate ownership or control of the site,” Kotcon said in a statement. “When Fundamental Data applied for their permit, they assured DEP that they did. But then when the West Virginia Department of Commerce asks, Fundamental Data insists that everything is ‘conceptual.’ West Virginia citizens have a right to know whether this company can deliver on their promises, and our state agencies should uphold their responsibilities.”
The conflicting information is the latest example of how unclear the parameters surrounding Fundamental Data’s proposed project are.
Nikki Forrester, director of communications for Tucker United, said in a news release that Fundamental Data’s misrepresentations feel intentional.
“Fundamental Data lives in the brackish zone between being a microgrid and data center-related project and not having anything to do with data centers so they can skirt regulations and state rules,” Forrester said. “The company has no prior experience with these types of developments and now it’s unclear whether they even own the land, despite claiming otherwise. We’re all for good economic development in Tucker County, but this project isn’t it. It’s time to invest in the people of West Virginia instead of out-of-state companies that have no interest in engaging with our community or following state regulations.” 
Fundamental Data has been pushing the proposed project since House Bill 2014 — which created the state’s certified high impact data center and microgrid program — was introduced, and later passed, in the Legislature in 2025. In the almost year-and-a-half since the company filed for an air quality permit, more questions have arisen regarding the company, which has no known experience operating, building or maintaining projects of this nature or scale.
Last month, the state Department of Commerce notified Fundamental Data that it was in violation of HB 2014 and its affiliated rules due to the company failing to file an application to be certified as a high impact data center. State code dictates that any company intending to build such facilities must file with the Department of Commerce within 10 days. There is no penalty listed for non-compliance.
Fundamental Data pushed back, saying the plan remained in the “conceptual phase,” and as such no violation existed. Representatives walked back previous statements that suggested the plans were more concrete. The state then rescinded its violation.
The letter containing the conflicting property ownership information from the Commerce Department was part of further communications between the state agency and the company regarding that rescinded violation. 
The constant back-and-forths and the growing questions over the legitimacy of Fundamental Data’s proposal have left community advocates frustrated.
Olivia Miller, interim executive director of the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy and a candidate for the state House of Delegates, said the company’s “ever-changing proposals” have forced community members as well as state officials to spend “significant time” attempting to reach the facts and boundaries of the project. She said this shows Fundamental Data’s plans “increasingly appear to be an amateurish, boom-chasing venture.”
In the letter, advocates urge the state DEP’s Division of Air Quality to perform its own investigation into the assertions made regarding Fundamental Data’s land ownership. If the company was not truthful in its claims, then they want to see the DEP “exercise its authority to suspend or revoke the permit for being based on false information.”
“Fundamental Data has yet to demonstrate that it has the experience, property control or realistic plan to carry out a project of this scale,” Miller said. “… West Virginia officials need to stop giving this company the benefit of the doubt and start rigorously enforcing the law. Our agencies exist to protect the public, not to help speculative developers profit from our land, natural resources and communities.”

title: Michigan Data Centers: The Weekly Download
description: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer unveiled her Michigan Affordable and Responsible Growth Action Plan, intended to ensure data centers don’t bring harm to Michigan residents. Her approach is two-pronged, calling on state lawmakers to pass protections for Michigan energy customers, while asking data center companies to commit to paying their own way, and abiding[...]
text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments 

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer unveiled her Michigan Affordable and Responsible Growth Action Plan, intended to ensure data centers don’t bring harm to Michigan residents. Her approach is two-pronged, calling on state lawmakers to pass protections for Michigan energy customers, while asking data center companies to commit to paying their own way, and abiding by energy and environmental regulations. As of Thursday afternoon, the Governor had secured commitments from six companies.
The Wixom City Council unanimously rejected a request to waive its data center moratorium for developers eyeing a 54-acre spot on Wixom Road, MLive’s Peg McNichol reports. The moratorium remains in effect until the end of August.
Lansing City Council has approved a 182-day moratorium on data center developments, blocking considerations of new proposals until Jan. 25, 2027, Emma J. Nelson reports for WKAR.

Updates

The Saline Township Board of Trustees approved the full amount of a tax break requested for the controversial data center under development in their community, backtracking on a decision to approve a significantly smaller tax break earlier in the week, MLive’s Jennifer Eberbach reports. Oracle America Cloud Services LLC requested a 50% reduction in property taxes for 12 years. While the board previously capped the valuation of the project at $4.8 billion, it would later remove the cap on advice from one of the township attorneys, approving the tax break at the the project’s current valuation of $43 billion.
Ingham County Clerk Barb Byrum has approved recall petitions for Mason Councilwoman Elaine Ferris, according to WLNS’s Trevor King. The recall effort was prompted by residents’ opposition to a data center proposed in the community.
Developers of the proposed Project Flex data center in Lyon Township are continuing to push forward, with WXYZ’s Christiana Ford reporting that the township’s planning commission is expected to review the project at its meeting on Monday, Aug. 24.

News of Note

Lucas Smolcic Larson and Danielle James of MLive report that between 2020 and 2024 data centers benefitted from $13 million in tax breaks that the Legislature approved in 2015.
On Tuesday the Huron Valley Area Labor Federation issued a statement calling for a pause on approving large-scale data center projects until safeguards are put in place. The group of 40 labor unions specified that in order for a project to move forward, eight minimum standards must be met.
Those standards include no tax incentives or subsidies, no cost shifting onto consumers, binding labor standards, full transparency and public disclosure, enforceable limits on resource use, no weakening of state climate commitments,  safeguards for community protections and accountability and democratic review, approval, and oversight of these projects.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Mixed opinions, limited information about $6.6 billion data center in Arkansas River Valley
description: CLARKSVILLE, Ark. — Karen Fawley first recalls learning of plans to construct a data center near the Johnson Regional Medical Center when a friend mentioned the project in passing two years ago.  Fawley said she wasn’t following the project closely. Then, in January, she watched the razing of a tree-covered hillside through her mother’s hospital […]
text:
The construction site for the Serverfarm data center in Clarksville, Arkansas on July 13, 2026. Construction on it began earlier this year. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)CLARKSVILLE, Ark. — Karen Fawley first recalls learning of plans to construct a data center near the Johnson Regional Medical Center when a friend mentioned the project in passing two years ago. 
Fawley said she wasn’t following the project closely. Then, in January, she watched the razing of a tree-covered hillside through her mother’s hospital room window.
“It was really a surprise,” Fawley said. “We knew that it was gonna happen, or we at least thought it was gonna happen, but we didn’t know when. And then I just looked out the window and it was just, it was happening.”
That hillside next to the hospital now has a tall crane that dwarfs the surrounding area and the beginnings of what will eventually become a data center. 
The groundwork for the project was laid quietly in 2022, and with the support of local officials — and an initial lack of public pushback — it has progressed steadily through various zoning and city council approvals without much controversy.
The $6.6 billion data center — one of six such projects announced in Arkansas — is being built by Serverfarm, a California-based company with facilities around the world. 
Unlike Little Rock and Pulaski County where residents have been vocally opposed to two planned data centers, opposition appears more muted in Clarksville, and some have expressed optimism online about the benefits the Serverfarm facility could bring. 
But there is also skepticism and frustration from those who say they were blindsided by the project — a common refrain at a time when many small towns across the country are grappling with data centers springing up in their backyards. 


Some Clarksville residents hope the center leads to good jobs and more money for schools, roads and law enforcement. Others have questions about environmental impact, utility costs and whether the city is giving away too much to receive too little.
The desire for more information was evident during a community-organized town hall at the University of the Ozarks last Monday. The event occurred immediately after the Clarksville City Council meeting where members tabled resolutions to issue up to $55 billion in industrial development revenue bonds for the Serverfarm data center. 
About a hundred people attended the sometimes tense town hall. Community members submitted more than 80 questions in advance, said Debra Hobbs, one of the event organizers. Hobbs is also a former Republican state legislator who is running as an independent candidate against Republican Rep. Aaron Pilkington to represent House District 45, which includes Clarksville.
‘They own it’: A split-screen view of data centers comes to central Arkansas

Town hall organizers invited Clarksville’s mayor, city council, city engineer and other local officials, including Pilkington, but only two of six city council members attended.
Pilkington told the Advocate he was out of the country, and Clarksville Mayor David Rieder held his own meeting at the same time as the town hall. Rieder did not respond to several interview requests.
In an emailed statement, Serverfarm spokesperson Kurt Widmann said the company is continuing to provide information to city leaders, and looks forward to sharing details of the project’s benefits, including hundreds of permanent jobs and millions in tax revenue, with local residents. Like other Arkansas data centers, Serverfarm has created a website for the project.
“We understand a project of this size generates questions, and we welcome these conversations,” Widmann wrote. “Our goal is to build a campus that benefits Clarksville and its residents while complying with all applicable environmental requirements.”
  Economic potential 

Clarksville, a town of just under 10,000 in the Arkansas River Valley, is the kind of town that packs the stands for a peewee baseball game and hangs vibrant blue banners that read “Welcome Home” from lightpoles along downtown’s main street. Nestled in between the Boston and Ouachita Mountains, it’s the home of the Johnson County Peach Festival, the University of the Ozarks and a Tyson Foods hatchery.
Though the hatchery has been economically beneficial, the closures of Baldor Electric and HanesBrands manufacturing facilities were a big hit to the region, Pilkington said. 
“Those were two big economic losses, and so while we’ve had some growth as well, we’re teetering on the edge,” he said.
A banner displayed in downtown Clarksville, Arkansas that reads “Welcome Home” on July 14, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
Pilkington, founder of a new group advocating for data center and AI infrastructure investment, said the region needs the jobs and tax revenue he says the completed data center will provide.
The Republican lawmaker has been a proponent for expanded financial incentives for data centers, and sponsored legislation in 2023 that established sales tax exemptions for such projects.
Eddie King, one of two city council members who attended last week’s city hall, said young people are moving away from Clarksville because of a lack of good jobs. King said the town wouldn’t have a main street if it weren’t for Tyson.
“We got plenty of convenience stores and Mexican restaurants and other kind of restaurants, but we don’t have jobs that people can go out and make a retirement on, other than Tyson and Red Wing,” King said.
  Many questions, few answers 

The project’s benefits remain an open question, in part because a “community benefits package” scheduled to be discussed at last week’s city council meeting was pulled from the agenda.
“A lot of it sounds like we got a lot of promises, but I don’t think I’m the only one that believes big corporations don’t always keep their promises,” Clarksville resident Bryan Connerly told the Advocate. 
A sign directing deliveries to a data center construction site in Clarksville, Arkansas on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)
King and Christel Thompson, the two council members who attended the town hall, said they were unable to answer many of the questions submitted by the community. 
“I was hoping that the mayor and some of these other folks who had the answers would be here tonight,” Thompson said.
Despite the current lack of details, Thompson, a former public school teacher and principal, said she’s hopeful the data center will benefit local public schools. Thompson said a visit to an operational data center in Oklahoma demonstrated how tax revenue supported construction of a facility focused on STEM — science, technology, engineering and math — that benefitted students.
“They were able to partner with universities near there to train those students to go get jobs…because of the property tax they were able to get,” Thompson said.
  A town engaged 

Efforts to organize people to push back against the data center have run into cynicism, Hobbs said, and what some described as lagging civic engagement with local government. 
She said “people feel powerless,” but the data center project “is challenging people to show up.”
Thompson said the city had not done a good job of “getting out in front of this” and informing the community of what was coming. Pilkington disagreed.
“If people feel like they’re kept in the dark, I don’t necessarily know what they wanted us to do unless they want us to be running TV ads about what the project does,” he said.
Clarksville City Council members Eddie King (left) and Christal Thompson (center) address attendees of a community-organized town hall about the Serverfarm data center on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate) 
No one group was at fault for the community being taken off guard by the data center, Fawley said. The city could have done more to alert residents, Serverfarm could have been better about conducting outreach, and residents could have been more proactive about learning what was happening in local government, she said.
Fawley said it felt like nothing could be done once construction began, but the town hall was a wake-up call.
“I just came away from it saying I need to know more about what’s going on,” she said. “That’s part of the reason why my husband and I have been really trying to get more involved in things, because it’s just what you should do.”

Circa 1751, Voltaire (left) travelled to Prussia in 1750, on the invitation of Friedrich II and was a permanent resident of court for two years. (Photo by Hulton Archive/Getty Images)Nebraskans sometimes enjoy the reputation of having common sense … as if the gods, Prudence and Perception, tilted the coasts and a whole bunch of wisdom and wit tumbled into Middle America. The lexicographers at Merriam-Webster say as much, defining common sense as “sound and prudent judgment based on a simple perception of the situation or facts.”
Now “common sense” — Thomas Paine’s pamphlet notwithstanding — has become a political touchstone, the phrase often bandied about by a Nebraska congressman and more recently a spokesperson for someone who wants to be one. “Common sense solution” has also become a favorite iteration of the construct, appealing to our practicality so as to avoid getting too far into the weeds trying to solve prickly problems or right listing ships.
There is, however, this little, semi-popular chestnut: “Common sense is not so common,” an observation so pragmatic that it surely came from a common sense, pragmatic Nebraskan or similarly situated Middle American. 
But that would be off by almost 5,000 miles and three centuries. French Enlightenment writer and philosopher Voltaire is credited with giving us “Common sense is not so common.” While a tireless advocate for individual rights, Voltaire was hardly a utilitarian or pragmatist, preferring the company of monarchs and aristocrats like himself.
He was on to something with his wry observation, however. 
Contemporary examples are instructive. To wit: As I’m sure some of you have, I’ve stopped eating leafy green salads. No Caesars or Wedges or Clubs for me as the diarrhea-producing cyclospora parasite is making its way around the country. Health officials have said that the culprit is likely fresh produce. Yeesh! 
As of this writing, 1,645 confirmed cases and 5,100 probable cases of cyclospora are under investigation across 34 states, including Nebraska. The CDC said about 10% of cases usually require hospitalization. The symptoms – diarrhea, low-grade fever, aches and fatigue – can last a few days and even a few months if untreated.
While no one has ever accused me of always making “sound and prudent judgment based on a simple perception of the situation or facts,” wouldn’t common sense dictate we should have kept an eye on that nasty little bugger? Seriously. We used to do just that until the HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. thought we could skip the mandatory monitoring of food products for six of eight sickening pathogens, cyclospora among that sextet. Nor did budget and personnel cuts to the agency help. The rest – or more accurately, the result – is explosive diarrhea history.
Wait, there’s more. The Epstein Files Transparency Act passed by unanimous consent in the Senate on Nov. 19, 2025 and by 427-1 in the House the next day. Would a senator be using common sense to vote to confirm an attorney general nominee who is largely responsible for slow-walking, outing victims and generally defying the act passed by both houses of Congress?
Closer to home, while we should view new political entities or parties as democracy in action, common sense may lead us to wonder if we are racing toward a time in Nebraska when we have more political parties than we do good ideas or solutions to problems. As a lifelong Independent, I welcome other points of view, even party platforms. The trick for voters will be distinguishing one party from another, which, ironically may also be a hurdle for the parties themselves.
The most challenging hurdle to clear in the common sense sweepstakes has to do with the phrase’s first word. We seem to have less in common with each other than we used to … or so we’ve been told. Even common sense’s cousin, common knowledge, has taken a hit. We often have a difficult time agreeing on a common set of facts, a phenomenon fueled by an ocean of disinformation and conspiracy theories sloshing from one end of the social media universe to the other, among the legacy media as it fights for relevance and now even presented in prime time.
Many adherents to the digital world’s “wild, wild west” motif preach bigger, faster, stronger, especially in the employ of artificial intelligence, lest our humanity slow us in the AI race to somewhere no one can seem to determine. The result? An obfuscation of the facts and an undermining of common knowledge.
The rampant conspiratorial nonsense reminds me that our Francophone friend, Voltaire, also famously said, “Those who can make you believe absurdities can make you commit atrocities.” 
The hope is that we do indeed find “common sense solutions” to our problems and when we do, they carry the trappings of shared benefits and diminished disadvantages.
Before that happens, however, we should start with a list of what we have in common.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: The Tuberville residency case is a test for the Alabama Supreme Court
description: The Alabama Supreme Court is about to face a test. It’s not about Tommy Tuberville’s eligibility to run for governor. At least, not yet. The question for justices: Can a court even determine whether a candidate for public office can serve in it? This should be easy. It says quite a bit about the state […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville gives an acceptance speech after winning the Republican nomination for Alabama's governor at his primary election victory tailgate at the Vulcan Park in Birmingham, Alabama, on May 19, 2026. A lawsuit challenging Tuberville's ability to run for governor was dismissed by a lower court earlier this month, but has been appealed to the Alabama Supreme Court. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Supreme Court is about to face a test.
It’s not about Tommy Tuberville’s eligibility to run for governor. At least, not yet.
The question for justices: Can a court even determine whether a candidate for public office can serve in it?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This should be easy. It says quite a bit about the state — and Alabama’s high court — that it isn’t.
But we deserve a hearing on the issue. Yes, Montgomery Circuit Judge Brooke Reid dismissed a lawsuit earlier this month alleging that the Republican gubernatorial nominee did not meet the seven-year state residency requirement to be governor.
This wasn’t a win for Tuberville, exactly. Reid said she lacked the authority to consider the merits of the case. But, she added, that didn’t mean the case lacked merit.
The plaintiffs argue that Tuberville does not meet residency requirements and has therefore “usurped” his office — in this case, the Republican nominee for governor.  
Tuberville’s attorneys — who insist he is constitutionally eligible to run for governor — argue that the Alabama Republican Party must determine its nominees. If there is a legitimate question about a candidate’s residency after nomination, they say, the Legislature may make that determination should the candidate win election.
This may work with the letter of the law. But it’s obviously in conflict with the spirit. It’s also impractical. A Republican-controlled Legislature — all but certain to be the outcome in November — is not going to dump its party’s choice for governor. Tuberville could probably deliver his inaugural address on tape delay from Santa Rosa Beach, Florida.
The central question is whether the legal path pursued by the plaintiffs challenging Tuberville’s residency, known as quo warranto, can apply to a party nominee. A quo warranto suit argues that an official does not have the right to hold an office or exercise a power because they lack the legal authority to do so. 
Because there was “no Alabama case directly on point” on the matter, Reid dismissed the lawsuit. But the judge also noted that the law recognizes party nominees as “quasi-officials,” and wrote that there was a “very strong argument” that quo warranto could apply to those seeking an office.
This is an issue for a higher court. And it’s an important one.
Tuberville has faced questions about his residency for years. And it hasn’t helped that he’s been largely evasive in answering them. There’s plenty of evidence (unearthed by Lagniappe in Mobile) to suggest Tuberville spent much of his time as Alabama’s U.S. senator in Florida, whether it’s holding a Florida driver’s license or flying frequently to the Sunshine State. At a minimum, the senator has been sloppy about putting down roots.
Now, sloppiness is not in itself conclusive. Tuberville has argued that his time as Auburn’s head coach should count toward residency, as should his purchase of an Auburn home in 2018 (though his name was not on the deed until 2024). This defies common sense but, perhaps, not the law.
These questions can’t be answered in a quick, Sunday afternoon rush job. Nor does upholding the dismissal without explanation seem wise. Do that, and you’ll open the door to candidates running for Alabama office from Florida or (heaven forbid) New York, so long as their party controls the Legislature and the courts.
Yet it’s easy to envision the Alabama Supreme Court taking that tack. The justices have shown a disturbing tendency to ignore the law when a powerful entity (particularly one run by or connected to Republicans) ends up at a defendant’s table.
This is a body that said in 2013, in clear violation of the state constitution, that the Legislature did not have to conduct meetings in public. It was hard to ignore that the ruling helped uphold the shady passage of the Republican-backed Alabama Accountability Act earlier that year.
In 2020, the justices deployed a comically labored reading of the word “meeting” to justify the Public Service Commission kicking out a person recording a hearing on Alabama Power’s ludicrous rooftop solar panel charges.
Maybe the all-Republican Supreme Court fears being primaried. Perhaps they believe Republicans can act with impunity.
But simply announcing that a quo warranto suit doesn’t apply to political nominees will undermine the Alabama Constitution. It will justify a kind of absentee officialdom, so long as one party calls the shots. And the deep disconnect between Alabama leaders and Alabama politicians will grow still wider.
So here’s the test for the court: Consider the practical reality of a decision that would let out-of-state politicians run for office unimpeded. If you still think the case can be dismissed — because of oversight or fuzzy language — spell out your reasons and suggest a remedy. But above all, don’t rein in the law the moment it touches a powerful person.
It’s not that much of a challenge. But it’s one we’ve seen the Alabama Supreme Court consistently fail.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Gov. Morrisey: If childcare is next, let’s have that discussion
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey, we have been paying attention. More importantly, so has the rest of West Virginia. You already told us what you are considering. You publicly said funding for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families was being looked at for School Clothing Vouchers, Family Resource Networks and childcare. Working families should believe you. I certainly[...]
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey announces a plan to expand programs in public schools aimed at helping children before they need the child welfare system in an effort to improve the state’s overburdened foster care system on Tuesday, Jan. 6, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)Gov. Patrick Morrisey, we have been paying attention. More importantly, so has the rest of West Virginia. You already told us what you are considering. You publicly said funding for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families was being looked at for School Clothing Vouchers, Family Resource Networks and childcare. Working families should believe you. I certainly do.
First came the uncertainty surrounding Family Resource Networks. Then came the School Clothing Allowance. Next it will be childcare. The pattern is hard to ignore. If history is any indication, we know what will come next. We will hear about “difficult decisions,” “tightening the states belt” and “fiscal responsibility.” 
Before the first proposal is even announced, let me save everyone a little time. If childcare is next on the chopping block, do not expect West Virginians to quietly accept it. Childcare is not just another government program — it is economic infrastructure.
Every morning, thousands of West Virginians go to work because someone else is safely caring for their children — the nurse, correctional officer, teacher, police officer, hospital employee, manufacturer, state worker and small business owner. 
You can cut childcare funding, but you cannot cut the consequences. Parents will not suddenly find another provider. Employers will not suddenly find more workers. Hospitals will not magically fill vacant shifts. Businesses do not become more competitive. They end up posting more “Help Wanted” signs. 
Childcare is not welfare. It is workforce infrastructure. You cannot claim to be pro-business while undermining the businesses that make work possible.
West Virginia does not have a childcare spending problem. It has a workforce shortage. Making it harder for parents to work is not an economic development strategy.
Here is what many people still do not understand: childcare does not just support businesses it is a business. We employ thousands of West Virginians, pay taxes, buy local and make it possible for every other industry to fill its jobs.
No childcare. No workforce. No economic growth.
For years we have heard elected officials talk about recruiting new businesses to West Virginia. That is great, but who is going to care for those workers’ children? You cannot recruit workers to a state where they cannot find childcare.
If classrooms close, the impact will not stop at our doors. Employers across every industry will lose workers, reduce production, shorten hours and struggle even more to fill open positions. That is not fiscal responsibility. It is bad economic policy.
So, Governor, if childcare is next, let’s have that conversation. Let’s have it with the parents who could lose their jobs, the employers who cannot hire without childcare, the hospitals trying to recruit nurses, the manufacturers struggling to fill positions, and the legislators who understand what is at stake.
Because this debate has never really been about childcare. It is about whether West Virginia wants people to work.
You often say West Virginia is open for business. Then stop threatening the one industry that makes every other industry possible.
If childcare is next, do not be surprised when parents, providers, employers, hospitals, manufacturers and members of the Legislature stand together to defend it.
Gov. Morrisey may see childcare as another budget line, but parents see it as the difference between keeping a job and losing one.
Employers see it as the difference between filling a position and leaving it vacant.
Providers see it for what it has always been — the foundation that keeps West Virginia working.
History will remember whether this administration chose to strengthen West Virginia’s workforce or weaken it.
Gov. Morrisey, if childcare is next, we are ready.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fifty for 150: First National Western Stock Show takes place in Denver in 1906
description: Ranchers and farmers gathered under a big top tent borrowed from the circus for the first official National Western Stock Show in Denver in January 1906. There had been previous stock show attempts, such as the 1875 Blood Stock Fair, the 1899 National Exhibition of Range Cattle and sporadic meetings of the Denver Fat Stock […]
text:
(Courtesy of National Western Stock Show)Ranchers and farmers gathered under a big top tent borrowed from the circus for the first official National Western Stock Show in Denver in January 1906.
 


This story is part of Colorado at 150. Each Fifty for 150 story focuses on an event that helped define Colorado over 150 years of statehood. Newsline is publishing one Fifty for 150 story every weekday in reverse chronological order until the sesquicentennial, Aug. 1, when the final of 50 stories, about the declaration of statehood, will appear.



There had been previous stock show attempts, such as the 1875 Blood Stock Fair, the 1899 National Exhibition of Range Cattle and sporadic meetings of the Denver Fat Stock and Feeder Show, but 1906 proved to be a rosy year for an official stock show, with six livestock and agricultural associations set to meet in Denver around the same time.
During that first show, 351 cattle, sheep and pigs went on display and area stockmen discussed breeding and feeding techniques. “CATTLEMEN OF GREAT WEST GATHER IN DENVER TO RIGHT WRONGS AND EXHIBIT STOCK,” said the headline in the Jan. 30, 1906, edition of The Rocky Mountain News.
“Beef magnates from the East, commission men from all the large packing centers, and a host of ranchers, farmers, horse fanciers, sheep herders and citizens of Denver made the formal opening of the Western livestock show at the Union stockyards yesterday afternoon an occasion both picturesque and interesting,” the report said. “The aristocratic cattle were curried within an inch of their lives, the horses had ribbons and straw braided into their manes until they were as festive looking as circus paraders, and the buildings at the yards were decorated with flags, bunting and large paintings, all of which made a gala background for the masses of people who had come miles.”
Following a meeting at the Brown Palace the previous day, the The National Live Stock Association and the American Stock Growers Association voted to merge into the American National Live Stock Association, an early precursor to the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association. By the end of the show on Feb. 1, the ranchers adopted resolutions about changes to interstate commerce and rules about livestock transport.
The program for Jan. 30 included livestock judging, a farmers’ congress and arrival by train of agricultural students from Colorado State University in Fort Collins. The next day, dubbed Denver Day, saw over 25,000 visitors according to local reports. At the public sale, cattle went for 10 cents per pound.
“Much of Colorado’s fine stock will be served on New York tables,” a Feb. 2 report from The Rocky Mountain News said. “A triumph was scored by the cattlemen of the West at the sale of stock at the live stock show, and prices far above the big Eastern markets were readily offered by the buyers.”
The first international entries to the show were in 1908, and a rodeo was added in 1931.
The National Western Stock show has substantially evolved since then and continues to be one of the most important annual events for Colorado ranching and agriculture. Today, it is held at the National Western Complex and attracts almost 700,000 visitors to the rodeos, horse shows, trade show, auctions and other events.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Altria’s recent gift to UK follows long history of corporate white-washing of tobacco
description: In 1996, the Cigarette Papers was published, revealing how Kentucky’s Tobacco and Health Research Institute at the University of Kentucky presented itself as an independent arm of a publicly funded university, but in fact it was run by tobacco manufacturers and their highly paid lawyers. Although the purported goals of the institute were to conduct […]
text:
In Kentucky, almost 20% of high school students use electronic cigarettes and 5% smoke, according to The Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids. (Getty Images)In 1996, the Cigarette Papers was published, revealing how Kentucky’s Tobacco and Health Research Institute at the University of Kentucky presented itself as an independent arm of a publicly funded university, but in fact it was run by tobacco manufacturers and their highly paid lawyers. Although the purported goals of the institute were to conduct research on smoking and health, the tobacco industry, not independent scientists, engaged in evaluating the research and participated in developing public policy that favored the tobacco industry. 
Over the past 30 years, scientists have used industry document research to verify the tactics used by the tobacco companies and other health-harming industries to disrupt public health. Using the industry’s own internal documents is a novel approach to understanding the corporate social responsibility playbook.
According to the playbook, it is common for tobacco companies to hide behind unwitting allies or front groups, like universities and community organizations, to improve their public image and garner goodwill. It is well-known that tobacco companies “capture knowledge” by suppressing scientific data on the health harms of their products or sponsoring research to tone down the harm. Commonly, the tobacco companies attack or discredit scientists who do not support the industry’s positions. As a scientist myself, I have experienced this tactic firsthand.
The tobacco companies continue to shape public narrative by building relationships with influential community leaders and using slick advertising and marketing campaigns to promote their products and downplay the dangerous health effects. They also indirectly promote tobacco products by sponsoring charitable causes, anti-health policy advocacy, disaster relief efforts, and youth efforts under the guise of “corporate responsibility” in exchange for good will. 
There are many reasons why the tobacco companies invest so heavily in generating public good will. I name just a few. First, the tobacco industry was found guilty of lying to the American public about the deadly effects of tobacco products for more than 50 years, in the 2006 landmark decision in the Racketeering Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act lawsuit. 
Second, the tobacco industry conspired to addict young people on nicotine leading to a class action lawsuit against Juul labs, contributing to a youth nicotine addiction crisis and debilitating health issues linked to vaping. 
Third, the tobacco industry has targeted Black Americans for decades with aggressive and targeted marketing of menthol cigarettes such as saturating urban neighborhoods with billboards, sponsoring cultural events like jazz festivals (giving away free cigarettes), advertising in popular publications such as Ebony and Jet, and more recently on social media. 
Many countries prohibit these unfair corporate social responsibility practices and debunk tobacco industry misinformation by signing on to the World Health Organization’s Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. The United States should sign on to this important public health treaty.
Now, 30 years later, the tobacco industry is at it again. Altria’s recent $2 million gift to the University of Kentucky to create the Endowed Professor of Tobacco Growers Sustainability is intended to ‘strengthen academic and extension capacity in tobacco-growing communities.’  While the focus is on supporting faculty who, in turn, will help our tobacco growers, tobacco is no longer the dominant agricultural commodity it once was. Nearly all the Kentucky farms that once grew tobacco no longer do. Today, leading agricultural commodities include corn, soybeans, cattle, and poultry, and Kentucky’s agriculture and agribusiness contribute billions to Kentucky’s economy. 
So why is Altria investing in tobacco growers now? Are they using the University of Kentucky College of Agriculture’s good reputation to boost their own credibility, influence public opinion, and soften perceptions? This is reminiscent of years prior to the tobacco buyout in the late 1990s and the Master Settlement Agreement in the early 2000s when tobacco was “king” in Kentucky. Since then, Kentucky has moved away from growing tobacco to diversify agriculture. 
During this same time, Kentucky has witnessed countless successful local smoke-free campaigns even in some of the poorest rural counties in the country. These laws have led to dramatic reductions in new cases of lung cancer, preterm births, hospitalizations for emphysema and visits for asthma, lower indoor air pollution from tobacco smoke, and significant reductions in adult and youth smoking in communities with strong smoke-free laws. We have made slow, steady progress in lowering the harm caused by tobacco use and exposure to tobacco. 
We now know that corporations harm people. In fact, five commercial products are responsible for nearly one-third of all deaths from chronic disease. Tobacco contributes to 7.2 million deaths per year globally (second only to the 8.1 million deaths from fossil fuels). The science is clear. Corporations are a well-known cause of disease. In fact, many universities have policies on taking money from health-harming industries. At the very least, universities need to create guardrails to disclose conflicts of interest and minimize harm from these corporations.
Don’t let Altria fool you. Their money and influence cannot hide the extraordinary toll that tobacco use has on Kentucky’s health and our economy.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: A Mercer County city wants to annex land for a potential data center. Another city has concerns.
description: An effort by the Mercer County city of Burgin to annex land into its city limits for a potential data center has embroiled the small community in a contentious debate over the impacts of such a project, something that’s also raising strong concerns from local leaders of the county seat. People packed inside the Burgin […]
text:
The Harrodsburg City Commmission, meeting on July 13, voted to have their city attorney send a letter to the city of Burgin objecting to its process for its annexation ordinance. (Screenshot/Facebook)An effort by the Mercer County city of Burgin to annex land into its city limits for a potential data center has embroiled the small community in a contentious debate over the impacts of such a project, something that’s also raising strong concerns from local leaders of the county seat.
People packed inside the Burgin Independent School building on July 9 for a special-called Burgin city council meeting where city council members voted 3-2 to advance an ordinance to annex from the county more than 1,000 acres of land — roughly doubling the size of the city — for a potential data center development. 
The council didn’t take public comment from those in the audience during that meeting. Burgin resident Bethany Corea, who attended the meeting, told the Lantern dozens of people were turned away from entering the building. 
“A lot of people in Burgin and Mercer County, but primarily Burgin right now, just feel like the process is being rushed, that their voices aren’t heard,” Corea said. “What it feels like to us is the local officials are going, ‘We don’t care what you think. More tax money.’” 
Corea, 40, a former volunteer firefighter and a volunteer with the community group We Are Mercer County that’s advocating for a data center moratorium, said she’s also strongly concerned with the community having enough firefighting capacity for a large data center.
Burgin has now canceled another special-called meeting planned for July 20 because, according to a post on the city’s Facebook page, the first special meeting was “not legally accurate as we have not had a first reading of the ordinance.” Voicemails and emails to Burgin city council members Melinda Wofford and Travis Irvin on Friday were not returned. 
Meanwhile, the Mercer County Fiscal Court and the city commission for the county seat of Harrodsburg are also taking action related to data centers. The city of Harrodsburg sent a letter to Burgin on July 14 objecting to the process it went about scheduling the special meeting for the second reading of the ordinance.
Harrodsburg City Attorney Norrie Currens told the Lantern that the city of Burgin didn’t give a 14-day notice, as is required by state law, for the annexation of property on which Harrodsburg’s municipal water utility has a water line. Currens said their city, which supplies water to the city of Burgin, has concerns about having enough water supply for a potential hyperscale data center. 
“If they annex this property, they have a duty to provide services to those to that area. They have to provide police fire protection, water, sewer, all the things. They are moving forward with the annexation without ever having discussed with the city of Harrodsburg supplying water to the location in question,” Currens said. 
The Harrodsburg Herald reported the county fiscal court at a July 14 meeting is also moving forward with considering a temporary moratorium on data center construction in the county, a move that would not affect property within the city limits of Burgin. 
In addition, the county’s planning and zoning commission is also holding a public hearing on July 23 on a draft ordinance to site and regulate data center construction in the county. Burgin does not have any planning or zoning body. 
Corea, who’s running for Burgin city council this fall, said herself and other volunteers with We Are Mercer County plan to advocate for a stronger planning and zoning ordinance at the county level. 
She said while whether Mercer County should be the location of a large data center is up for debate, she’s personally concerned about the potential water usage and environmental impacts from a data center, especially for a place that her family moved to a rural lifestyle. 
“You’re taking away what makes Burgin, Burgin,” Corea said. “So much of the citizens here, so many of them feel that way.” way.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Is the Colorado River in a climate doom loop?
description: As negotiations and potential lawsuits over the Colorado River intensify, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation – which is ultimately in charge of managing the river – would be smart to pull back from the high-stakes gambit and take a hard look at the science. To make it easy for the Bureau, I’ve packed the best […]
text:
The Colorado River is pictured where it flows near Hite, Utah, just beyond the upper reaches of Lake Powell, on Friday, Sept. 19, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)As negotiations and potential lawsuits over the Colorado River intensify, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation – which is ultimately in charge of managing the river – would be smart to pull back from the high-stakes gambit and take a hard look at the science.
To make it easy for the Bureau, I’ve packed the best and most recent science into four tight paragraphs below.
First and foremost, in a new report from the University of Colorado Boulder, the best scientists in the business predict that flows in the Colorado River could drop 30% more by 2050 due to climate change, and that pre-climate flow levels are not coming back.
Second, a new scientific study by the group, Tell The Dam Truth, describes how the massive damming of the Colorado River is a source of greenhouse gas emissions. Not only do the reservoirs and hydropower turbines themselves emit GHGs, but the dry-up of two million acres of wetlands in the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, caused by the dams, is the biggest source of GHG emissions in the whole system.
Third, another new scientific study in Nature Communications describes how in dryer climates impacted by climate change, human interventions to try to capture and manage water cause further drying. The study indicates that “pumping water for farms, clearing land, and damming rivers primarily intensified dry conditions.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Finally, a recent scientific study in Nature Water indicates that as the climate warms, reservoirs will become warmer and more polluted and emit even more GHGs than they do now. The study estimates that reservoir emissions at the latitude of Glen Canyon Dam could increase between 20% to 80% by the end of this century depending on how bad climate change gets.
I call this a “climate doom loop,” where the damming and diversion of the Colorado River causes GHG emissions that dries out the Southwest, causing decision-makers to try to accelerate the damming and diversion that accelerates the GHG emissions and the drying. Further, hydroelectricity that uses dams and reservoirs to generate power causes GHG emissions, and those emissions increase as climate change intensifies.
In plain English: We caused a problem and our efforts to fix the problem are only making the problem worse.
In 1936, social scientist Robert K. Merton was the first person to formally analyze this concept, commonly known as the “law of unintended consequences.” This law also combines tightly on the Colorado River with what economists refer to as the “sunk costs fallacy” that drives bureaucracies to continue a failing endeavor because they have already invested so much time and money into it.
The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation’s current attempts to “save” Glen Canyon Dam, Powell Reservoir, and its hydroelectricity are perfect examples of these loops, laws and fallacies. Glen Canyon Dam has the unintended consequence of causing the emission of GHGs that further dry out the Southwest U.S., but the Bureau has so much time and money sunk into Glen Canyon Dam that they want to save it, which, as climate change intensifies, causes more emissions and drying that makes it even more unlikely to save the dam.
Likewise, the ongoing and proposed dam-building flurry in the Colorado River’s upper basin states of Colorado, Wyoming and Utah further exemplifies these loops, laws and fallacies. Denver Water is desperately trying to bring a new diversion online — the Gross Reservoir Expansion Project, for the stated purpose of “climate resilience” – that would further drain the Colorado River at the tippy-top of the Continental Divide, thus accelerating the downstream chaos all the way to Mexico and the Sea of Cortez.
Many of the same social scientists and economists also point to a solution for these problems that centers around looking forward rather than backwards. “Ignore the past,” they say, and instead ask this question: “Knowing what I know today, would I still choose to do this?”
The inconvenient truth of the climate doom loop on the Colorado River will force us to look forward, not backward, for solutions to address it. The sooner the Bureau of Reclamation starts looking forward, the faster those solutions will appear. To be clear, those solutions will be hard and controversial, but the opposite will be even more so.
