name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansans who banded together to save PBS deserve better than this
description: In normal times, a group of citizens banding together and pitching in to save a public institution like PBS would be rewarded. They would be lauded for putting their money where their mouths are. But these aren’t normal times, as Arkansans who fought to keep PBS programs in the state are learning the hard way. […]
text:
Supporters of PBS held up signs at the Arkansas TV commission meeting held on Thursday, March 12, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)In normal times, a group of citizens banding together and pitching in to save a public institution like PBS would be rewarded. They would be lauded for putting their money where their mouths are.
But these aren’t normal times, as Arkansans who fought to keep PBS programs in the state are learning the hard way.
Arkansas TV’s decision to remove one PBS news program from its lineup and reschedule another is a betrayal to those who were trying to do the right thing. The decision is also going to make it harder for Arkansans to trust the public television network’s leadership.
Supporters of public television barely had any time to celebrate their victory in convincing the Arkansas TV commission to reverse course and keep PBS before learning of the network’s plan to water down offerings. Billed as an effort to increase local programming, Arkansas TV announced it would no longer air “Washington Week with The Atlantic” and would move “PBS Newshour” to a late-night schedule.
The head of Arkansas TV, former Republican state Rep. Carlton Wing, says the changes weren’t politically motivated and are part of the network’s goal to increase its local programming from 5% to 30%.
But it’s hard to ignore that the changes affect programming that has long come under fire from Republicans in Arkansas and elsewhere. 
That includes GOP state Sen. Dan Sullivan, whose wife sits on the Arkansas TV Commission and who has referred to “Washington Week” as left-leaning. Sullivan, who has unsuccessfully pushed for abolishing the Arkansas TV Commission, said he didn’t have any role in the programming changes.
The changes raise questions about what PBS will look like in Arkansas in the years ahead. Supporters successfully raised more than the $2.1 million needed to pay PBS dues, staving off efforts to cut ties with the national network altogether.



Let us know what you think...


 


The bipartisan coalition of viewers and donors led by former first ladies Gay White and Barbara Pryor weren’t fighting to keep a watered down, Diet Coke version of PBS in the state. Imagine the response they would have gotten from donors if they knew they were donating money to keep PBS in Arkansas in name only, a version stripped of any content that could draw objections.
The backlash from viewers, as reporter Tess Vrbin’s story last week showed, demonstrated the danger of trying such a bait-and-switch on PBS viewers and donors. One viewer wrote that “trust has been broken” and another complained about being “jerked around by politics.”
Donors didn’t give money because they wanted less PBS. They saw the value in keeping quality educational and cultural programs on the state’s airwaves for all ages, from Mister Rogers to Ken Burns.
That includes news programs like “PBS Newshour” and “Washington Week.” There’s a reason why PBS is consistently ranked as one of the most trusted news sources in polling, with only the Weather Channel ranking higher.
PBS’s news programs underscore the value of having a strong public television network that helps viewers connect with the news at home and nationally. That relationship is built on trust.
Trust is also vital in keeping the public’s support for an institution like Arkansas’ public television. Viewers across the state mobilized, donated and spoke out when they saw PBS under threat. They weren’t fighting for PBS in name only. They were fighting for the kind of programming that audiences can’t find in commercial media, and that means programming that may make some uncomfortable.
When he promoted his critically acclaimed documentary series on the American Revolution, Burns frequently cited the neon sign he kept in his studio that reads, “It’s complicated.” It was a reminder that history never boils down to simple black-and-white narratives.
Arkansas should reward the efforts of PBS supporters who fought hard to keep that kind of perspective on the air. More importantly, Arkansas should trust that its citizens don’t need to be protected from complicated stories.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The story behind rows of unmarked stones at New Haven cemetery
description: Roughly 2,200 people are buried at Blake Street Cemetery, many in graves marked only with numbers. Researchers want to tell their stories.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

For more than a century, Anna Horan’s gravesite was one of the thousands marked by squat, featureless headstones arranged in uneven rows along the hillside in New Haven’s Blake Street Cemetery.
The only identifying marking, the number 685, was slowly eroded away by the elements until it, too, was gone.
Horan, the daughter of Irish immigrants, died penniless at the Springside Almshouse in 1907. Her life was marked by occasional misfortunes recorded in the city’s newspapers: her father died during her infancy, and later in life, she was abandoned by her husband, forcing her to place her own children in a orphanage. A run-in with the police in 1891 led her to file a slander lawsuit seeking $5,000 in damages, for which she received just $25.
Her body was taken to the Blake Street Cemetery, which served as New Haven’s paupers’ graveyard — a place to bury poor and unclaimed bodies — between 1884 and 1931.
A few years ago, some Horan’s descendants — aided by modern genetic testing and online records — began researching their family tree, and Horan’s hardscrabble life in New Haven began to emerge from obscurity.
Seeking more information last year, they contacted Sherill Baldwin. 
Baldwin is an amateur genealogist who has spent the last five years researching the identities of the roughly 2,200 people who are buried at Blake Street Cemetery, the vast majority of them in graves marked only with numbers. Using census records, newspaper archives and other historical records, Baldwin has pieced together narratives about their lives, which she publishes on her blog, Buried Stories.
“New Haven is trying to uncover stories that are not always told,” Baldwin said. “And people who are buried here, while they may have been sort of economically disadvantaged, they contributed in some way into the creation of the community.”
After connecting with one of Horan’s great-grandchildren, Michael Knappman, Baldwin began researching Horan’s life and searching for her final resting place among the rows of stones.
The search was hampered by the fact that Horan’s gravestone, like many at Blake Street, had eroded to the point that it could no longer be identified.
But Baldwin hit a break when she and Knappman discovered the names of two men who had died within weeks of Horan, and were given sequential burial numbers that lined up with Horan’s. Incredibly, Baldwin said, both men had headstones engraved with their still-legible names right next to each other.
The third stone in the row, Baldwin concluded, must be Horan’s.
In August, Baldwin messaged Knappman that she had located his great-grandmother’s grave and included a photo of the stone marked with a small orange flag. Knappman, who lives in California, coordinated with his sister in Louisiana and a pair of cousins from Maine and North Carolina to purchase a new headstone engraved with Horan’s name and the dates of her birth and death.
Earlier this year, the family gathered in New Haven to see the new headstone and memorialize Horan’s life for the first time.
“Just the thought that Anna’s gravestone was uncared for and not acknowledged was just — it was so sad,” Knappman said. “I felt so much satisfaction knowing that we could put a stone back there with her name on it and recognize her, even though who knows when we might be able to get back to New Haven and lay some flowers down there again.”

Sherill Baldwin holds a photo of reunited family members of Anna Horan next to her headstone in Blake Street Cemetery in New Haven on July 2, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

What is this place?
Baldwin, a native of Cape Cod, first became interested in genealogy as a teenager, researching her own family’s history at local cemeteries near her hometown of Harwich, Mass. While the interest never developed into a professional career, she later received a research certificate from Boston University after conducting a survey of the people buried in a plot that had belonged to her family since 1862.
Baldwin moved to New Haven in the 2000s and began working for the state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck, Baldwin said, she was unable to make regular trips back to Massachusetts and she began exploring old cemeteries near her home, starting with Fair Haven’s Union Cemetery.
Eventually Baldwin’s interest led her across town to the larger Westville Cemetery and adjacent cemetery owned by the Congregation Mishkan Israel. Behind those two cemeteries is the small, hillside parcel with thousands of small, numbered headstones — Blake Street Cemetery.
“One day I found this, and I was just like, ‘What is this place?'” Baldwin recalled. “I was just bitten. I wanted to know the stories: who’s buried here? What’s going on with this place?'”
Baldwin’s search for more information led her to the Charles R. Hale Collection at the Connecticut State Library. Hale, a necrologist who originally focused on the graves of Union Civil War veterans, was hired by the Works Progress Administration in the 1930s to survey burial plots at more than 2,000 cemeteries across Connecticut.
“It’s phenomenal if you’re a researcher,” Baldwin said. “He had staff that transcribed every single headstone in every single cemetery they could find in Connecticut.” 
Even during Hale’s time, however, most of the stones at Blake Street did not have engraved names. Instead, Hale relied on a written list that included names and plot numbers of the 2,200 people buried there.
As a result of Hale’s research, military veterans buried at Blake Street Cemetery received new, larger headstones with engraved names. Those stones are still largely standing today, providing an easier reference point for researchers like Baldwin to navigate the cemetery.
After obtaining a copy of Hale’s list, Baldwin converted it into a digital spreadsheet that allowed her to sort the plots by name, age and date of death. One of the quirks of Hale’s collection, Baldwin said, is that it identified the race of people buried at Blake Street — something she said was uncommon for the time period.
About one quarter of the people buried at Blake Street were of African American descent, Baldwin said. Seeking a challenge, Baldwin said she decided to focus her initial research on those names.
One of the first names that attracted her interest was that of Lois Tritton, who, at 95, stood out for being the oldest person buried at the cemetery.
Baldwin soon discovered that Tritton was also one of the most famous people to be buried there. Around the time of her death in 1894, Tritton was the subject of numerous newspaper articles that noted she was the last living person sold at auction on the New Haven Green.

Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Sherill Baldwin shows the manumission for Lois Tritton, the last enslaved person sold in New Haven. Tritton is buried at Blake Street Cemetery in New Haven.At right, Baldwin holds a printed drawing depicting Tritton.
Much of the information about Tritton’s life has been collected by Jill Snyder, a community historian who first came across the story in the 1990s, when she was looking into the history of New Haven’s St. Luke’s Church, one of the nation’s first predominantly Black Episcopal congregations.
Snyder said that Tritton was born a slave in Nova Scotia and was later brought to New Haven along with her mother, Lucy. The mother and daughter were sold, for $10 each, to help cover their owner’s debts in 1825. Sydner said the man who purchased them, Anthony Sanford, claimed to have freed the pair but actually made Lois work for several years as an indentured servant. (Connecticut began the gradual abolition of slavery in 1784 but did not formally ban the practice until 1848.)
From there, Tritton worked as a laundress in New Haven, where she became historical curiosity as one of the state’s last living linkages to slavery.
“She had her 15 minutes of fame, if you will, and and then was forgotten,” Snyder said.
Spurred in part by Snyder’s research, the Trittons’ story has seen a resurgence in recent years. In 2022, a pair of witness stones were placed in front of the steps of Trinity on the Green Episcopal Church, near the spot where Lois and her mother were paraded and sold. Last March, the church held a special service in conjunction with St. Luke’s to mark the 200th anniversary of the event.
Members of both congregations also began a collection to raise money to place a new headstone at Tritton’s grave at Blake Street. The new stone, featuring the names of Lucy, Lois and Lois’s son Frederick, was placed during a dedication ceremony at the cemetery in June.
“They’re almost alive in my mind, I’ve spent so much time with them,” Snyder said. “Their story is so representative of what happened to African women, being used in such a terrible way, kept enslaved. So they’re very representative, but theirs is also a triumphant story because they were free, and Lois was able to live out her own life, which was rare.”
Hard lives
To date, Baldwin has published articles recounting the lives of around two dozen people buried at Blake Street. They include John Bray, a Civil War veteran who fought with the 29th Regiment of Connecticut Volunteers — the state’s first all-Black infantry regiment — and Charles Coe, a mason who helped construct the old State House on the New Haven Green.
There’s also Mary Hazelton, a woman who was murdered and found stuffed in trunk inside her apartment in 1909. Hazelton’s husband, James Hazelton, who was known for a history of abuse, was immediately suspected of the crime. He was later captured in New York City, tried and sentenced to life in prison for the crime, only to be pardoned in 1928.
“I just hope she’s found a better place, because she lived a very hard life, and it was really hard researching and reading about her demise,” Baldwin said. “And I’m hoping that this is a better spot for her, which is why, to me, I think we need to take care of cemeteries in general.”
After Blake Street Cemetery stopped accepting new burials in 1931, New Haven began relying on another paupers’ cemetery located on Woodin Street. By the 1990s, the responsibility of handling unclaimed and unidentified bodies had shifted to the state’s Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, which works with local funeral homes to arrange burials and cremations.
In addition to her blog posts, Baldwin has begun hosting tours of Blake Street Cemetery, to share her research, and clean up days to remove weeds and litter from around the headstones.

The headstone for Charles P. Geyer in Blake Street Cemetery in New Haven on July 2, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

The full story of Anna Horan, the woman whose identity was recently discovered by her family, is another that Baldwin has shared on the Buried Stories website.
In 1885, Anna’s husband Thomas Horan sold all the family’s furniture and left his wife and oldest child without a place to stay or anything to eat, according to a notice about “a cruel husband,” which Baldwin found published in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier.
At some point, Thomas returned, and he and Anna had four more children, according to Baldwin’s research. When he left the family again, Anna was forced to place her children in the St. Francis Orphan Asylum, while she went to live in the almshouse.
The Horans’ youngest child, John, died at the orphanage at age 8, while the older children later spread out across the country. In some cases, they took steps to conceal their family tree.
For example, Anna’s third child, Thomas, later changed his name to Horace Theodore Sanford when he joined the Army and was sent to Texas, according to his granddaughter, Caron Wilbur.
Knappman — the man who reached out to Baldwin last year to fine Anna’s grave — said his grandmother, Maude, erroneously told him that her parents died in a fire in Baltimore. His mother, Maude’s daughter, would occasionally respond to her kids’ begging with the admonition, “You kids are going to send us all to the poorhouse” — a phrase that stood out to Knappman in the 1950s, and which he now believes was a clue into the family’s background.
“I think my grandmother was hiding some of her history because of shame or just anger, or we’re not sure,” Knappman said. “Maybe she was trying to give us some misdirection to not find out her true birthplace.”
It was not until Knappman and Wilbur completed DNA testing through Ancestry.com in 2019 that they became aware of each other. Even then, it took hiring a professional genealogist to discover the mutual relative: Anna Horan.
The cousins met for the first time in person in New Haven, where they shared pizza and caught up on family stories.
“Without her, we wouldn’t be here today, and for me it brings some closure in this emotional feeling of the unknown, not knowing who your family is,” Wilbur said. “It brings a little bit of a connection, I think, to this human aspect of family.”
Baldwin said she’d eventually like to see every one of the small, numbered stones raised in places where they have sunk into the ground, and to have missing stones replaced. In the meantime, she said, people who believe they have a relative buried at Blake Street should reach out to her to see what information she can uncover.
“It’s regular people, and some of them have very sad endings, but I’m enjoying telling [their] stories,” Baldwin said.
Gravestones in Blake Street Cemetery often have carved numbers to identify burial sites.   Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The ‘developer’ of a Kansas data center swore under oath he wasn’t involved. My town is bamboozled.
description: The sales pitch for what could be the state’s largest data center is built on a hyperscale whopper. In sworn testimony from a federal bankruptcy proceeding, Gary Pinkston, the businessman touted as the developer of the proposed “Flint Hills Digital Campus” at Emporia, said he wasn’t familiar with the project. Come again? “I have no […]
text:
Organizers of a petition to put a proposed data center for Emporia to a public vote gather signatures on July 13, 2026, outside the cty offices. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)The sales pitch for what could be the state’s largest data center is built on a hyperscale whopper.
In sworn testimony from a federal bankruptcy proceeding, Gary Pinkston, the businessman touted as the developer of the proposed “Flint Hills Digital Campus” at Emporia, said he wasn’t familiar with the project.
Come again?
“I have no interest at all in that project,” Pinkston said under oath last month in reply to a question about the Emporia data center.
Pinkston has been the folksy plaid-shirt-and-jeans ambassador for the hyperscale project since shortly after its announcement last month. The scheme aims to transform 1,000 mostly rural acres on the west edge of Emporia into a data center complex that might eventually attract billions of dollars in investment. Mentally stress “might” in that sentence, because not enough information in the project has been released to judge its chances of success.


 Kansas Reflector video
The debate over the data center proposal has been fierce in Emporia, mirroring arguments in Kansas and across the rest of the country. A coalition composed of unlikely demographics — the young and the old, the rich and the not so rich, tree huggers and Bible thumpers — has emerged to fight the data center, with yard signs and petitions and passionate testimony at public hearings. Those in favor of the data center, led by pooh-bahs at the local chamber of commerce and the local regional development association, have crowed about jobs, progress and an enlarged tax base.
All of this has unfolded in my town, most of it within walking distance of my home on Constitution Street. The rift has strained or broken friendships, prompted passionate discussion in bars and restaurants, caused distrust among some and brought others together. It has revealed the frustration that the average citizen feels as they are buffeted by decisions that are moving too fast and are beyond their control. Mostly, the data center debate has ignited a conversation about who deserves the public’s trust.
The score thus far: A day after the data center was announced, the Emporia City Commission unanimously annexed the designated acreage into the city. The opposition had one petition to force a public vote bounced by the county clerk on a technicality, but a new petition has been submitted. The local planning commission recommended, 6-1, to include the rezoned land in the new “digital infrastructure overlay” zone, after hours of public hearings in which sentiment was so hostile that many turned their chairs around when Garrett Nordstrom, representing the proposal, approached the microphone to address the planning commission.
The next step is a July 22 meeting in which the city commission will consider the recommendations for rezoning and creating the digital infrastructure zone. The commission was scheduled to vote July 15, but that was scrubbed so city staff and commissioners could attend a two-day educational “summit” in Topeka, hosted by Kansas Municipal Utilities, about data centers and energy use. Protestors attended the summit as well, or at least they demonstrated outside the Docking State Office Building, as KMU declared the event off-limits to anybody but paid attendees. It would have cost a member of the press or public $295 to attend, a KMU official told me.
In most appeals on behalf of the data center, the town pooh-bahs — a term derived from a pompous character in Gilbert and Sullivan — cite the economic benefits and bemoan “misinformation” circulating among the resistance. I’ve lambasted civic leaders before, including in a column last year about Emporia being the new unemployment capital of Kansas. But this twist in the data center story, in which the man promoted as being the developer of the proposed data center swore he was not the developer, takes the cake.
Where is the due diligence?
Shouldn’t the local chamber, the city staff, city commissioners or those on the planning commission have noted the red flag that Pinkston had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and followed up on it? The local planning commission, a seven-member volunteer board, has taken months to deal with a zoning variance for a drive-through coffee stand near the local Walmart. But it took a week after the first public hearing for the commission to recommend approval — in the face of heavy public opposition — of the data center requests.
Nordstrom, the spokesman for Pinkston and the data center, deflected questions about the bankruptcy filings. Instead of focusing on the bankruptcy, Nordstrom said, the public should ask instead whether the data center project demonstrated the financial, technical, and other requirements needed for success.
But the fact that Pinkston’s creditors were asking about the data center as part of the bankruptcy proceeding — and that Pinkston told a substantially different story than the one made for public consumption — should validate the public’s concerns.
Nordstrom did not reply to requests for comment on Pinkston’s bankruptcy testimony, sent via both email and voice message. Brad Kraft, the vice president of the Regional Development Association of East Central Kansas and a vocal advocate for the data center, also did not respond to email and phone message requests for comment.
At 84, Pinkston has spent most of his career as a real estate developer in California and Hawaii, but he grew up on a ranch in nearby Chase County. In a media campaign aimed at winning over local residents, an image has been heavily featured of Pinkston in cowboy hat and rumpled blue shirt posing on a horse against a suspiciously generic rural background. Pinkston has been portrayed as a savvy businessman who came back home to help bring growth and jobs to the community.
But when he’s allowed to speak for himself — as he did on local radio June 19 — the folksy demeanor drops and he engages in the kind of fearmongering once heard from the likes of John Birchers.
“If you folks would like to learn Chinese to watch Netflix, just stick around,” Pinkston said of those opposed to the data center plan.
AI is used for everything now, he said, from video streaming to billing for the local hamburger shop.
“If you want all of that run out of China, just keep pushing back,” he said.
The implication is clear: If you oppose the data center, then you’re a godless communist who hates America. You may also hate horses, cowboy hats and plaid shirts.
During the segment, which aired on Emporia’s KVOE radio, Pinkston said data centers are like business centers: “It just has machines instead of people.”
He said he expected his bankruptcy to be “wrapped up” within 60 days. As the “master developer” for the project, Pinkston said, he would be involved at every level of decision making, had already engaged in discussions about water and power supplies, and was already fielding inquiries from potential end users.
But when questioned under oath just four days later during a proceeding in connection with his bankruptcy, he disavowed any interest in the project.
What follows is the exchange between Pinkston and Keith M. Lusby, the attorney representing Hydra BV and Meridian Pacific Holdings, during a 341 Meeting of Creditors Proceeding, from an audio recording made by the Office of the U.S. Trustee in Atlanta. I obtained the audio through an open records request. Lusby is attending the meeting remotely.
Lusby: “Mr. Pinkston, can you tell me a little bit about a company known as Flint Hills Digital Campus LLC?”
Pinkston: “I’m sorry?”
Lusby: “Are you familiar with a company called Flint Hills Digital Campus?”
Pinkston: “No.”
A gravid pause follows.
Lusby: “Ah, related to a campus project in Emporia, Kansas, a data center?”
Pinkston: “My daughters are working on a data center in Kansas.”
Lusby: “You have no interest in that project at all?”
Pinkston: “I have no interest at all in that project.”
Pinkston also denied a relationship with Kanza Park Place LLC, the business entity registered in Kansas for the data center project. He said his daughters “owned” that limited liability company. Pinkston said he was receiving no compensation of any kind from the Emporia project.
A few minutes later in the proceeding, Lusby came back around to the data center, after apparently pulling up the Flint Hills Digital Campus website on his computer. He then mentioned the open letter to the community.
Lusby: “Is this something you authored?”
Pinkston said he had no idea what Lusby was looking at, then added that his children owned Kanza Park Place, and that he was helping them with no compensation. Lusby then read the first two sentences of the message, purportedly from Pinkston, which identify him as the developer.
Lusby: “Is that something that you wrote?”
Pinkston: “No, I did not write that.”
Lusby: “Then somebody forged it, on your behalf?”
Pinkston: “I can’t answer that, I’m sorry.”
A 431 meeting is held so that creditors can ask questions of the debtor and the bankruptcy filings to date, and the exchange between Lusby and Pinkston took place during an hour-long session of a proceeding that took several days. Pinkston has filed for personal Chapter 11 bankruptcy, and similar protection for more than a dozen LLCs he either owned or managed, so the cases have been combined into one massive Dickensian legal affair.
To trace the labyrinth of connections among Pinkston’s companies would require a team of auditors. What’s significant is that all the cases were filed May 14, less than three weeks before the public announcement of the Emporia data center project.
Pinkston said during the creditors meeting that he filed the bankruptcies because he was the victim of a “predatory” lending scheme to wrest control of his condominium project in Hawaii. He often seemed confused about the worth of his holdings or how many other assets he had. An attorney representing the IRS said during the meeting that Pinkston still owed money from 2012 and had not yet filed his 2023 income taxes.
To this point, Pinkston’s daughters have not been publicly identified as owners of the data center or otherwise connected with the project. They are, however, listed in court filings as sharing 98% ownership in TC Clovis, an LLC registered in Delaware that Pinkston manages, and that is associated with the Chapter 11 bankruptcies. Pinkston owns the remaining 2%. They also own various smaller interests in other associated trusts and LLCs.
Crystal Pinkston lives in Hawaii and Tiffany Myers (formerly Pinkston) lives in California, according to court records. Gary Pinkston’s residential address is listed as Tiburon, in Marin County, California.
At the upcoming meeting of the city commission, officials should ask Nordstrom just who the hell really owns Kanza Park Place LLC. What has been presented to the public thus far appears to be a lie, based on Pinkston’s bankruptcy testimony. If Pinkston didn’t write that letter to his “neighbors” in the Flint Hills, who did? Why did Pinkston tell a local radio audience that he was the “master developer” of the project, in charge of all decisions, when he contradicted himself in the creditor’s meeting?
The other day I talked with a member of the planning commission who justified their vote to recommend approval because, they said, otherwise the city would be at risk of a lawsuit. That is, simply put, nonsense. While people can sue for a variety of reasons or no reason at all, planning commissions are under no obligation to recommend action that might result in harm to the character or the quality of life of a community. The data center proposal is a poor fit for a small rural community that has long considered itself the “front porch” to the Flint Hills, and whose premiere tourist event is the summer Unbound Gravel bicycle race. There is a very real need to consider the soul of a community when contemplating the seismic cultural shifts that would be caused by a hyperscale data center.
The economic development system is broken.
That a proposed data center could progress with such speed through the slow and deliberate machinery of municipal government is alarming. That the proposal could advance while the true owners and developers, whoever they may be, are shielded by the secrecy of limited liability companies is outrageous.
To fix things, the public must insist on greater transparency in the economic development process. Groups such as the Regional Development Association need to be reformed to serve the public, instead of catering to power and influence. Ownership structures of LLCs asking for public support should be clearly understood, and that information shared with the public, before any project advances. That would require a change in the way LLCs are registered under Kansas law, to require more than just the name of the registered agent, but it would be a change for the better. I couldn’t get a permit to replace my roof without identifying myself. Why should the rich be allowed to hide behind shell companies?
Planning commissions should use wider discretion when making recommendations, weighing a community’s character and the quality of life in their deliberations, and they should take public opposition seriously.
But none of this will happen.
The system is built to reward money and influence, and nothing is likely to change as long as wealth is prized over humanity. But every so often we get a glimpse behind the curtain, and we are rightly appalled.
Jay Vehige, an Emporia activist who is among the principal organizers of the resistance to the data center, told me he was distressed by Pinkston’s bankruptcy revelations.
“Working families, farmers and neighbors across Emporia and the great Lyon County region are seeing one red flag after another with bankrupt Gary Pinkston,” Vehige said. “It’s becoming harder to understand why our city leaders seem so reluctant to slow down or stop this process and demand complete transparency.”
It’s time for city officials to demand Pinkston and Nordstrom come clean about what’s really going on. If there’s a reasonable explanation for the whopper that Pinkston was the developer, then let’s hear it,
The public deserves the truth.


 
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hot and bothered – summer’s transportation meltdown
description: The effect of last week's heat wave on trains, planes and automobiles is worth remembering, and planning for, because this kind of weather will return.
text:
Last week’s heat wave was neither the worst nor the last we’ll see this summer. But its effects on our trains, planes and automobiles are worth remembering, and planning for, because this kind of weather will return.  Heat can take a serious toll on our travels.
Just consider…



Wildfire smoke: Fueled by hot and tinder-dry conditions in Canada, last week’s smoky skies contributed to flight delays and travel disruptions.  Drivers were warned to keep their windows closed, switch the ventilation system to recirculate, and make sure the cabin air filter was clean.
Trains: Heat can make railroad tracks lengthen by an inch (in an 1,800-foot piece of track) for every ten degrees of temperature.  Because much of the track in the Northeast is welded rail (without many expansion joints) that can lead to buckling, known in the biz as “sun kinks,” where tracks get seriously out of alignment.  That can force the railroads to slow their trains down, in Amtrak’s case to just 80 mph in extreme cases, to avoid derailments.
Heat can also cause older fixed-tension catenary wires to expand and sag.  Much of Metro-North’s original overhead power system was more than 100 years old before Connecticut replaced it with modern constant-tension equipment.  But when the old wires sagged, a passing train’s pantograph could snag them, bringing down the power system and halting service.
You may remember just such an incident in 2011 on the then-hottest day of the summer with Manhattan pavement heating to 147 degrees.  A train near Westport got its pantograph tangled in the sagging power lines, stranding over 200 passengers onboard with no air conditioning and no windows that could open.  The passengers, understandably,  panicked and called 911 seeking rescue by local first responders.  One positive outcome was improved emergency planning, including provisions for supplying water to passengers on stranded trains.
Planes: Aviation also has trouble with the heat, in some cases because it’s just too hot to fly.
Hot air is lighter than cold air, right?  Add higher elevation to the mix (think Denver, where the air is already thinner) and the physics of flying just doesn’t work.
In 2017 Phoenix’s Sky Harbor Airport had to cancel dozens of flights when the air temps hit 120 degrees.  Where runways are shorter, some aircraft, particularly smaller regional jets, may not be able to operate safely without reducing their weight or waiting for cooler conditions.
Automobiles: Your car is not immune to heat, either, especially its tires. Sustained high temperatures can accelerate tire deterioration, while an underinflated tire flexes and builds up even more heat as it rolls, increasing the risk of tread separation or a blowout.  Check tire pressures when they are cold and use the recommended pressure printed on the driver’s-door.
But it’s your car’s cooling system that’s strained the most, working overtime to keep the engine temperature stable.  If the temperature gauge starts climbing, turning off the A/C can reduce the load on the engine.  But if the car is actually overheating, pull over safely and shut it down.
And the road itself is also under attack: concrete can buckle (from expansion) and asphalt can soften and start rutting.  As with the trains, the safest solution is to slow down and watch for trouble ahead.
We like to think of Connecticut summers as reliably hot.  What we’re not prepared for is heat this intense… or wildfire smoke this frequent.  
Our trains, planes and roads weren’t designed for heat this extreme and this persistent. Neither were we. The heat is coming again. The only question is whether we’ll be ready.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Public health improvements stall amid Trump’s DEI crackdown
description: THOMASVILLE, Ga. — As Earl Williams drove through a historic Black neighborhood known as Dewey City in his hometown, he hardly recognized what he saw. Homes that once belonged to friends, family, and neighbors had siding covered in mold. Some were boarded up. Others had holes in their roofs.  Black churches once used Oquina Creek, […]
text:
Earl Williams, community development director of the Thomasville Community Development Corp., stands in front of a building the city hoped would be turned into a healthcare clinic in Dewey City. The predominantly Black neighborhood in Thomasville, Georgia, faces blight and health challenges. (Briah Lumpkins/KFF Health News)THOMASVILLE, Ga. — As Earl Williams drove through a historic Black neighborhood known as Dewey City in his hometown, he hardly recognized what he saw.
Homes that once belonged to friends, family, and neighbors had siding covered in mold. Some were boarded up. Others had holes in their roofs. 
Black churches once used Oquina Creek, which runs along the border of the neighborhood, to baptize their congregants. Today, fecal bacteria and other contaminants have made the water unsafe due to an aging wastewater system.
Black churches once baptized their congregants in Oquina Creek in Thomasville, Georgia. Today, fecal bacteria and other contaminants make the water unsafe. (Briah Lumpkins/KFF Health News)
“Sometimes you get the feeling like you’re in a Third World country,” Williams said. After three decades in Washington, D.C., he returned four years ago with a mission to revitalize communities such as Dewey City, which he said are “part of what makes Thomasville, Thomasville.”
A $19.8 million Community Change Grant from the Environmental Protection Agency was supposed to shift the tides of the neighborhood Williams grew up in.
The city and the Thomasville Community Development Corp., where Williams is the community development director, applied for the grant in 2024. It was part of a $2 billion effort initiated under the Biden administration to help disadvantaged communities address environmental health risks and create clean energy and climate resiliency projects.
But three months after winning the grant, Thomasville became one of 80 communities across the country — from Hawai‘i to Alabama to Massachusetts — to see the funding stripped as priorities shifted in Donald Trump’s second presidency.
On the first day of his second term, Trump signed an executive order titled “Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing.” It stated that the Biden administration “forced illegal and immoral discrimination” through diversity, equity, and inclusion programs.
In an emailed statement, EPA spokesperson Mike Bastasch said the administration is “fully committed to being a great steward of taxpayer dollars.” He added that the “radical agenda” of DEI and environmental justice “preferencing” are not within the agency’s core mission of protecting human health and the environment.
Thomasville, Georgia, about 15 miles north of the Florida border, received nearly $20 million in federal money for improvement in areas like Dewey City, a historic Black neighborhood. But months later, the Trump administration pulled the funds, citing shifting priorities. (Briah Lumpkins/KFF Health News)
Environmental health advocates argue, though, that the decision to cut the grants was not rooted in science. They say that equating environmental justice to DEI is an act of bad faith and that withholding the money forces disenfranchised communities to delay long-overdue updates needed to protect public health for marginalized populations.
“I unfortunately believe we’re going to see a reversal in the health profile of this country,” said Jalonne White-Newsome, an associate professor at the University of Michigan who served in the Biden administration as the first federal chief environmental justice officer.
“This current federal regime has decided that humanity and public health and justice don’t mean anything,” she said.
‘Why Us?’
Thomasville, near Georgia’s southwestern border, is home to just over 18,600 people.
The city had hoped to improve health outcomes in neighborhoods on its southern and western sides where, according to the grant proposal, “historical redlining created a legacy of disinvestment.”
Those areas have a deep history: Dewey City, for example, was the first neighborhood in the city where Blacks could build homes after the Civil War. It’s also home to the closed Douglass High School — the first public school for Blacks in Thomasville, established in 1902.
“This place has been neglected,” said Williams, who occasionally hosts historical walks through the community. “But it’s worth bringing it back online.”
The proposed “Restoring Resiliency” project featured a plan to remove toxic substances such as mold, lead paint, and asbestos from homes, repair a nearly 82-year-old wastewater system, and convert part of a shuttered high school band room into a health clinic.
The Rev. Jeremy Rich, a pastor, teacher, and Thomas County commissioner, says a clinic in the Dewey City neighborhood of Thomasville, Georgia, would have increased trust in healthcare providers. The Trump administration’s cancellation of a federal grant funding the project was a major loss, he says. (Briah Lumpkins/KFF Health News)
“This was a long and storied attempt to bend the arc of justice closer,” said Jeremy Rich, a Thomas County commissioner and the pastor at First Missionary Baptist Church. “Justice in healthcare. Justice in environmental impact.”
Having a clinic in the community would be a “game changer,” Rich said. During the covid pandemic, he said, older residents who rely on public transit were reluctant to go to the nearby hospital or the county health department to get vaccinated. When his church offered shots from Black nurses, he said, vaccination rates improved.
Many residents don’t have the financial means to remove mold, lead paint, and other toxic materials, said Thomasville Mayor Pro Tem Lucinda Brown. “They just have money to live with every day. That’s it,” she said. “If they can make that happen.”
The grant meant hope, and its reversal left many asking, “Why us?” Williams said.
In the EPA’s May 2025 letter announcing the grant termination, it said Thomasville’s project promoted “initiatives that conflict with the Agency’s policy of prioritizing merit, fairness, and excellence.” The grant was “inconsistent with, and no longer effectuates, Agency priorities,” the letter said.
Environmental justice projects are rooted in science, not DEI, said Jillian Blanchard, the senior vice president of climate change and environmental justice at Lawyers for Good Government, a national nonprofit that provides pro bono legal assistance in focus areas such as health equity, immigration, and environmental health.
“Where is the water dirty? Where is the air unclean?” she said. “That is where the money should go.”
In June of last year, nearly two dozen communities and organizations around the country filed a class-action lawsuit to get the Community Change Grants reinstated. The lawsuit argued that the projects — such as efforts to create energy-efficient housing in Kalamazoo, Michigan, and empower Houston residents in the pollution permitting process — were vital.
The case was dismissed by a federal district judge in 2025 but is being appealed.
Thomasville was not named in that lawsuit. But the city did appeal the EPA’s decision on its project with the support of Blanchard’s group. The city and the EPA continue to dispute the issue.
This March, the EPA’s deputy inspector general, which serves as an independent watchdog for the agency, released a report concluding that the process for determining the awardees was fair.
Such federal funding is needed because large-scale change is difficult for small municipalities to achieve without getting stuck with high-interest loans, Blanchard said.
“It’s next to impossible,” she said. “That’s one of the reasons the things haven’t been done.”
‘It’s Not Over’
The city of Thomasville has found other ways to make some improvements in the meantime. With the help of a nearly $3 million federal Community Development Block Grant from the Department of Housing and Urban Development, it made repairs to portions of Dewey City’s sewer, water, and drainage systems.
In a community of mostly older residents who rely on public transportation, a healthcare clinic planned for this building would have increased access to care and built trust, local advocates say. (Briah Lumpkins/KFF Health News)
The Thomasville Community Development Corp. has begun building affordable housing in Dewey City and intends to convert a portion of the closed Douglass school into apartments for seniors.
The corporation has also applied for $764,000 in congressional funds through the office of Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) that it hopes to use to construct a community health clinic in Dewey City. Decisions on these funding requests will be made this fall.
“It’s not over,” said Williams, whose legacy in Thomasville runs deep. At the center of what locals call The Bottom — a two-block stretch of downtown where independent Black and other minority-owned businesses once thrived — is a plaque honoring his father, Earl Williams Jr., the city’s first Black mayor.
As he peered at his father’s memorial on a muggy afternoon, he reaffirmed his intentions.
“There’s more work to be done, and I’m able,” he said. “I like pouring into the community.”
But he has little hope the initial grant will be restored under the current administration.
“That was our shot. We didn’t do anything to miss it,” he said. “We just did it during the wrong period of time.”
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee County Exec. David Crowley reenters Wisconsin governor’s race with Gov. Evers’ endorsement
description: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley announced he was reentering the Democratic primary for governor Saturday, reversing his recent decision to drop out of the race. “Wisconsin, we can not afford four years of Tom Tiffany,” Crowley told dozens of excited supporters gathered to hear his announcement Saturday morning in downtown Milwaukee. Crowley suspende[...]
text:
David Crowley, Milwaukee County Executive, joins his supporters as he relaunches his campaign to become Wisconsin's next governor. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley announced he was reentering the Democratic primary for governor Saturday, reversing his recent decision to drop out of the race. “Wisconsin, we can not afford four years of Tom Tiffany,” Crowley told dozens of excited supporters gathered to hear his announcement Saturday morning in downtown Milwaukee.
Crowley suspended his campaign just 10 days ago and endorsed Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez. But a crippling campaign finance mismanagement scandal forced Rodriguez to drop out of the race Friday. This left a four-person Democratic field consisting of Rep. Francesca Hong (D-Madison), Rep. Kelda Roys (D-Madison), former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, and former secretary of the state Department of Administration Joel Brennan. Barnes has raised the most money among the Democratic contenders, while  Hong and Roys have the most cash on hand. 
Mayor Cavalier Johnson at David Crowley’s campaign re-launch. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Crowley started his campaign with the most money raised, but reports filed this week showed he had not kept up with his opponents still in the race. He started the year with $602,181 in the bank, raised $250,047 over six months and spent $537,050. He ended the last reporting period with $315,178 in cash on hand. 
Crowley had endorsed Rodriguez after suspending his own campaign last Wednesday — the same day Rodriguez said she learned about the financial troubles that ultimately sank her campaign. “I believed that I was supporting the strongest candidate at the moment,” he told the Examiner Saturday.
The crowd that came out to hear Crowley jump back in the race included a who’s who in Milwaukee politics and organizing. Among those in attendance were activist Vaun Mayes, former state legislator David Bowen who is now executive director of Wisconsin Voices, a statewide coalition of progressive advocacy groups, state Sen. Melissa Ratcliff and Milwaukee Mayor Cavalier Johnson as well as the mayors of Sheboygan, Waukesha and Wauwatosa, members of the Milwaukee County Board and Common Council and union leaders.
Ericka Crowley, wife of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, speaks at her husband’s campaign re-launch. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Crowley was also joined by his wife Ericka, introduced by the mayor  as “the next first lady.” She told the crowd that she wasn’t thrilled when “people were encouraging him to get back into this race.” The couple had closed that chapter, she said, and they were beginning to focus on spending more time with their family. “But the phone calls didn’t stop,” Ericka Crowley said. “Friends called, community leaders called, people from every corner of Wisconsin called, and they were like, ‘David, please reconsider,’ and still, the answer was no!” 
Ericka said the family relied on their Christian faith and prayed for a sign. She saw a cardinal, she said, a significant religious symbol to them. Then Rodriguez,  dropped out. “And in that moment, everything that we prayed about just felt different,” she said . “It was like the atmosphere shifted.” Crowley told reporters that both dropping out of the race and then reentering it were “very hard” decisions to make.
Evers’ endorsement and the ‘Democratic establishment’ 
Crowley returns to the primary race with departing Democratic Governor Tony Evers’ endorsement, a benefit none of the other candidates, including Rodriguez, Evers’ lieutenant governor, received. 
“I have indicated I did not plan to endorse anyone in the race for governor because I know each of the candidates and I wanted them to have the opportunity to make their case to Wisconsinistes first, just like I did,” Evers said in his statement endorsing Crowley Saturday. “I also believe that, in a race this close, Wisconsinites deserve to have the perspective of someone who’s done the job, who understands what it takes, and who’s had the benefit of spending years quietly watching how others in politics conduct themselves and treat people when they thought no one was paying attention.”
“David is not only the best candidate to beat Tom Tiffany,” Evers continued, “he’s the right candidate for the people of Wisconsin. He’s created thousands of new jobs, cut the county’s local carbon emissions in half, and passed a balanced budget, all while delivering the largest property tax cut in the county’s history, and I know he’ll continue to deliver results statewide.”
David Crowley, Milwaukee County Executive, speaks to media at his Milwaukee campaign event. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“It’s just an honor to receive his endorsement,” Crowley told the Examiner. He recounted Evers’ victory over former Republican Gov. Scott Walker, his leadership  guiding Wisconsin through the COVID-19 pandemic, and his tenure as “the best damn goalie that Democrats could have from stopping the Republican-controlled Legislature from having its way.” 
In addition to Evers’ endorsement, he said, he has received  “a groundswell of support from volunteers, from other elected leaders, as well as labor unions.” 
Responding to criticism that his re-entry into the race represents an effort by the Democratic party establishment to push forward someone to defeat Democratic Socialist candidate Francesca Hong, who had repeatedly finished at the top of public polls, Crowley said, “This isn’t about any of the other primary candidates.” Rather, he said, “this is about making sure that we have the best candidate that can defeat Tom Tiffany and his extreme MAGA agenda,” a goal he said he shares with all of the other Democratic candidates. 
Yet when he addressed the crowd of supporters in Milwaukee Saturday, Crowley took more direct aim at his opponents. He pointed to the Republican Governors Association’s recent $2 million ad blitz featuring Hong. The ads portray Hong, a self-described Democratic Socialist, as “too liberal for Wisconsin” and denounce her for wanting to return the state to its “progressive roots.” Barnes has called the ads “counterintuitive,” saying they appear to feature political attacks but are actually designed to increase Hong’s popularity among Democratic voters instead of hurting her chances. Many Democrats have concluded that the ads are designed to boost Hong, the Republicans’ preferred target in November, and that the Republicans are holding back stronger criticism they plan to deploy against her in the general election. 
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany addresses the 2026 Republican Party of Wisconsin convention. (Screenshot/WisEye)
Crowley seemed to endorse that theory at his campaign relaunch event, saying that the ads are meant “not to attack the Democratic party, but to boost one up.” He told  the crowd that Republicans are “deciding the Democratic nominee that they want to beat in November. They’re making an investment right now, and this should all be a five-alarm warning sign to all of us. We cannot allow the GOP to choose the Democratic nominee for governor of the great state of Wisconsin. Period.” 
Crowley told the Examiner  that people should be alarmed that Republican money is being used in a Democratic primary. “At the end of the day, there’s clearly an agenda there if they’re spending money in our primary,” he said. 
Democratic candidates respond
The Barnes campaign immediately blasted   Crowley’s reentry into the race in statements issued Friday and Saturday, claiming that Crowley’s campaign has ties to big corporations, that he’s trying to emerge as the “leading establishment Democrat” despite under-performing in multiple polls, and highlighting a county health insurance scandal earlier this year. 
A March Marquette Law School poll showed support for Crowley among voters at 3%, compared with 14% for Hong, 11% for Barnes and 3% for Rodriguez, with most respondents still undecided. 
Crowley discounted claims that he’s being hand-picked by the Democratic establishment, saying that “a 40-year-old Black man” isn’t what people think about when thinking about the “Democratic establishment.” He told the Examiner, “I know where my roots come from,” including  growing up in the impoverished 53026 zip code, “being the son of loving parents who struggled with mental health and drug addiction, who did everything that they could to make sure that their children were successful.” He added, “I look at my story as Wisconsin’s story.” He called the attacks by the  Barnes campaign “unfortunate,”  particularly because they are, by extension, also attacks on “a governor that he actually served alongside with during his first term.”
Francesca Hong speaks at a healthcare forum for Wisconsin gubernatorial hopefuls in April 2026. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)
Hong took a less combative tone, welcoming  Crowley back into the race. “I look forward to the perspective he’ll bring as we each make our case to Wisconsinites over the next three weeks,” Hong said. “Competition is good for democracy, and voters deserve a substantive debate about the future of our state. Our campaign will remain focused on building the working-class coalition it will take to defeat Tom Tiffany and deliver permanent affordability for Wisconsin families.”
Brennan’s campaign released a statement saying, “Joel Brennan is in this race to win it. Wisconsin needs a candidate who can beat Tom Tiffany in November and get to work for Wisconsin families from day one. That was true yesterday, and it’s still true today — no matter who else is in or out.”
A spokesperson for the Roys campaign said, “We need to move forward and unite behind the strongest candidate to beat Tom Tiffany and deliver a Democratic legislature, which is Kelda Roys. We have been on TV statewide for over a month and still have more cash on hand than most of the field, the most endorsements by far, and the most momentum. We are laser-focused on winning August 11 and delivering a trifecta on November 3.”
The Republican Governor’s Association issued a statement mocking both the demise of the Rodriguez campaign and  Crowley’s decision to reenter the race: “Watching Wisconsin Democrats is like watching a clown car crash into a parked semi-truck,” RGA  communications director Kollin Crimpton said. “From financial scandals to re-launching failed campaigns, these Democrats shouldn’t be in charge of a lemonade stand let alone the state of Wisconsin…Tom Tiffany is fighting to lower property taxes, protect Wisconsin land, and require health care price transparency. The choice is clear for Wisconsinites: commonsense versus crazy.”
Beating Tiffany will require a focus on “policies that people care about,” Crowley told the Examiner Saturday, highlighting his campaign’s Badger Basics Plan to increase affordability, care and opportunity. “People care about making sure that we fully invest in our public schools,” he said, “that we increase the reimbursement rates for special education; that childcare and 4-K is affordable and accessible; that we expand Badger Care across every community across Wisconsin.” 
State Sen. Kelda Roys is taking her second shot at running for governor. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Repealing Act 10 and “enshrining workers’ rights directly into our Constitution” are also priorities, he said. “We have to speak directly to what people care about. And we can’t get caught up, you know, in the misinformation, in the disinformation, in the distractions quite frankly that Tom Tiffany, the Republican Party, as well as the Trump administration continue to throw our way.”
 Addressing voters across Wisconsin from the podium as he relaunched his campaign, Crowley declared, “Let’s ride, not just on Aug. 11 but in November.” He added,  “My goal is to get as many people to the table as possible,” so “if you see me out there, please don’t be afraid to come speak and spark up a conversation.”

title: Kennebec Democrats consider the candidates, the issues and Platner’s legacy at nominating meeting
description: AUGUSTA — Hundreds of potential delegates and voters from around Kennebec County filled the Augusta Civic Center Saturday to select delegates to represent the county at next weekend’s Democratic Party convention.  People milled around the space, many stopping to peruse the signs listing the nearly 300 people on the ballot to become a delegate, with others […[...]
text:
Volunteers with the Kennebec County Democratic Committee offer technical support as voters begin the virtual method to select delegates to represent the county at next weekend’s Democratic Party convention. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)AUGUSTA — Hundreds of potential delegates and voters from around Kennebec County filled the Augusta Civic Center Saturday to select delegates to represent the county at next weekend’s Democratic Party convention. 
People milled around the space, many stopping to peruse the signs listing the nearly 300 people on the ballot to become a delegate, with others holding flyers from Senate campaigns listing out the names of potential delegates that have declared a pact for a specific Senate candidate.
When not sorting through the long lists of names, people spoke with the Senate candidates that made it to the meeting, and chatted with fellow voters, creating a cheerful atmosphere in the space. 
The 40 delegates picked here on Saturday will be among 601 delegates tasked with selecting a Senate candidate to replace Graham Platner, who withdrew from the race last week.
Among the crowd in Augusta was Lisa Ingraham, from Waterville, who was still undecided on who she liked best among the 12 Senate candidates, let alone the hundreds of delegate candidates. But she preferred delegates who were uncommitted. 
“The ones that kind of appeal to me are the ones who haven’t quite made up their mind, are keeping an open mind and listening to the people in their communities and what they would like to see,” she said. 
Other voters, like Ruth Stevenson, who wore a green Nirav Shah shirt and held a Shah sign, were clear about which Senate candidates they preferred, and planned to choose delegates that were like-minded.
“I worked in healthcare during COVID, and he did a wonderful job leading us through that,” she said. “He’s very well spoken. He has some interesting ideas, particularly about funding rural hospitals, and I think he can beat Collins.” 
She felt it was important to participate in the delegate process because “the nature of our politics in our country today is very distressing. And for my children and my grandson, I have to make a difference now.”
Democrats outside the Augusta Civic Center read signs listing the nearly 300 people on the ballot to become a delegate, and will represent the county at next weekend’s Democratic Party convention. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)
Mary Jean-Byk, from Litchfield, had supported Shenna Bellows in the gubernatorial primary last month, but said now she felt Troy Jackson was the best choice for Senate. 
“I feel like the people sort of already voted for him as a governor — he came in second — so that and also talking with people, he’s from the north or the 2nd District, so I really want to look at it from a political point of view,” she said. 
Patrick Banks, from Augusta, was another Jackson supporter in the room Saturday. 
“I think he has what it takes to win,” he said. “So he’s kind of unpolished, but in a good way. So I think he’s the one for me.”
The focus among Democrats was very much looking ahead to the general election, and who will be able to take on Collins. But when asked about Platner, there was a mix of opinions. 
Jim Betts, a Bellows supporter running to be a delegate, said as a veteran himself, he’d given Platner the benefit of the doubt in some of his earlier scandals, but the latest accusation was too much for him. 
“I think he’s genuinely rehabilitated,” Betts said. “I think none of the things that happened would happen today, but he’s carrying too much baggage. It’s unfortunate. Amazing speaker, and right on the issues, I’ve never heard anyone talk like he has when it comes to the issues. It’s very disappointing.”
Ingraham, the undecided voter, said she had never been a big Platner supporter, because she felt like the campaign was veering into a cult of personality around him. 
“So my radar went off pretty quickly with that candidate,” she said. “But I understand people’s disappointment.”
Jean-Byk, one of the Jackson supporters, said she would have voted for Platner in November if he’d stayed in the race. She said she felt there was a lot of money spent to target Platner, and he was pushed out of the race. And it felt hypocritical of Republicans, she said, when Trump has faced sexual assault accusations and they still voted for him. 
“I know the background of Trump, this guy hasn’t even gone to court or hasn’t had that, so I’m not going to go by just what people are saying, because I know there’s too much money out there,” she said. “So I don’t even trust them, and I don’t trust the money.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine Democrats select delegates as the party begins the abnormal process of replacing Platner
description: Maine Democrats on Saturday began the unprecedented process to select a new Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.  County Democratic committees met online and in person to select delegates, who will then attend the party’s first-of-its-kind convention in Bangor July 25, to select a Senate candidate to appear on the ballot in November.  “Now, this probably […]
text:
Hundreds of potential delegates and voters from around Kennebec County filled the Augusta Civic Center Saturday to select delegates to represent the county at next weekend’s Democratic Party convention. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)Maine Democrats on Saturday began the unprecedented process to select a new Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. 
County Democratic committees met online and in person to select delegates, who will then attend the party’s first-of-its-kind convention in Bangor July 25, to select a Senate candidate to appear on the ballot in November. 
“Now, this probably couldn’t happen in most states, but as we know, Maine is not like most states,” said Cumberland County Democratic Committee Chair Joseph Zamboni. “The fact that we are here today, at this moment, ready to elect delegates, is a testament to the strength, resilience and commitment of Maine Democrats.”
It’s uncharted waters for the party, which had just a few days to decide the process to select a new candidate, after Graham Platner withdrew from the race last week. And it’s a tight turnaround, because a new candidate must be selected by July 27. 
There are a dozen candidates vying to be the new nominee and take on incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But that field may narrow next week, when candidates must submit 500 signatures in order to be considered. 
This weekend, county committees will select a total of 500 delegates, with another 101 delegates made up of the party’s state committee. The Maine Democratic Party said earlier in the week that nearly 4,000 people were interested in becoming a delegate. 
And with more than 11,000 people pre-verified to vote by Thursday evening, the party opted to use a virtual voting method, allowing people to vote from home. 
“From the beginning, our goal has been to build a nominating process that is secure, accessible and transparent,” said Maine Democratic Party Executive Director Devon Murphy-Anderson in a statement Thursday. “Every verified voter will be able to cast their vote securely from home, ensuring that safety measures and accessibility barriers don’t prevent participation.”
The online voting process didn’t stop a crowd from forming at the Augusta Civic Center for the Kennebec County meeting Saturday. 
Many Democrats arrived right at 10 a.m. when check-in began, and took the opportunity to speak with potential delegates and Senate candidates who made the trip to Augusta. 
Several Senate candidates shared lists of delegates that were backing them, to make it easier for supporters to vote for those people among the long list of names. 
But not every potential delegate said they were committed to a certain candidate. On the Democratic Party’s voter guide for the delegate candidates, some said they were undecided but shared their priorities for selecting a Senate candidate. 
The catch is that those delegates are not required to vote  for a particular candidate at the convention next week. And if the convention process goes through multiple rounds of voting, a delegate may be forced to change their vote if their preferred candidate is eliminated.
Some Democrats said the process for selecting a new nominee wasn’t ideal, but probably was the best option given the short timeframe — the party only has until July 27 to get a new candidate on the ballot. 
Several Senate candidates traveled to the Augusta Civic Center Saturday, and shared lists of delegates that were backing them, to make it easier for supporters to vote for those people among the long list of names. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)
Patrick Banks, from Augusta, said he would have preferred a traditional caucus, where delegates stand in separate corners of the room to show what candidate they support. He said that would be easier to understand, rather than having to sort through the voter guide to find people’s details. 
But, Banks said, “they had to do this on the fly, so I can’t get too mad at them.”
Jim Betts, a Bellows supporter running to be a delegate, said the process was a step up from the 2024 presidential election, when President Joe Biden dropped out and was replaced by Vice President Kamala Harris. 
“It’s the best we can do,” he said. “It’s a heck of a lot better than the presidential race.”  
Just after noon, Kennebec County Democratic Committee Chair Joanne Mason called the meeting in Augusta to order. 
Democrats, in the room or at home, got an email or text once the county opened voting, with a link to their ballots. Mason said voting would be open for an hour, but ultimately the process was extended to closer to two hours before voting was closed. 
“I recommend that you vote your conscience, vote your best and do the best you can to support the people you know,” Mason said. 
Mason said before voting began that if there was a tie, the names would be drawn from a hat to make the selection — but that was not needed. 
It was a similar start at the virtual meeting in Cumberland County, which Zamboni brought to order promptly at 4 p.m. Saturday. 
He also walked through the voting process, which was the same as it was at the in-person meetings. 
“I want to thank you all for participating in this process, democracy can be exciting, and we have illustrated that this week,” Zamboni said. “Now we will begin the voting period and distribution of ballots, and start the process to replace Susan Collins once and for all.”
In Kennebec, each voter could pick up to 40 delegates — the total number being sent; in Cumberland each voter selected 149 names. 
In Augusta, the party had volunteers set up with tablets, to assist anyone who could not connect to the voting system on their phones, or needed other technical assistance. 
In contrast to the hub of activity ahead of the meeting, once voting was open the convention center was nearly silent as people hunched over their phones, waiting on the links and searching through delegate names. 
After casting their votes, many people left without hearing results, but there was still a sizable group that stuck around until 3 p.m. when Mason was able to announce the results. 
“I want to remind everyone that our work doesn’t end here,” Mason said. “Although you may not get chosen for this specific delegation, this meeting is important because the work ahead of us is incredible, the Kennebec County Democrats are committed to supporting every candidate on our ballot, from the top of the ticket all the way down. We need each of you to stay engaged, energized and show up at the polls in November.”

title: Large protest against ICE draws more than a 1,000 people to Monument Square
description: As the public outcry against the fatal shooting of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by federal immigration agents continues, more than a thousand people gathered in Monument Square in Portland to protest U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement. Mainers have taken to the streets all week, starting hours after the Biddeford resident and young father[...]
text:
Protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)As the public outcry against the fatal shooting of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero by federal immigration agents continues, more than a thousand people gathered in Monument Square in Portland to protest U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement.
Mainers have taken to the streets all week, starting hours after the Biddeford resident and young father was shot as he was leaving for work Monday morning. In the days since, community organizers and political leaders throughout Maine have rallied against the federal agency, with many publicly calling for its abolishment.
Saturday’s rally was no different. Several speakers highlighted the need for continued community organizing, and holding elected leaders accountable for their actions.
“Johan’s death did not happen in isolation. It exposed the reality that immigrant communities had been living with for months,” said Safiya Khalid, a community leader from Lewiston.
“It was a result of an immigration system that has increasingly become punitive, increasingly militarized and increasingly disconnected from the humanity of the people it touches.”
Three days after Guerrero was killed by federal immigration agents, his wife Karolina Rojas Alvarez spoke to the press, remembering him as a loving and devoted father and husband who took care of their family, went to the park with his daughter every afternoon and held her until she fell asleep every night.
Speaking through tears, Rojas Alvarez said her husband “always dreamed big, and he had so many dreams left to fulfill.”
Protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. Jillian from Brunswick, who declined to give her last name, was among many attendees with signs denouncing Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, who is running for a sixth term in November.  “She’s been complicit all along,” Jillian said. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Safiya Khalid speaks during a protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. Numerous attendees denounced Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, who is running for a sixth term in November. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Dale Knight of Portland, a former law enforcement officer, at a protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. ICE agents “will protect themselves and they will protect one another -- and that’s wrong,” he said. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Annette Lemek of  Portland at a protest against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Portland’s Monument Square on July 18, 2026. “It’s terrorizing the whole community,” she said of ICE. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security confirmed earlier this week that Guerrero was not the target of the agency’s investigation. An ICE spokesperson told Maine Morning Star that the agency was doing targeted surveillance on the last known address of someone with a final order of removal. “The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon,” the statement from an unnamed ICE spokesperson read.
Dale Knight of Portland, a former law enforcement officer, said ICE agents “will protect themselves and they will protect one another — and that’s wrong.”
Multiple news media have reported the name of an agent alleged to be responsible for the shooting, which also appeared on protest signs Saturday. Maine Morning Star is not naming the agent because the information has not been independently confirmed by the Maine Attorney General or the Department of Homeland Security.
Throughout the week, protesters have called out Sen. Susan Collins, criticizing her vote in favor of adding $70 billion in funding for ICE. At Saturday’s rally, many attendees held up signs that said “ICE pulled the trigger. Sen. Collins gave the gun.” After the speeches, people marched through downtown Portland through the rain to Collins’ office.
